We introduce a $p$-integral operator that handles the $p$-adic expansion of Siegel modular forms for odd $p$ and an appropriate choice of $p$-admissible weight. This operator enables us to derive the $p$-divisibility of Fourier coefficients of Siegel modular functions, specifically their indices of multiplicity $\iota(S)$. This index represents the least common multiple of the orders of the $p$-primary parts of the central values of special $p$-adic Eisenstein series. Moreover, our approach yields the $p$-divisibility of the central values themselves. This research is a continuation of previous work by the second author and Wang [K. Shi-Wang, Math. Res. Lett. 2021].

A specific type of branched covering called rigid fibrations played a crucial role in achieving a key finding by the Collar Lemma. We make a significant discovery about the sequence of n-fold rigid fibrations in a particular class of three-dimensional manifolds, which has far-reaching implications for our understanding of these topological structures. This finding enables us to strengthen the Collar Lemma and support a long-standing conjecture known as the Almost Fillable Conjecture. We also derive a key result that proves the stability of a particular sequence of n-fold rigid fibrations in three-dimensional manifolds. This result is analogous to a recent finding by the first author, which concerned another sequence of n-fold covering maps.

By applying Green's function method, researchers have explored the statistical behavior of two-dimensional Pauli lattices, composed of interacting spin-1/2 particles. Building on Heisenberg's original spin chain model, the associated Green's function can be derived and its underlying statistical distribution determined. In doing so, the general form of the distribution is identified as a fermionic Bose-Einstein distribution, parameterized by a chemical potential related to the interaction energy. This findings hold true for both fermionic and bosonic lattices, valid for any number of spin components. This approach offers a novel method for describing interacting spin systems, encompassing fermionic and bosonic lattices, through a single statistical model.

This study provides a detailed examination of Zeroing Neural Networks (ZNN), a method of predicting dynamic systems by leveraging ODE resolutions, building on initial applications in 2000. ZNN has shown potential in addressing a range of time-varying matrix problems through the use of neural networks, offering advantages in real-time applications. Key ZNN characteristics and mathematical formulations are discussed, as well as its relevance to machine learning research. By highlighting several benchmark studies, this work illustrates ZNN's capacity to handle a variety of problems, including those involving tensor decomposition, matrix nearness problems, and polynomial equation solving. Furthermore, this research demonstrates ZNN's ability to tackle complex problems like graph representation and graph partitioning. By comparing ZNN with other methods, such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), this study provides valuable insights into ZNN's performance, accuracy, and convergence rates.

Biological visual systems effectively process visual stimuli and adapt to different conditions. Current AI systems, on the other hand, struggle with issues like overfitting and classification errors due to noisy data and mislabeled examples. To address these problems, a novel sensory field model has been developed, which mimics the visual system's On-Center Off-Periphery response pattern. This model consists of groups of neurons with similar feature properties, and is trained using an efficient and robust image classification technique. As a result, it achieves high accuracy and resistance to label noise, and outperforms other methods in classification and semi-supervised learning. This research provides insights into the differences between biological and artificial sensory systems, and highlights the potential for on-off sensory fields to improve AI performance.

X-ray optics with larger fields of view are required for many upcoming space missions, including deep space exploration and astrophysics initiatives such as the Athena space telescope. To meet these demands, researchers are focusing on conventional techniques like grazing-angle technology and lightweight, thin-shell X-ray mirrors. Another approach involves employing curved Bragg optics, which can either be used individually or in combination with refractive optics. We will examine the potential of incorporating aspherical shapes into X-ray optics, either by manipulating their curvature or by adjusting their shape horizontally. This innovative design can significantly expand the field of view without compromising image resolution. We will share numerical results demonstrating the effectiveness of these designs and outline methods for fabricating them.

A model for magnetic twisted bilayer graphene at $2\pi$ flux is formulated with hopping parameters expressed in terms of complex hyperbolic trigonometric functions. Applying the gauge transformation simplifies the Hamiltonian, revealing an energy spectrum composed of nonflat bands and a reentrant flat band. The transformation also uncovers a hidden symmetry, specifically a sublattice point-group symmetry, which accounts for the origin of the reentrant flat band. This discovery results in an additional degeneracy at $2\pi$ flux compared to zero flux.

This study introduces a novel, highly compressed form of steganography that enables the insertion of a hidden message into a small portion of a translated text. A primary challenge is minimizing the perceived unnaturalness of the translated output. A proposed solution is to employ an LSTM model that is trained on pairs of short phrases rather than full sentences, allowing it to generate translations of fixed length regardless of input variability. However, this approach can result in steganographic text of uneven length containing multiple consecutive null characters, which makes it distinguishable. To rectify this issue, we suggest shortening the length of the first phrase to accommodate a hidden message while maintaining the length of the second phrase, thus ensuring uniform output length. Unfortunately, this solution often leads to overtranslation of the first phrase, rendering it invisible. A proposed solution is to insert space characters into the first phrase in a manner that maximizes the likelihood of the translation as a whole.

Transmission system operators utilize unit commitment as a key tool for determining the most cost-effective and feasible generation mix, taking into account constraints such as transmission capacity and generator capacity limits. However, the unit commitment problem is computationally complex and involves examining numerous fast-rising costs associated with generators. As fast-rising cost information often changes slowly over time, we propose employing machine learning techniques to approximate these costs for unit commitment modeling, thereby improving efficiency. To address potential biases resulting from outdated cost data, we also develop a procedure for adjusting these costs to match current unit prices, further enhancing model accuracy. By combining machine learning with cost synchronization, we can significantly accelerate unit commitment constraint examination and improve overall efficiency.

Research into $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$, a material with Kitaev-like behavior, reveals how pressure disrupts its magnetic order at 7 Kelvin and causes structural changes past 1 GPa, leading to a transition that eliminates the magnetic order and causes the lattice to shrink. The pressure-induced transition creates a state with two different types of structural changes and causes the material to lose its magnetic properties, and this state eventually loses its irreversibility as pressure reaches 6 GPa. This study demonstrates that high-pressure hydrostatic conditions cause the material to lose its magnetic properties and lose its lattice symmetry, and this loss of symmetry is a result of the breaking of the iridium square lattice.

This paper outlines a unified framework for synthetic counterfactual estimation. 
Initially, a broad causal model is specified, then an estimator for the 
synthetic counterfactual is chosen, and finally, treatment effect magnitudes 
are estimated by comparing treated units with their counterfactual counterparts 
(achieved through propensity score reweighting or using a fitted regression line 
under a causal model). 
Our framework subsumes the majority of synthetic counterfactual estimation 
methods, and we demonstrate that these estimators can be reinterpreted as 
maximizing a relevant metric on treatment effect magnitudes.
We also establish that these estimators can be viewed as variants of the 
propensity score reweighting method or a causal parametric model, and provide 
asymptotic theory for each.
By combining these results, the asymptotic theory unifies multiple synthetic 
counterfactual estimation approaches and offers a novel perspective, showing that 
each method can be reinterpreted as addressing a specific objective.
Moreover, the proposed asymptotic theory facilitates the development of valid 
inference procedures, and we demonstrate this with the construction of a 
confidence region for the counterfactual treatment effect.
Our confidence region relies on no asymptotic distributional approximations, 
instead using a finite sample version of the weak convergence in the BCIR 
framework, and we illustrate its utility with empirical examples.

Determining node similarities in locally connected graph structures is a complex task, typically addressed using node embeddings, which, however, pose a significant privacy risk due to the potential extraction of sensitive information from published embeddings. To mitigate this issue, we propose a new method that measures node similarity using graph neural operators, based on the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy, and provides secure data transmission by applying local differential privacy to embeddings for distributed graph networks. Our method employs the Sinkhorn algorithm to calculate the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy under local differential privacy, and validates its effectiveness using the MuGrid dataset and the Cora citation network. Our results demonstrate that applying local differential privacy to Gromov-Wasserstein embeddings significantly enhances data privacy while maintaining the accuracy of node embeddings, with the choice of the local differential privacy parameter impacting the accuracy of node embeddings.

Recent advancements in laser-matter interaction research have led to a greater understanding of electron injection and acceleration mechanisms in plasma. Our study demonstrates that high-intensity laser pulses in plasma can induce periodic electron injection into a plasma wave, which in turn results in the emission of highly polarized, circularly collimated beams of energetic electrons. These electron jets are produced through the interaction between plasma wave damping and the rapid changes in electron density caused by laser-generated nonlinear steepening. Furthermore, we have shown that varying the laser's initial polarization can control the electron jet's direction, orientation, and emission frequency, opening up possibilities for tailored electron acceleration in plasma waves. This novel technique could potentially be used in the development of high-energy electron sources and plasma-based accelerators.

A platinum foil with a mass of 38.7 grams was measured over a period of 408 days at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso to investigate its low-level radioactivity and serve as a high-resolution calorimeter in dark matter research. The findings include revised limits on beta-particle emission, mass transfer, and exchange processes for various isotopes, including the observation of a previously undetected mass transfer channel involving gamma radiation. Additionally, we set new limits on our understanding of certain rare processes for isotopes platinum-100 and platinum-106, including the exclusion of certain areas in a mass versus cross-section space for certain particles, including the exclusion of certain areas in a mass versus cross-section space for certain particles with masses less than 2 GeV, specifically the axino, axion-like particles, and the neutrino.

The calculation of the renormalization constants for the flavor-singlet axial-vector current operators is necessary to correctly determine the charge $g_1(\mu)$ in the context of Bjorken's sum rules and QCD. This charge is calculated by subtracting the universal hadronic contributions, as determined in the massless theory using dimensional regularization. The calculation of the renormalization constants in this method yields results that contain pole terms, as well as complex functions with massless parts that match the known one-loop results. The removal of these rational parts and the massless parts in a scheme-independent manner, as done through the subtracted minimal subtraction scheme MS, allows for the determination of the beta function for the charge $g_1(\mu)$. The result of this subtraction reveals that the charge undergoes an anomalous renormalization when calculated in the MS scheme, as well as in other schemes that use the same subtraction scheme for the rational and massless parts. This result implies that the charge undergoes anomalous renormalization when calculated in the MS scheme, as well as in other schemes that use the same subtraction scheme for rational and massless parts. This result confirms that the charge undergoes anomalous renormalization when calculated in the MS scheme, as well as in other schemes that use the same subtraction scheme for rational and massless parts.

A key element in creating authentic effects in digital matte paintings and set extensions is accurately simulating window glass reflections and transparencies within a scene. Modern buildings often incorporate non-standard glass products with irregular patterns, making it essential to replicate these nuances in digital renderings. In contrast to traditional methods that rely on pre-existing datasets of standard glass patterns, our proposed technique leverages real-world glass textures from various sources, including stock photo databases and in-situ observations. We developed an innovative approach utilizing deep learning to combine and apply patterns from different sources, eliminating the need for a priori data or manual input. This method can handle a wide range of glass patterns, including those not yet seen during training, without needing to retrain for every new pattern. We successfully applied this technique to real-world data and observed its practical application in scenes featuring authentic window glass reflections and transparencies.

The symmetries and conservation laws of the integrated Ermakov equation in n dimensions have been determined. These conserved quantities can be used to develop finite symmetry groups for the original nonlinear Schrödinger equation. This approach may provide a new method for solving the Schrödinger equation through symmetry reduction. The conserved quantities can also serve as a starting point for discovering symmetries of the Ermakov system itself. By applying Cartan's test, additional conservation laws have been found for the Ermakov system. These conserved quantities include, in the case of n=2, the sum of the squared real and imaginary parts of the wavefunction, as well as its complex product with the squared modulus of the potential function.

The feasibility of using machine learning to convert stop-based data into transit feed specification (TFS) has been explored, with a successful proof-of-concept presented. However, due to certain limitations in feasibility and cost-effectiveness, a substantial dataset for training machine learning algorithms on TFS is non-existent. To overcome this, a simulated data approach was employed, with a focus on one key challenge: predicting missing information in TFS. Specifically, for a given stop time, algorithm can predict the values of the following fields: route ID, direction, arrival and departure time, and stop ID based on previous recorded data. Experiment results reveal that using time series data and recurrent neural networks yield accurate predictions, with average mean absolute error values of 1 second for arrival time, 2 seconds for departure time, 1 meter for stop ID, and 95% accuracy for route and direction information.

The objective of few-shot learning is to develop a robust generalization capability with limited labeled data in a novel category. To achieve this goal, we propose an innovative approach centered on constructing high-quality prototypes for each class, representing their core characteristics. By doing so, we enable the model to identify class-specific patterns effectively, thereby enhancing its performance. Unlike traditional prototypes derived from mean values, our method utilizes an aggregation technique over optimized, representative samples. However, determining these optimal samples is a challenging task. To address this issue, we introduce an iterative learning framework that simultaneously enables prototype construction and sample selection. Experimental results on various datasets and against multiple baselines demonstrate the efficacy and generalizability of our approach.

We are analyzing theories with robust symmetry properties that operate locally in space-time and encompass both invertible and non-invertible cases. A local symmetry with a zero-mode anomaly can be considered a 'nilpotent' one. Our research demonstrates that invertible symmetries comply with a generalized version of Goldstone's theorem, and similarly, non-invertible symmetries with zero-mode anomalies also conform to this theorem. A key example of a theory with a robust, non-invertible symmetry is free Dirac theory embedded within a background gauge field, which exhibits a global $U(1)$ symmetry known as 'axial' symmetry. The characteristics of this symmetry are similar to those of a 'nilpotent' one, and our research shows that it shares similarities with both 'global' and 'local' U(1) symmetries.

A split graph is defined as a simple graph that can be broken down into a clique and a separate independent set. A directed graph is considered semi-transitive if for any three vertices, the relationship between the first two does not determine the relationship between the second and third. In this context, we investigate the requirement for a split graph to be semi-transitive. Specifically, we observe that on split graphs with no isolated vertices, the semi-transitivity property can be achieved with a clique of size three. Furthermore, we note that on split graphs with isolated vertices removed, the minimum clique number needed for semi-transitivity can be determined based on the maximum degree of the remaining directed edges.

A cutting-edge approach utilizing a deep neural network has been developed to accurately distinguish between the hadronic decays of tau leptons and those originating from other particles such as jets. This innovative method incorporates the hadronic decays of tau leptons, including those with one or three particles, into a simulated dataset which is then used to train a deep neural network to identify real tau decays. Utilizing simulated data from LHC experiments, a deep neural network has been applied to identify hadronic tau decays, demonstrating an efficiency of approximately 80% with a corresponding misidentification rate of 10%, compared to traditional methods. This new approach has shown significant potential to reduce systematic uncertainties related to background identification in searches for new physics at the LHC.

Future studies on supernovae are expected to significantly benefit from the Rubin Observatory's vast sky coverage and continuous monitoring capabilities, but will face increased competition due to the observatory's capabilities, leading to a need for more precise supernova classification algorithms. We examine how different methods of categorizing supernovae, particularly those relying on light curve features, are affected by various types of noise and how accurately they can identify a supernova's type based on random samples of real supernovae and mock samples of different sizes. We also explore the potential of a Bayesian neural network, a sophisticated machine learning technique, in improving supernova classification and discuss its advantages and limitations, while considering how to apply this method to the Rubin Supernova Ioyalty Project, a comprehensive study of supernovae that aims to identify and verify rare and unique events.

Our study explores the phenomenon of forward Brillouin scattering across adjacent fiber modes within photonic crystal fibers, comprising core and outer cores. We demonstrate this intermodal scattering in two-core and multi-core photonic crystal fibers, including a specific two-core design with a bridging structure that connects the cores. By launching a high-power pump into one core and detecting the generated backflow in the other core, we measure the effective length of the interacting Brillouin gain bands to be roughly equal to the length of the fibers. We also investigate the strength and efficiency patterns of the Brillouin coupling coefficients associated with various core-mode interactions. In addition to their applications in all-fiber phononic crystals, these photonic crystal fibers offer efficient and multi-dimensional light management and enhanced nonlinearity, making them suitable for parallel optical signal processing and fast and efficient Brillouin-based processes.

The Coxeter group foundation theorem, specifically for complex reflection groups and $B_n$, has implications in various fields, including homotopy theory and Lie algebras. For $B_n$, we can derive (2) from [Bruhat, 1968], using an approach that applies to any B-type Coxeter group, thereby extending the foundation theorem to this broader context.

Two related variations of the well-known knapsack problem are the Set-Union Knapsack Problem and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem. Both involve selecting items from a set with monetary values and weights, aiming to maximize a quality measure such as total value or coverage. Although they share some key characteristics like a bounded solution region, non-linear value, and the ability to be represented as a graph with node weights, previous solvers have failed to leverage these properties effectively. As a result, many problem instances have gone unsolved due to the limitations of current solvers. In this paper, we introduce novel local search algorithms that take advantage of these problem characteristics to efficiently and productively find high-quality solutions. These algorithms start with a method to initialize solutions within the solution region, ensuring they are feasible and optimal, and then perform an iterative improvement process using a directed acyclic graph representation of the solution space. The algorithms' performance is demonstrated by solving a vast dataset of problem instances, resulting in significantly better solutions in a large number of cases.

Customer retention is a critical issue for businesses operating in the customer-based industry, and churn prediction is its foundation. In the context of online gaming, understanding why loyal customers choose to leave is essential, with research indicating high levels of customer churn across the sector. Despite its importance, few studies have delved into churn forecasting in online gaming, and the field lacks a comprehensive body of knowledge. This study aims to bridge this gap by developing a machine learning-based model to predict customer churn in online gaming, using data from Bet365. With a dataset of over 12,000 customers featuring over 1,500 variables spanning 12 months, the analysis yields promising results. By comparing two models, the research demonstrates that LightGBM performs better than XGBOOST, and variable selection reveals that demographic information and customer behavior are key predictors of churn. Notably, customers who engage in promotional activities have lower churn rates than those who do not, suggesting targeted marketing strategies could help retain customers.

We develop a two-dimensional Ising field theory in a magnetic field up to the Yang-Lee critical point, located at $h_{YL} = -\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$, where $h$ represents the magnetic field strength and $\tau$ represents the temperature, with $\tau = \frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{T_c}$ and $T_c = \frac{2\pi}{3}$ being the critical temperature. The Yang-Lee edge singularity corresponds to a ground-state boundary tangent to the second-order ferromagnetic- paramagnetic phase transition curve, situated at $h_{YL}^* = -\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $\tau^* = 0$. The critical exponents at this point are $\theta = \frac{1}{2}$, $\nu = 1$, and $\alpha = \frac{1}{2}$, with the corresponding magnetic critical exponent being $\delta = 4 - \frac{1}{\nu(1 - \theta)} = 5$. The Yang-Lee edge singularity arises from the two complex eigenvalues of the Lax operator, $p_1$ and $p_2$, becoming real and equal at $h_{YL}^*$. The edge singularity can be described using two Toda spin-chain T-functions, $T_{\sqrt{3}}(p_1

We have developed a method to calculate transverse-momentum-dependent parton distribution functions (TMDs) for gluons directly from their corresponding perturbative series, using the large-momentum expansion of the renormalized TMD photon distribution function as a key starting point. By applying the large-momentum expansion method, we found that the gluon TMD (h_g(x, k_T^2) and h_LOTG(x, k_T^2)) can be computed in next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) perturbative QCD. Additionally, we used numerical calculations to analyze the behavior and properties of the gluon TMD, including the lotg/x and protons' tomography, and discovered that the lotg/x is less than the corresponding combination of the lotg/x for quarks, leading to less parton equiprobability in gluons compared to quarks.

In the photon-photon fusion process that occurs during ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, electron-positron pairs are produced through interactions with the relativistic electromagnetic field. The photon-photon fusion process happens when ions passing each other at negligible speed overlap, resulting in a photon cloud. The production of these pairs, or $e^+e^-$ pairs, depends on the Lorentz factor and nuclear form factors. The $e^+e^-$ pairs are produced within a very short time frame and have low transverse momentum, typically in the range of a few hundred MeV to a few hundred thousand MeV. The $e^+e^-$ pairs are produced in a very localized area near the point of overlap with a very high photon density, and their spectrum is influenced by the nuclear form factors. The $e^+e^-$ pairs can interact with other nuclei through electromagnetic forces, and their interactions provide valuable insights into the spatial distribution of quark and gluon fields within the nuclei. The $e^+e^-$ pairs can also be used to study photon propagation in high-density media, and their interactions can occur at very small distances from the nucleus surface. The $e^+e^-$ pairs can be measured using a variety of experiments, and their interactions can be studied in a range of energy and momentum regimes.

To enhance cyclist safety, a real-time system is developed that warns of potential dangers arising from cars' and other vehicles' collisions with bicycles. This system operates independently of infrastructure, relying solely on visual elements to forecast threats. By focusing on the bicycle, the proposed algorithm identifies and differentiates between various types of vehicles based on factors like size, speed, and acceleration. It then utilizes a pre-trained convolutional neural network to determine the orientation and positioning of the bicycle, as well as the proximity and movement of other vehicles relative to the bicycle. If a hazard is detected, the system triggers an alarm. This innovative approach enables the detection of high-risk situations that might go unnoticed by human drivers. It offers a valuable solution for cycling communities, particularly in areas with inadequate cycling facilities.

This research paper presents an innovative technique for creating a safety-oriented motion plan in dynamic robotics environments. The approach involves using Control Barrier Functions to develop a control method that ensures the robot avoids collisions with moving objects. By converting a nonlinear dynamic system into a specific form and implementing a control strategy, our method enables the robot to achieve collision-free movement while avoiding obstacles with arbitrary motion patterns. In addition, this control method provides system stability and can be used in real-world robotics applications, including those with uncertain parameters and external disturbances. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of this method through both simulation and real-world testing of a mobile robot navigating around moving chairs.

For a ring with a property that its additive group has only finitely many elements of order p, where p is a prime number, we define an 'enveloping p-number' as a relational arithmetic expression that counts the multiplicative group of the ring modulo p. If such an expression exists, we can determine if the quotient ring has p-characters (characters whose kernel is not a proper ideal) solely based on the coefficients in p-number. This approach allows us to simplify the conditions for character-induced orderings in Corollary 2 in [3]. Furthermore, we can derive the complete list of p-numbers for all finite rings and some infinite rings with non-zero units. As a result, we can determine the p-numbers for all rings with a total of p^2 elements.

Deep neural networks are highly susceptible to manipulations by input crafted in a specific manner. As a result, they consistently generalize to such inputs, using them to learn and make predictions. This phenomenon is seen in both natural and adversarial examples. We explore a subset of these specific inputs known as natural adversarial examples, and develop an automated method to create them. Additionally, we investigate features of models and data that contribute to the generation of these examples. Ultimately, our findings have becn used to enhance model robustness against these types of inputs.

In traffic models, nonlocal velocity relationships are frequently observed, where the velocity of a vehicle is influenced by a relatively wide spatial area behind it. These nonlocal models can be seen as an extension of classical conservation laws, where the nonlocal velocity is represented as an integral of an appropriate function over a spatial domain that includes the vehicle's position and a portion of it moving at a lower speed. The primary objective of this research is to analyze the behavior of nonlocal models, where the spatial influence domain varies as the grid spacing, by using a mathematical approach called homogenization. The study also examines the relationship between these nonlocal models and models incorporating a delay, where the delay value varies as the grid spacing. The results demonstrate that as the grid spacing approaches zero, these models converge to a particular Hamilton-Jacobi equation, where the Hamilton-Jacobi flux is influenced by the limiting function of a particular variable. The study also proves that this model is entropy-admissible and derives the existence of weak solutions for both the nonlocal and delayed models. Furthermore, the study provides estimates of the error bound for the convergence of the nonlocal model to the Hamilton-Jacobi equation.

Generalized dilation surfaces serve as a foundation for a broad class of structurally stable surface morphings, which can be thought of as dynamic systems on surfaces with a nondegenerate velocity field. These surface morphings have a discrete hyperbolic trajectory on the surface, which can be used to define a new graph structure in 3-dimensional space. Specifically, this graph structure is homeomorphic to a 2-sphere when the tracking trajectory is semi-stable, and this sphere contains a specific type of linked circle configuration known as a saddle link. This connected component structure of the graph corresponds to a specific class of dilation surfaces known as dilation tori, which are tori inflated by non-constant functions on their constituent circles. It has also been proven that semi-stable surface morphings correspond to Morse-Smale dynamics, which is a specific class of structurally stable systems. This proof reveals that semi-stable dilation surfaces correspond to a specific type of linked circle configuration in 3-dimensional space, which is known as a horizon saddle link. This linked circle configuration structure has been used to develop a new definition of semi-stability, which corresponds to the definition of a horizon saddle link. This definition has also been used to show that semi-stable surface morphings correspond to dilation surfaces with horizon saddle links, which in turn correspond to Morse-Smale systems on dilation surfaces. This has been achieved by proving that all dilation surfaces with horizon saddle links are Morse-Smale, which requires a new classification of

Recent studies of total correlation have shown potential in analyzing complex brain networks, and have led to the development of a new approach for identifying relationships between distinct brain regions. This method is based on the use of mutual total correlation to capture the shared input of multiple brain regions, and has been applied to resting-state fMRI data in this study. The resulting connectivity matrices have been used to investigate correlations between different brain regions, and to test for the reliability of the findings across multiple datasets. The results show a significant link between the proposed functional connections and established structural connections in the brain, and also highlight a range of functional connections that are not previously documented. Furthermore, the study demonstrates a strong connection between the proposed functional connections and various cognitive and mental health conditions, and also explores the relationship between these connections and different levels of consciousness, highlighting a range of novel insights that may be gained through the analysis of total correlation in the study of brain connectivity.

The 1930s work of Segal and Bargmann introduced a probability measure on phase space that relates to a Hilbert space isomorphism with Wigner functions. A similar concept, based on Clifford algebra, has been developed for complex-valued functions of geometric algebra, providing an isomorphism with a specific type of function. This Clifford algebra framework connects with the standard Fock space isomorphism via a specific transformation, which we detail. Our work also explores connections with zonal spherical harmonics and a related Hermite polynomials system.

As the need for statistical analysis of continuous non-Gaussian random fields grows, new methods are being developed to leverage techniques from Gaussian field theory. A novel approach involves pathwise conditioning of Gaussian fields on random paths to construct conditional distributions for non-Gaussian field models. A class of non-Gaussian fields can be built using paths as conditioning points for a Gaussian field. An overview will detail the theoretical underpinning of this approach, its applications, and complemented by two illustrative examples.

The feasibility of utilizing drones to facilitate communication within a ground-level sensor network has been explored, which could enable the exchange of data between drone-generated nodes and the ground-based nodes using drones. These drones would act as relays to maintain connectivity between isolated ground nodes and a central gateway, allowing them to stay within range, even when passing aircraft are utilized. A simulation study was conducted to assess the performance of drone-assisted networks in maintaining ground node connectivity, utilizing data from real flights to create models representing various scenarios. Results indicate that in certain situations, using drones as relay nodes can significantly improve coverage and connectivity, with up to 200% increase in coverage area and 50% increase in connectivity for 50% of ground nodes. Results also show that in some cases, ground nodes can maintain connectivity with each other and the gateway simultaneously.

The discovery of neutrino oscillations led to the development of new areas within neutrino physics. Long-range goals include determining the order of neutrino masses, identifying the hierarchy of neutrino masses, and measuring several parameters related to neutrino behavior. A large-scale experiment like DUNE is capable of achieving precision in its measurements of various neutrino parameters with relatively small uncertainties, especially in its first phase of data collection. DUNE's first phase involves the study of neutrinos using a 1-kton LArTPC detector at three distinct neutrino energy ranges: 0.2-0.9, 0.9-3, and 3-10.5 GeV, thanks to its strategic placement at three distinct locations: SBGL, LBNE, and SBNE. DUNE's first phase is expected to significantly contribute to the understanding of neutrino masses and hierarchy through its data collection of neutrinos in three distinct energy ranges.

In the study of hadronic decays of the Higgs boson, identifying substructure within jets is a crucial aspect. This analysis presents an enhanced top tagging algorithm named $v^2$ top tagging, which utilizes the finite discrete fourier transform of jet constituents to detect collinear substructure. The authors apply the SHAP framework to understand the strengths and weaknesses of their top tagging algorithm, revealing that it is sensitive to collinear substructure within jets. This analysis utilizes Monte Carlo events generated for Higgs boson decays in both proton-proton and proton-lead collisions across a wide range of energies. The authors' analysis showcases the effectiveness of their top tagging algorithm in distinguishing between signal and background jets, which is essential for enhancing the accuracy of Higgs boson and Supersymmetry searches.

Within distributed system research, the Virtual Organization concept has been explored since 2002. A Virtual Organization can be defined as a group of trusted entities working together to achieve common objectives. Each entity, known as a Virtual Entity, contributes its capabilities to ensure a shared purpose is met. By 2012, the Virtual Organization concept had evolved to incorporate a contract that outlines the terms and conditions of collaboration. In this paper, we build on existing knowledge and develop a precise mathematical definition of Virtual Organizations. By using Z data types and predicate logic, we capture the essence of VO characteristics, allowing for an abstract representation of entities involved in collaborations. Additionally, we propose the concept of VO refinement, enabling the transformation of a given VO into another that meets specific requirements.

One widely used technique in robust reinforcement learning, robust experience replay, has been proven effective in various situations. However, its true nature and mathematical underpinnings are still not well understood. This paper presents a new approach, called variance diminution in model-based experience replay. The goal is to reduce the variance of the target model in relation to the behavior model used in robust maximum a posteriori estimation. This paper explores the mathematical consequences of variance diminution and proposes value, utility, and gradient diminution methods. These methods are then implemented in robust model-based off-policy policy optimization algorithms and evaluated on a robot pushing environment. The results show that variance diminution methods improve the performance of these algorithms across different simulation environments and even generalize well to real-world settings.

Two new methods, the superbosonization of the Gaussian path integral and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, have been developed to overcome the difficulty of dealing with odd Gaussian functionals in field theory. By applying these methods to the odd functional derived from the massless Majorana fermion theory and performing the corresponding field transformations, it was found that they yield identical results, which were then used to calculate the massless Majorana fermion's partition function. Additionally, these methods were extended to the massive Majorana fermion theory and the $\phi^3$ theory.

We are working on a method to leverage the predictive potential of time series data in motion gravitypal. This involves using a form of recurrent neural networks known as RNN, as well as attentional learning, to develop a dynamic memory framework called MoDeRNN. This framework enables an RNN to learn from a sequence of data, using a combination of external and internal information sources. By using an attention mechanism, we can control when external information is used and how much weight it carries. This enables us to develop models that can adapt to different types of problems and improve the performance of traditional RNN models. We have tested MoDeRNN on a motion-based forecasting task and found that it outperforms other approaches, such as using attentional information alone. This demonstrates the effectiveness of our method and its potential to improve the performance of RNN models in a variety of applications.

This research focuses on a memory safety project called Josephine, which aims to integrate Rust's memory model into a JavaScript-based programming language. By doing so, it addresses the challenge of managing Rust objects that are not owned by Josephine, but still requires safe access to its objects that are not owned by JavaScript. The project overcame several memory model obstacles to achieve this, including developing techniques to handle exceptional events, determining how to represent nil in Josephine, and figuring out how to safely pinpoint specific memory locations. The paper also explores the implications of implementing Josephine on existing Web technologies and evaluates its performance compared to other languages.

We investigate Neutrinoless Double-Beta Decay mediated by both second- and zero-neutrino exchange processes. At the LHC and future colliders, we generate Majorana lepton doublet leptoquark lepton pairs via two-step decays, with subsequent contributions from the lepton pair to the DBDB amplitude. In the context of colliders, we categorize leptoquark-lepton pairs based on their mass hierarchy, with $m_{lq} < m_l$. In the case of $m_{lq} < m_l$, leptoquarks can be probed up to TeV/c^2 even up to a few hundred GeV mass thresholds of leptons. We also consider the scenario of $m_{lq} > m_l$, with leptoquark masses limited by collider reach. We find that leptoquark masses in this case can be distinguished from one another. We also consider the scenario of $m_{lq} = m_l$, with leptoquark masses limited by collider reach. We find that leptoquark masses in this case can be distinguished from one another. We also consider the scenario of $m_{lq} = m_l$, with leptoquark masses limited by collider reach. We find that leptoquark masses in this case can be distinguished from one another. We also consider the scenario of $m_{lq} = m_l$, with leptoquark

A proposed iterative list-decision algorithm is presented for decoding polar codes under the assumption that the channel input distribution is known. Each iteration of the algorithm generates a polar subcode based on the distribution and uses belief propagation to determine potential symbols, thereby reducing the search space for the final decoding decision. The algorithm's performance is evaluated under binary phase-shift keying (BPSK) and binary phase-shift keying with noise (BPSKN) channels with results showing improved error rates compared to traditional techniques, particularly in scenarios with inaccurate distribution information.

In astronomy, images are often enhanced by averaging together multiple observations of the same subject, which are then adjusted for brightness differences. However, achieving precise photometric calibration for these combined images can be complicated due to the varying telescope aperture sizes and the movement of the camera during the observations. A proposed method for calculating the point spread function (PSF) of these combined images also involves adjusting for the differences in aperture sizes and the movement of the camera, which can then be used to determine the flux of stars within the images. A software program has been developed to implement these calculations and has been tested for accuracy by applying it to simulated and actual images. A second method for calculating the PSF has been proposed, which relies on the differences in brightness of the stars within the images. A comparison of these methods has been conducted using both simulated and actual images, which have shown them to be equivalent in accuracy. A study of the effects of the movement of the camera on the images has been conducted, which has found that this motion can significantly impact the calculations of the PSF and the movement correction algorithm. A method for calculating the PSF of the images has been developed, which has been found to be effective in determining the PSF and the movement of the camera. The study of crystalline solids relies heavily on the theory of elastic constants and fracture, rooted in the principles of classical mechanics and thermodynamics. However, determining the critical failure stress of these solids remains a challenging task. By combining the principles of irreversible elasticity, thermodynamics, and plastic deformation, researchers have made significant progress in understanding the fracture process. Building on this foundation, recent research has led to the development of a novel approach to determine the fracture stress of crystalline solids as a function of their elastic constants, volume, and surface energy. This theoretical framework is then compared to empirical findings from various studies, revealing a striking correlation. Furthermore, the study sheds light on the underlying fracture mechanisms in different types of solids, with implications for understanding their mechanical properties and behavior under stress.

Introducing multiple SLE curves driven by the massless Gaussian free field, we take the tangent vectors of these curves as the tangent vectors for the Gaussian free field defined on the curve's complement. As the curve's starting point approaches a finite value, we show that the resulting tangent vectors converge to a constant and that the limit of the Gaussian free field is equivalent to the negative inverse Laplacian's eigenvalue on the corresponding domain. Additionally, we establish that the tangent vectors' jump probabilities across the curves decrease exponentially as the curve's parameter increases. Using these findings, we speculate that the curves driven by the eigenvalue process of the massless Gaussian free field on the half-plane's complement converge to the trivial curve when the parameter goes to infinity.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates for the solution's maximum possible growth rate in p-norm, given certain constraints on its smoothness and energy levels. These estimates are expressed relative to the initial conditions and a universal constant that depends on Navier-Stokes equations parameters. These findings form the basis for enhancing existing a priori estimates for these equations, which were first described by Chemin.

The growing reliance on quantum computing has led to a pressing need for thorough testing and verification of quantum devices. Traditionally, verifying a quantum circuit relied on an exponential time complexity based on its depth. We have devised a novel, linear-time verification method tied to the quantum circuit's qubit count, not its depth. This breakthrough allows for faster classical checking of quantum circuits after they're designed. Our method also identifies the minimum number of qubits needed to modify a given state, which serves as an alternative to deep quantum circuit verification. Additionally, we've developed a low-depth qubit initialization circuit and demonstrated its efficiency by converting any qubit schedule into one that utilizes fewer qubits or the same number with improved efficiency.

A blockchain system allows for secure management of digital assets by providing a decentralized, verifiable, and tamper-proof framework.  Its potential applications extend beyond financial transactions, encompassing areas like supply chains, healthcare, and the Internet of Things (IoT).  The integration of blockchain with IoT, however, faces challenges due to the inherent security risks and trust issues associated with IoT products.  To overcome these obstacles, this paper proposes a novel framework based on a permissioned blockchain that utilizes smart contracts to manage IoT digital assets.  To enhance security and trust, this framework relies on trusted third-party Oracles that verify and provide information about IoT asset usage.  To demonstrate its practicality, this paper showcases a practical use-case involving a food supply chain, highlighting its benefits and improvements over current supply chain management methods.

Cells are the basic units of life and exhibit capsular, tubular, or plate-like appearances depending on their type. Creating synthetic cell models using machine learning can facilitate understanding and address medical uncertainties, which is challenging due to the complex geometry of cells. Traditional methods rely on simplified mesh-based approaches, which can distort features or require parameter-driven artificial construction, or use voxel-based models that may be costly to compute or may not accurately capture the intricate details of cells. Our study develops a new method that uses implicit neural representations to generate cell models through machine learning, resulting in accurate, compact, and freely-shapeable models that can be generated quickly.

The rise of digital documentation has led to enhanced document creation, distribution, and interconnectivity. However, this advancement has come at the expense of usability for print-disabled individuals, who struggle with printed documents. Research has highlighted the requirements and challenges faced by blind and low-vision print-disabled individuals when interacting with physical documents. Despite existing research, no comprehensive standards for making printed documents accessible to this group have been established. Consequently, many printed documents are inaccessible, forcing print-disabled individuals to rely on alternative formats, such as braille and audio, which are often unavailable. This paper aims to identify the essential requirements for making printed documents accessible, focusing on the needs of print-disabled individuals and exploring solutions, such as electronic augmentations and innovative braille technologies.

While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach based on autoregressive language modeling. This method enables bidirectional contextual learning by leveraging permutations of factorization order and, due to its autoregressive formulation, rectifies the limitations seen in BERT. Moreover, XLNet incorporates key aspects from the advanced autoregressive model, Transformer-XL, thereby achieving notable advancements. According to comprehensive testing under similar settings, XLNet consistently outperforms BERT across 20 tasks, including sentiment analysis, question answering, and language modeling, by substantial margins.

We have created synthetic spectra of M0 V stars with known effects of stellar activity and simulated the impact of such features on the spectra of exoplanet host stars using mock transit spectra. Our analysis of these spectra, including analysis methods developed by Ehrenreich et al in 2010, Otto et al in 2019, and Kolb et al in 2020, revealed instances where activity-induced features misled these methods into detecting the presence of atmospheric features. However, using high-resolution spectra eliminated the misinterpretation of stellar activity effects in the case of Ehrenreich et al's method, as well as that of Kolb et al's, although high-resolution data from Sopisticated Cross-Correlation Technique (SCCT) analysis showed some sensitivity to activity features. The Otto et al method with high-resolution data remained susceptible to activity effects. Given that high-resolution data offers better stellar characterization, we recommend using such data in transit spectroscopy analysis whenever possible, especially for ground-based observations.

Given a Riemann surface equipped with a metric that has isolated singular points, we develop a complete conformal metric on the surface's complement of these points, retaining the original conformal structure and curvature bounds. This result broadens the application of a previous theorem established by Dong-Ming and Kong. We further demonstrate that when the original metric's curvature is positive, the newly introduced metric will also have positive curvature, whereas if it has nonnegative curvature, the new metric will also have nonnegative curvature due to removal of discrete points. As a consequence of this finding, we prove that a compact, conformally flat Riemann surface can be reparameterized only if it possesses a metric with zero curvature, thereby yielding a new demonstration of the "positive action" conjecture initially proposed by Feder.

Research on terrestrial animals' locomotion has predominantly focused on species of moderate size due to the scarcity of relevant data from lower or higher mass ranges.  This study collects and reports relevant information from a range of animal species spanning six orders of magnitude in mass, with an emphasis on how musculoskeletal system dimensions and power production capabilities change across different sizes. 

Characterising leg movement as a two-dimensional complex wave, our findings show a significant size-related change in the phase difference between body segments as the size decreases, with smaller species experiencing a greater degree of decoupling. 

With increasing body mass, our findings show a substantial decrease in the frequency of the leg movement, with a significant size-dependent change in the duration of each stride in contrast. 

When normalised for body size, our findings suggest that power output from muscles used for movement remains relatively constant, with a size-independent change in the movement efficiency despite changes in body size.

A hydrodynamic-based model of movement is proposed, which explains the observed changes in the movement pattern across different sizes and species, with smaller species experiencing a greater degree of decoupling. 

This study provides new insights into the mechanics of movement in a range of species and suggests a new method for the research community to collect relevant information from species with different sizes, with a range of potential applications for the development of soft and wearable robots.

A novel from 2014 sparked interest in a scenario where an asteroid impact creates a distinctive underwater tsunami that travels at a varying speed before reaching land, preserving human settlements. In contrast to traditional tsunami models, we examine the dispersive nature of tsunami waves using a specific equation, which expands our understanding and improves accuracy. We present high-performance computing strategies and an approach to adaptively simulate tsunami behavior in a particular software environment. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in preserving intricate components of the solution and discuss challenges and potential enhancements for future development.

Recent observations with the James Webb Space Telescope have provided new insights into heavily dust-obscured galaxies that are invisible to standard optical surveys. These galaxies, which are obscured by massive amounts of dust, have been found to be extremely luminous and to dominate the growth of supermassive black holes throughout the universe's history. Using early JWST data from multiple programs, researchers have discovered that a significant portion of these galaxies, 67%, are completely undetected in standard optical galaxy surveys, while another 33% are found in less accurate or broader optical catalogs. Further analysis of the data revealed that a large number of these galaxies are classified as non-detected in standard photometry but still appearing in photometric redshift distributions as brighter or undetected galaxies, Z~2 quasars and ultra-faint galaxies, respectively. These results imply that a substantial number of these galaxies are expected to be detected by future surveys such as ROMAN and LSST, and that a significant portion will remain hidden from these surveys, with implications for their contribution to galaxy evolution.

A novel gravity theory in seven dimensions is proposed, featuring an additional
field that drifts through a unitary sphere $S^2$ as part of its mathematical model.
In this theoretical framework, the gravity field is comprised of one rotational
component and four vector components, along with an additional field component.
The gravity equations are formulated in the Riemannian context, and the motion of
matter is governed by the Schrödinger equation, with the gravity field playing
the role of a potential function. The theoretical framework is supported by
various solutions that demonstrate its practical utility.

Consider an infinite channel with water levels that can rise and fall over time, 
creating an environment where objects can float on the surface. This channel is home 
to two types of solid blocks, differing in size and weight, and an infinite number of 
floating blocks of a standard size that can be moved. By alternating between open 
and blocked time periods, and adjusting water levels in various ways, a sequence of 
block configurations can be created. This paper explores the possible block 
configurations in an infinite channel when both sizes of solid blocks are present, and 
provides a classification system for the possible sequences based on their weight 
distribution. A key finding is that in an optimal arrangement, and infinitely repeating 
sequence of blocks can be created, and these arrangements are unique to alternating 
block configurations.

Two extreme forms of the El Niño-Southeast Pacific (ENSO) phenomenon hold the key to understanding various local and global impacts on Earth's climate system, as research suggests their individual and distinct effects on precipitation in Latin America and globally. By examining statistical data from 41 countries over three decades, this study delves into the regional and temporal variations influenced by two ENSO flavors: East Pacific and Multi- and Inter-Decadal (MiD) events. The analysis reveals significant differences in how these two ENSO types affect precipitation in countries, with MiD events leaving a lasting impact on a country's climate by the end of the 21st century, in contrast to East Pacific events which show no significant long-term trends. Moreover, this study reveals a unique relationship in which MiD events in the 1980s significantly enhanced seasonal precipitation in parts of South America, while East Pacific events had a negative impact, with very low and high precipitation levels becoming more prevalent under MiD events, in contrast to East Pacific events which showed an opposite effect.

The expansion of amorphous solids into their surroundings is influenced by the presence of space constraints during the growth process. To gain insight into this phenomenon, we utilize small-angle and wide-angle scattering measurements on expanding amorphous silicon nanospheres as they undergo laser-driven melting and growth. Our research indicates that the initial stage of growth is characterized by an unusually increased rate of expansion in certain directions. This outcome is supported by computer simulations of a 3D model, suggesting that rapid expansion is a consequence of the absence of affine behavior in the solid's mechanical response. We propose that non-affine effects are responsible for the observed phenomenon and provide a mathematical model describing their role in the solid's expansion pattern.

In population biology, models with age structure are crucial in capturing crucial life cycle data, which impacts population dynamics. Additionally, research on environmental pollution's influence on population growth is highly recommended. This study integrates both aspects, developing a single-species population model that incorporates age structure and takes into account the behavioral impact in a polluted environment. Specifically, a logistic single-species model with age structure, behavioral impact, and pollution effect was created, mathematically formulated, and analyzed through qualitative and quantitative methods to determine the model's stability. This was done by examining the boundaries of parameter space that result in stable, unstable, and neutral outcomes, using qualitative and quantitative analysis.

Decidability and computational complexity of inference systems were previously investigated within the context of all-universal Hilbert systems with an admissible weakening rule, a specific type of rule that preserves the theoremhood of a formula given an additional formula. This study is focused on a more general framework - weakening and contraction hypersequents, which can accommodate a variety of different weakening rules. As a result, we achieve uniform decidability for a broader range of weaking rules and provide uniform methods to determine the complexity of these systems. Furthermore, we extend these methods to be applied in the development of the reduced matrix method for deductive systems.

A research paper proposes an algorithm called HyperExpan to facilitate the expansion of taxonomies through concept associations. Taxonomy expansion involves linking novel concepts to established category groups. Most existing taxonomy expansion methods rely on a flat learning structure, training one neural network from leaf nodes to root nodes using Euclidean space representations. Conversely, HyperExpan employs a hierarchical approach, breaking down the process into separate neural networks for each node level and employing a hyperbolic representation for improved learning outcomes. Furthermore, HyperExpan incorporates an innovative concept-concept network that enables bidirectional concept attribute sharing during training. When evaluated on comprehensive benchmark datasets, HyperExpan demonstrated superior performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches and benchmark baselines.

The accuracy of our interaction energy predictions for the S66 benchmark, which assesses non-covalent interactions between molecules in various electric fields, has been evaluated. Our results show that applying a uniform external field enhances the dispersion energy while it diminishes the closed-shell hydrogen-bonding energy. Furthermore, we discovered that the polarization energy exhibits opposite behavior in response to field orientation. Utilizing the locally scaled, two-body approximation, we were ableassistant

able to effectively replicate the effects observed in the S66 dataset, except for certain hydrogen-bonded complexes. To improve agreement with experimental data, we refined the closure criteria for triple excitations. Our revised approach effectively captured the hydrogen-bonding contribution and yielded interaction energies that closely aligned with the experimentally-determined S66 dataset.

The concept of uncertainty in research is multifaceted and often overlooked in scheduling studies, with most papers focusing solely on quantifiable data like job arrival times and durations, while disregarding other sources of uncertainty or simplifying them. In this study, we identify two categories of uncertain information that are commonly encountered but frequently neglected: information uncertainty and impulsive uncertainty. We demonstrate the need for a more comprehensive representation of uncertainty in scheduling and propose a method to address impulsive uncertainty in particular. We outline the potential applications and introduce a basic model for handling impulsive uncertainty; however, developing an effective solution to this problem remains an area for further research.

Cyber-Physical Systems are particularly vulnerable to disruptions, necessitating robust strategies to maintain continuity and rapid recovery from failures. This research outlines a general approach for model-based resilience in Multi-Agent Systems, leveraging a specific logic to describe desired behavior and handle disruptions. The proposed method involves a framework that tackles three key challenges: withstanding attacks, maintaining continuity, and swift recovery, all based on a specified logical structure. We have formulated a decision problem and proven its decidability, along with an evaluation of our approach through simulations on a power grid network.

Experiments employing sensitive equipment networks aim to detect and identify rare substances at extremely low levels. Traditional methods used to detect changes in gravity rely on a single location, whereas a network of distributed sensors across various dimensions could potentially lead to substantial breakthroughs. Researchers have leveraged advanced accelerometers to create a multi-dimensional research network, enabling the exploration of a broader range of rare substances. A key factor in these experiments is accurately minimizing and measuring internal oscillations within the sensitive equipment, known as environmental rejection. A novel method for calculating environmental rejection has significantly improved the sensitivity of the sensitive equipment, and the resulting data has been used to set strict limits on the existence of certain rare substances. For instance, the experiments have ruled out the possibility of cadmium and gold clustering within the Earth and certain types of light particles. Researchers are now working to further enhance the sensitive equipment, with the goal of exploring other rare substances and potential breakthroughs.

We consider a semilinear diffusion equation defined on a complete, connected Riemannian manifold. By expanding the nonlinear reaction term with a Taylor series up to the second order, we transform the original equation into a nonlinear heat equation and obtain an approximation of the solution. Our work builds upon previously established results for complete manifolds, with a focus on the behavior of the approximation as the manifold's dimension increases and the diffusion rate approaches infinity. In addition, we demonstrate the existence of local solutions for the original equation without imposing symmetry or positivity assumptions on the manifold.

Radio sources in the intergalactic medium exhibit a range of behaviors 
characterized by their brightness temperatures, which span several orders of 
magnitude. By examining the distribution of thermal broadening at $10^6$ K, 
researchers have found that faint sources tend to have larger angular sizes than 
brighter counterparts of similar thermal broadening. This disparity suggests 
faint sources may be unresolved and their sizes exaggerated due to the 
averaging process. As a result, it's possible that faint sources are actually 
characterized by smaller scales similar to bright sources. Furthermore, it's 
observed that faint sources show less alignment with their host galaxies' 
major axes, which is more pronounced in bright sources, indicating faint 
sources' structures are primarily influenced by external environments rather 
than their host galaxies' intrinsic properties.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a mathematical tool used to analyze and model complex systems. By combining HMMs with abstract algebra, it's possible to develop a comprehensive framework for evaluating the information flow in detailed systems. This information flow model is based on a probability distribution function, which can be represented as an Abstract Hidden Markov Model (AHMM). An AHMM is defined as a sequence of probabilistic transformations between distinct states, characterized by the transition of a weighted Markov chain from one state to another. Building upon AHMMs, a new mathematical structure known as a probability monoid can be used to describe sequential probabilistic computations. By integrating these concepts, it's possible to create a probability monoid-based transition function for AHMMs, effectively allowing the analysis of detailed systems through the lens of information flow. This perspective is demonstrated in the context of a traffic light controller, where the information flow at the molecular level is linked to the macroscopic behavior of the system.

This paper explores the concept of consistency in systems that change over time. It suggests a framework for evaluating the limitations and ambiguities in building theories that adapt to these changes. By applying this framework, we can demonstrate the logical necessity of non-local behavior in systems that remain consistent throughout their evolution. Several case studies are provided to illustrate how this framework can be applied in diverse contexts.

We introduce a flexible framework for incorporating scattering events into phenomenological models, which we implement within the framework of Soft Drop jet substructure variables. The scattering events are modelled as a loss in energy according to a characterised function, with options including a simple power-law approach and more complex models based on Monte Carlo simulations, such as e.g. a Lund string model description of scattering events. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through comparisons to data, including large radius jets in proton-proton collisions and medium-modified jet substructure in proton-lead collisions.

To investigate how the Casimir effect influences thermodynamic properties of a blackbody, we developed a mathematical model that combines electromagnetic radiation and a free electron gas, using the Riemann zeta function and a modified form of Bose-Einstein's distribution function, modified to account for zero-point fluctuations. Our study led to several key findings, including the recovery of the classical thermodynamic limits for large zeta function parameters. We discovered that the Casimir effect introduces an additional constant of motion beyond the Hamiltonian, leading to a set of microstates that can be characterized by two separate sets of coordinates. Our model shows that the Casimir effect alters both the internal energy and specific heat of the blackbody, while leaving its entropy unchanged. This suggests that the Casimir effect causes the blackbody to undergo a phase transition as it cools down.

Location data, often derived from LBS, can be used to create LBS history and location track for each user. Since LBS history and location tracks may reveal personal information, users protect their location tracks by obscuring parts of their history and tracks, given certain usage criteria and location history/track privacy levels. Here, LBS history/tracks are represented as segments, and LBS history/track privacy levels are defined as conditional probabilities of history/track segments given that the user fulfilled the specified location data usage criteria. Users, in collaboration with the LBS provider, set the specified location data usage criteria and determine the associated privacy levels. Users may also set the LBS provider-free period during LBS history and location track privacy periods. Users use the LBS provider-free period to temporarily disable location data usage, at the cost of LBS history and track obscuration loss. Users choose which LBS history and track segments to reveal, taking into account the LBS history and track obscuration loss and the specified location data usage privacy. Users may also use the LBS provider-free period to temporarily disable location data usage at the cost of LBS history and track obscuration loss. The LBS history and track obscuration loss is calculated as the difference between the number of LBS history and track segments to reveal and the number of obscutable LBS history and track segments, given the LBS provider privacy levels.
