Our analysis involves the combinatorial aspect of the Fox-Hatcher loop, a specific element within the second homotopy group of the space $B_{n}$. This space is defined as the mapping class group of a genus $n$ surface, which we represent as a surface with one hole. By studying the behavior of long, thin rectangles within this surface, we establish a relationship with Vassiliev invariants of order three. This connection demonstrates that there exists a sequence of Vassiliev invariants with increasing order that all converge to a specific, order-three Vassiliev invariant. This invariant is derived from the Fox-History loop and can be further characterized by its behavior in the tautological ring of $B_{n}$. This loop also shares similarities with a specific graph that appears in the work of Korn, Reshetikhin, and Sawicki.

We've investigated the properties of LiFeAs, a unique iron-based superconductor with three-dimensional crystal structure and remarkable tolerance to pressure. By employing advanced four-dimensional ESR spectroscopy, we discovered that spinning LiFeAs crystals at high pressures does not trigger a nematic phase transition, in contrast to iron-based superconductors with tetragonal symmetry at lower pressures. The absence of electronic and magnetic changes in LiFeAs rules out the notion that LiFeAs shares common underlying mechanisms with iron-based superconductors and further complicates the already complex picture of high-temperature superconductivity.

This study examines the alignment of two-Higgs-doublet models with global fitting techniques, taking into account a comprehensive set of data including the Higgs boson signal, decays, related parameters, electroweak measurements, radiative b quark decay, meson mixing, and recent B meson decay observations.  We used the two-Higgs-doublet model as the benchmark model to test the reliability of the global fit method in finding the optimal model to match experimental data.  We discovered that future collider results can significantly influence the global fit outcome, underlining the importance of aligning theoretical models with empirical observations.  We also investigated how varying the significance of collider findings in the global fit affects the model analysis.

In a simulated environment where microorganisms compete for limited resources, our research focuses on understanding how naturally evolved creatures adapt to outsmart opponents that can think ahead. We've developed a learning algorithm that gives local organisms the ability to evolve and create effective group strategies, allowing them to coordinate and learn beyond their basic instincts. By studying the behavior of these evolved creatures, we've found that complex and efficient patterns of cooperation can arise from simple and efficient individual bodies that don't have the capacity for complex thought. This self-organizing process allows early successes against both logical and illogical opponents, setting the stage for a battle between cooperation and competition.

We investigate the anomalies in chiral gauge theories with various groupings of chiral fermions, focusing on theories including an SU(2) gauge field, as well as SU(2) with additional adjoint and triplet Higgs fields. Our analysis utilizes the robust anomaly approach, as introduced in a previous study. This method yields consistent results for established theories, including QCD and SU(2) with a fundamental Higgs field. In contrast, the robust anomaly method produces contradictory outcomes for certain accepted results in the literature: the presence of SU(3) breaking in QCD with three left-handed quark flavors, robust anomalies in the Standard Model, and SU(2) baryon number anomalies in the presence of Higgs fields.

This study investigates the well-posedness and ill-posedness of the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in Besov space, specifically under $p<1$ and with a fixed H\"older exponent $\sigma$ in $[0,1]$. Our analysis focuses on a perturbation theory of the solution to the equations when the viscosity is zero, using a specific type of space denoted as $B^0_{p,\infty}(\dot{B}_\sigma(0,h_0)$. By doing so, we demonstrate that the Navier-Stokes equations with a small nonlinearity and a fixed viscosity become ill-posed when the viscosity is sufficiently large, provided that the H\"older exponent and the parameter $p$ satisfy specific conditions. Our results generalize the works of Cannone (1995) and Planchon (2004) and extend the scope of these generalizations to Navier-Stokes equations.

We investigate the phenomenon of phonon-induced magnon squeezing in
antiferromagnetic materials and its relationship with a spectral shift in magnons.
Using the Jaynes-Cummings model, we derive a general quadratic Hamiltonian
expression for magnon-phonon interactions in antiferromagnetic materials with
specific examples in cuprate and nickelate systems. Our analysis reveals that the
interaction between magnons and phonons causes both modes to become thermally
squeezed, exhibiting non-classical properties. Moreover, we find that the spectral
density of magnons undergoes a shift in energy due to phonon-induced interactions,
which can be observed experimentally via magnon-photon interactions.

This paper proposes a pair of modifications to enhance the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem. Originally based on Gabidulin codes, the system has a well-documented vulnerability to preimage attacks, which this paper addresses by introducing a new decryption method. This new approach involves a system of polynomial equations, leveraging the capabilities of Gröbner basis computation and rational points on elliptic curves. A key benefit of this modification is the increase in its Niederreiter variant's security, ranging from Niederreiter200 to Niederreiter400, with varying parameters outlined in the accompanying table.

To improve the robustness of large language models like BERT, which have limitations in understanding word meanings outside general context, we've developed a novel pre-training strategy. This approach leverages a dictionary by creating a set of synthetic sentences that help BERT generalize word meanings in different contexts. Through rigorous evaluations on various tasks, including noun replacement in sentences and word sense disambiguation, our method has shown significant performance gains, with up to a 12.3% improvement in the most challenging tasks. Notably, our approach is efficient and adaptable, as it only relies on a basic dictionary tool and doesn't require any additional supervision or complex processing.

In our investigation, we consider the behavior of the minimum spanning acycles over the edges of Erdős-Rényi random graphs as the number of vertices increases without bound. We demonstrate that the distribution of the minimum weighted acycles that form a cycle changes in two distinct ways as the number of vertices grows, with a transition occurring at a specific threshold that depends on the edge weights. These findings are also applicable to the minimum spanning acycles in Cayley complexes formed by randomly connecting vertices in two-dimensional space. We also show that the persistence diagrams resulting from these acycles contain information about the mass of the resulting persistent structures and provide a method to calculate this information.

In cross-repository federated learning scenarios, data owners collectively train a machine learning model by sharing their data with a centralized server. However, several security breaches that exploit the training process have previously been demonstrated, taking advantage of horizontal federated learning (multiple clients sharing horizontal data distributions) by a malicious server. This paper explores a new set of attacks that occur in vertical federated learning (separate clients sharing vertical data distributions) and reveal a more insidious form of malicious behavior. The authors present several practical attacks that occur during the training process, demonstrating how a rogue server can infer sensitive information about individual users. The presented attacks are not only theoretically feasible but also validated through real-world implementations, highlighting the need for further research in vertical federated learning security.

A novel, purely theoretical method, named BOSR, is applied to examine the dark side of B-meson decay into a proton and a dark antibaryon. Utilizing the valence parton distribution functions derived from QCD light-cone perturbation theory, the BOSR method yields numerical results for the branching fraction and transverse momentum distribution of B-meson decay, indicating that with suitable dark-hadron distribution functions, the method can account for observed anomalies in B-meson decay.

The increasing reliance of cities on cyber-infrastructure systems like power and water makes them vulnerable to sophisticated, multi-faceted cyber threats that could potentially cause widespread physical damage. To study a city's response to such threats, a resource management game has been developed that simulates the defense of a city against socio-cyber-physical (SCP) attacks. In this game, SCP attacks combine physical and cyber elements and target a city's infrastructure to cause maximum damage. To counter these attacks, a city must manage its available resources, including personnel, equipment, and financial resources, to restore infrastructure and prevent damage. The game represents the city as a graph of nodes, including infrastructure sites, where attacks can be prevented or caused. The city's defense strategy is determined by a leader-following control method, where infrastructure defenders adjust their strategies based on the actions of other defenders and the node controller, and the node controller makes decisions based on the overall city well-being. The well-being of the city is measured by a utility function that reflects the impact of SCP attacks and the effectiveness of the city's defense. To test the city's response to SCP attacks, a case study has been conducted using a modified version of the ATENA attack model. The results of the game demonstrate the city's response to SCP attacks and the effectiveness of its defense strategy.

The research presents an investigation into how thermal and quantum fluctuations are impacted by a cavity confinement for a black hole in a state of equilibrium. The study focuses on a specific model consisting of a black hole in a flat, two-dimensional space, which exhibits no rotation and is coupled to a radiation field that satisfies certain energy and spatial constraints. The Horowitz--Perry method is employed to analyze the influence of the radiation field on the black hole's thermodynamic behavior. The investigation demonstrates that the black hole's transition temperature, which marks the difference between a black hole and a black hole "island," can be altered by the radiation field's temperature and confinement, ultimately leading to changes in the phase transition temperature. The study finds that a "phase shift" occurs, which can be described as the relationship between the cavity's size and the temperature of the radiation field. The research also explores the effects of the radiation field's entropy on the black hole's thermodynamic behavior and presents a specific model to illustrate these effects.

In the field of information retrieval, ranking documents is a crucial task where we assign labels to unlabelled documents for organizing purposes. However, document labels are often corrupted due to various errors, which hinders the effectiveness of traditional ranking models. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that employs bag-level representations, where documents with similar characteristics are grouped together. By leveraging BERT and PCA, our method mitigates the negative impact of noisy labels, resulting in superior performance on MsMarcos, TRECVID, and Corel datasets.

Recent advancements in Few-Shot Graph Classification tasks have been observed, primarily utilizing Graph Neural Networks models to achieve accurate results. However, these models typically rely on abundant labeled data, which is often scarce in real-world applications. To overcome this challenge, this paper presents an innovative solution by leveraging pseudo-labeling techniques to improve the accuracy of GNN models under limited labeling conditions. Our approach, Informative Pseudo-Labeling for GNNs (IPGNN), combines pseudo-labeling and semi-supervised graph classification methods to increase the effectiveness of few-shot GNN models. Our experiments, conducted on four benchmark graph datasets, demonstrate the superior performance of IPGNN over existing baselines under various labeling conditions.

Betatron radiation spectroscopy in vacuum or surrounding media can provide precise, undisturbed measurements of the wakefield's amplitude and phase. This technique has been successfully applied in prior experiments and is now being employed in the AWAKE Run 2 experiment, utilizing a self-modulated proton beam to generate a focalized electron bunch at 412 MeV. A simulation of this process using the Expert-Like Particle Tracker for Electromagnetic Waves program has been conducted to compare predictions with actual experimental data. The simulation's outcomes are as follows: Analyzing betatron radiation spectra at various distances from the interaction point in both vacuum and surrounding NF3 gas, while accounting for experimental conditions and electron bunch variations. The comparison of proton and NF3 gas focusing performance in generating comparable betatron radiation spectra at different distances from the interaction point. The estimated amplitude and phase of the betatron oscillations, along with corresponding uncertainties.

This study addresses the challenge of learning private decision trees in a distributed setting where participants contribute data while maintaining its confidentiality. Existing methods for private decision tree learning have achieved notable advancements; however, they are often limited by strict assumptions or significant privacy losses. In this research, a new framework for private decision tree learning is presented, which ensures that local data shared among participants contains at least one relevant example for making informed decisions. The proposed framework leverages a new method of quantile estimation that offers better accuracy and privacy than existing quantile estimators. The integration of this quantile estimation technique results in enhanced learning outcomes, applied here to distributed learning scenarios. The proposed framework's effectiveness is further demonstrated through experiments and theoretical analysis, showcasing its ability to make informed decisions with significant privacy losses while minimizing unnecessary data sharing. The quantile estimation technique, independent of its application to decision tree learning, exhibits promising results and can be applied to other differential privacy applications.

A new class of methods for optimizing regularized divergences is developed and applied to R\'enyi divergence with optional constraints. Leveraging the connection between Bregman prox algorithms and the proximal gradient method, a unified framework is established to derive closed-form expressions for the proximal operator and gradient of the objective function, which are central components of the Bregman proximal gradient (BP-G) algorithm. This algorithm is demonstrated to maintain monotonicity and convergence in the context of the BP-G method, which is further augmented with a non-standard line search condition to enhance its performance. Through numerical experiments, the efficacy and versatility of this algorithm are illustrated, particularly in its ability to capture the underlying structure of data, which aligns with theoretical findings.

This research introduces a novel approach to selecting chain event graph models using Bayesian maximum a posteriori estimation. The proposed method generates multiple models for each observation and identifies the most suitable chain graph models for PEAs. A simulation study and real-world analysis of smoking data are conducted to compare this method to others, revealing that it outperforms simulated models and produces results on par with other methods in model selection. Notably, this approach offers a level of interpretability and uncertainty quantification not available with other model selection techniques.

In a Hilbert space, we investigate the convergence properties of a point-of-interest $x^*$, which solves an underdetermined system of equations through the least-norm solution. This task is accomplished by applying a Tikhonov regularization parameter $\epsilon$ to the system under the influence of damped inertial movement. As time progresses, the movement is assumed to be non-stop and the Tikhonov parameter $\epsilon$ simultaneously decreases towards 0, with the step size and damping coefficient being sufficiently small. Under these conditions, it is found that the sequence of interest converges strongly towards the least-norm solution $x^*$ and, additionally, the sequence of iterates converges towards $x^*$ at a uniformly accelerated rate. This investigation is a continuation of prior research in which it was demonstrated that the sequence of interest converges weakly towards the least-norm solution and, further, the sequence of iterates converges towards $x^*$ at a uniformly accelerated rate when the Tikhonov parameter is adjusted manually after each step.

Our research explores how a basic robot tasked with navigating a long, straight path near a perpendicular wall behaves when its field of view is limited by the presence of obstacles. These obstacles can be either fixed or moving, and their impact on the robot's movement is studied in relation to the distance between the obstacles and the robot's viewing angle. The analysis reveals a complex and dynamic response in the robot's movement pattern, which transitions from orderly to disordered states as the viewing angle diminishes. The disordered state exhibits characteristics of chaos, with distinct patterns emerging at intermediate angles and viewing distances, such as clusters, waves, and spatio-temporal patterns of fluctuation. The observed behaviors are also replicated using a particle dynamics model based on simple attraction and repulsion forces.

In cuprate science, there's an ongoing debate about whether or not impurities affect microwave conductivity in the same way it does in typical metals. Recent research found that by changing the impurity level and positioning within the Fermi surface, researchers can manipulate the microwave conductivity's energy and temperature response extensively. Our research employing a two-dimensional t - U model shows that this effect is highly unlikely to occur if the impurities are located near the Fermi surface. On the other hand, if the impurities are positioned deeper within the hole pocket, we discovered that the microwave conductivity exhibits a contrasting behavior in comparison to conventional metals, with three distinct critical points instead, characterized by a second-order phase transition at one of them.

This passage discusses an anisotropic curvature flow, referred to as the motion by crystalline-like average curvature. This type of flow has far-reaching applications in fields such as materials science, nanotechnology, and crystallography. The survey covers a comprehensive range of relevant topics, including the emergence of this type of flow in the early 2000s, its connections to other related ideas, and current research developments. The main focus is on the first two authors, highlighting their key contributions to the field. The remaining sections are dedicated to the fundamental aspects of the motion by crystalline-like average curvature.

Our novel, interactive learning environment, GrowSpace, teaches individuals plant
care fundamentals through hands-on game-playing. As the first interactive learning
system focused on plant cultivation, GrowSpace enables players to develop their
skills by nurturing artificial plants that require periodic attention. These
artificial plants are represented by a suite of modular, interconnected systems
(similar to the xerus) that players must adjust to promote healthy growth. To do
this, players must learn the interdependent relationships between these systems
and make strategic decisions to optimize plant care. To effectively learn this
complex content, GrowSpace features a unique, modular curriculum that adapts to
player performance, incorporating both artificial intelligence-powered feedback
and a diverse range of game levels. Our evaluation results, obtained from a 32-
participant study, indicate that GrowSpace is an effective and engaging learning
system.

We present an outline of a novel approach that derives the SLE loop measure, based on a combination of two key insights. Firstly, the loop measure can be obtained by examining quantum disks in the Jacobi ensemble and then taking their union. Secondly, the quantum disks can themselves be obtained by performing a conformal welding of the unit disk and the punctured unit disk along the unit circle. These ideas draw inspiration from the direct coupling method in quantum mechanics and conformal field theory.

As image biomarkers become integral to clinical trials and precision medicine, we recognize the need for standardized workflows and a unified understanding of data analysis processes. This understanding is crucial for replicating and validating biomarker metrics across different imaging data. We propose a standard workflow for validating and normalizing image biomarkers across diverse datasets. This involves establishing a baseline using a widely available training dataset, and then evaluating and refining biomarker metrics based on their performance on independent validation datasets. This approach facilitates accurate biomarker metrics and enhances their clinical utility. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method using a training dataset from the PROTECT study and the NCI-ISIC skin cancer dataset for validation purposes. This work is a collaborative effort of the Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI) to develop standardized workflows for normalizing biomarker metrics across diverse datasets.

The role of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances in $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction off the nucleon is investigated, using a isobar model that includes the $N(1530)$, $N(1650)$, $\Delta(1620)$, $\Delta(1700)$ and $\Delta(1750)$ resonances. Calculated $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ differential cross sections and polarization observables are presented for existing experimental data at specific $K$-lab angles, examining the impact of each resonance's contribution. Notably, the $N(1650)$. $N(1700)$, $\Delta(1620)$, $\Delta(1700)$ and $\Delta(1750)$ resonances significantly influence both $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ cross sections, especially at forward $K$-lab angles. This study provides insights into the resonance contributions and is necessary for understanding the experimentally measured $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ cross sections, especially in the region of interest for J-PARC DiCharmEII's spin and flavor program.

This research describes a method for preprocessing images using OpenCV, employing a multi-stage approach to correct alignment, illumination, and imperfections in the morph II dataset, consisting of 5657 high-quality images, divided into Class A (5013 images) and Class B (644 images) based on ethnicity. Preprocessing commences with removal of subpar images from both classes via Class A and Class B, followed by application of a 10-fold iterative approach for refining rotation, scaling, translation, and illumination adjustments to rectify image orientation, size, positioning, and illumination levels.

This research explores the possibility that primordial black holes (PBH) formed as a result of a failed curvaton. With the curvaton contributing to inflationary perturbations turning into short-scale gravitational waves after inflation, these waves might have been responsible for the PBH formation. However, due to the constraints imposed by the curvaton potential's steepness and non-linearity, PBH formation has been considered unlikely. This study demonstrates that these constraints can be overcome if the inflationary perturbations originated from the curvaton, with its potential characterized by a short mass-scale, $\Lambda_s$. With the curvaton mass, $m_{\phi}$, much larger than $\Lambda_s$, it's shown that PBH formation is feasible, with observed properties matching those of the PBHs, potentially accounting for the dark matter and recent Galactic events like the microlensing, the GeV gamma-ray signal, and the 3.5-day periodic Gravitational Wave (GW) events, with $P_0=0.01$, with the curvaton mass, $m_{\phi}=O(10^{-3})m_{Pl}$, with the potential allowing for the curvaton contribution to the tensor to scalar ratio, $r$, with the remaining contribution possibly coming from the inflationary perturbations.

This paper delves into the application of latent variable models for analyzing educational pathway patterns. By considering various factors such as students' socio-demographic characteristics, school and program type, as well as the influence of social background, we aim to uncover how these elements shape educational choices. Leveraging a large dataset of students in Quebec, Canada, we explore the utility of different model approaches, including the application of non-parametric and parametric models, as well as the incorporation of supplementary flexible time-series models. Our findings indicate that student social background plays a pivotal role in educational pathway decisions. The estimated model can also inform policy makers on average transition patterns between educational stages, as well as the impact of school and program characteristics on these transitions.

This research investigates the issue of linked and automated vehicle formation control as it pertains to the establishment of multiple connected vehicle chains. We propose a new model that incorporates the effects of following distance and speed, as well as the influence of the lead vehicle's acceleration and jerk, and demonstrates that the control of these vehicles can be achieved through a differential game with a single controller. We have also derived a closed-form solution for the control inputs necessary to achieve the desired vehicle formations, and verified the stability and convergence of the system through both theoretical and simulation-based approaches.

In counterfactual estimation, a new method generates predictions for logistic regression without training a model, by directly estimating the log-odds. This approach relies on observed data, no gradients, no assumptions of causal structure, and no neighboring information. It's demonstrated to be a valid logistic regression predictor, to improve upon existing predictions, and to be scalable for large tasks, including a 64 billion parameter prediction. Additionally, it's shown that such estimates can be used under the ignorable treatment assumption to counterfactual logistic regression, and even nonignorable treatment scenarios through the use of neural lattices. Finally, interactions are shown to be impossible to represent within this framework, which are then formally characterized.

The generation of headlines by artificial intelligence is ubiquitous in today's world, and their application is diverse, spanning news agencies, social media, and even as supporting tools for human journalists. Given the prevalence of AI-generated headlines in everyday life and their widespread use, it is surprising that there is a shortage of studies focused on assessing their quality. In this study, we examine the feasibility of using deep learning models to identify AI-generated headlines with a high degree of accuracy. We compiled and released a dataset of genuine headlines and their AI-generated counterparts, and employed various models, including fine-tuned transformers, to conduct a comparison of their performance. The findings of our study indicate that AI-generated headlines are increasingly being surpassed by their human counterparts in terms of quality, and highlight the need for further research into the development of systems capable of detecting AI-generated headlines with precision.

Research on frustrated magnets with time reversal symmetry is becoming increasingly important due to the potential for discovering unusual ground states and unique phase transitions. A specific magnet, ${\mathrm{K}}_2Cu_3Cl_4$ ($D = 2$), is studied in both amorphous and polycrystalline forms, which enables a detailed investigation of the spin liquid phase and associated phase transitions. A theoretical model, based on hexagonal close-packed lattice and incorporating nearest neighbor and next nearest neighbor Heisenberg interactions, is used in conjunction with density functional theory and Monte Carlo simulations. These studies reveal a transition from a paramagnetic phase to a long range ordered state and then to a short range ordered spin liquid within which the long range order remains suppressed. Furthermore, the influence of symmetry and the nature of interactions on the stability of spin liquid and long range ordered states is also identified.

Future large-scale radio interferometers, aiming to detect 21\,cm signals across vast distances, may struggle with the high turnover rate of new sources appearing in the field of view due to their broad bandwidth and large sky coverage. Traditional calibration methods have a computational complexity that increases rapidly with the number of antennas, making them impractical for large-scale projects. We introduce a new approach that simplifies the calibration using matrix operations on a regular grid, resulting in a much more scalable complex growth of $O(N\log{N})$. This approach also offers additional benefits, such as the flexibility to adjust antenna pointing without recalibrating, and the ability to easily extend to sub-hertz resolution using Fast Fourier Transforms.

For several decades, the Markowitz model has been the standard for portfolio optimization by minimizing volatility in investments. Recent advancements in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have enabled the generation of realistic synthetic data, previously restricted to pure noise. A deep learning-based method is presented that produces a real-world investment portfolio with the potential to outperform the traditional Markowitz model in terms of both volatility and returns. A new type of GAN called Autoencoding Conditional GAN is developed, using an autoencoder to combine a conditional GAN and an autoencoder into one entity. This entity takes in a portfolio and produces a similar, synthetic portfolio as a result. A major advantage of this method is its ability to create diverse portfolios that can be used to enhance returns. A large dataset of investment portfolios is used to test the new approach, demonstrating its ability to create a variety of successful portfolios. A significant aspect of this research is its ability to create a variety of successful portfolios.

We have derived the analytical expression for the polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ at the next-to-next-to-leading order in QCD, which is necessary for the variable flavor number scheme. This result complements the $A_{gq}^{(2)}(N)$ matrix element and completes the necessary analytical expressions for the polarized transition matrix components in the context of the variable flavor number scheme. Using differential equations and soft over hard matching, we have obtained the analytical expression for $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ in terms of multiple polylogarithms. Furthermore, we have verified our result by comparing it with existing numerical results and the anomalous dimension. Our findings are the first complete analytical results for the transition matrix components at $O(\alpha_s^3)$ in the massless case.

A novel machine learning technique utilizing Bayesian neural networks is employed to accurately classify Fermi-LAT blazar categories. By comparing BNN predictions to spatial and temporal morphology annotations from the Fermi catalogue, it is demonstrated that BNN models are in concordance with expert judgments. Furthermore, BNN models are found to be superior to traditional machine learning models, such as CNNs, which are commonly utilized in blazar studies. It is envisioned that BNN models will become a valuable tool for blazar research and other astrophysical applications.

This study focuses on the challenges and benefits of enabling users with disabilities to create social media content. We evaluated seven key obstacles users with disabilities face when creating content, gathered feedback from users, and identified potential solutions to overcome these challenges. We also explored how to utilize accessible content creation on social media to promote greater accessibility and understanding.

In this paper, we present a hypergraph model where each hypergraph G is represented as a tensor, capturing the relationships between edges and higher-dimensional connections. The tensor is generated by combining individual edge matrices. By analyzing how these combined tensor structures evolve, we gain insights into the properties of these connected networks. Our findings demonstrate that the spectral characteristics of these combined tensors align with the properties of the associated edge hypergraph H and adjacency spectrum hypergraphs. This insight enables us to identify patterns in the spectra of associated tensors, revealing the patterns in the spectra of associated tensors, which in turn correlates with the properties of the associated edges.

A proposal for a space-based spectroscopic and imaging space telescope, INSIST, has been submitted to ISRO with a proposed mirror size of 1.5 meters. Our medium-resolution spectroscopic capabilities will cover the 380-5400 Angstrom wavelength range with high precision, while our imaging capabilities will have a precision of 20 milliarcseconds for nearby objects. With an estimated mass of 1500 kg and a launch payload of 1800 kg, INSIST will offer spectroscopy with a resolution of R=40000 and R=50000 through its 500-5400 Angstrom and 380-500 Angstrom spectrographic setups. A 30 square degree field of view will be shared between our imaging and spectroscopic instruments. With an estimated annual science budget of 450 million INR (~6.5 million USD), our science strategy includes observing various astrophysical objects like active galaxies, black holes, local universe, etc.

To assess the progression of Alzheimer's disease in clinical trials, we develop an approach that integrates data from cognitive assessments and brain imaging scans using a combination of cubic splines and summary measures. Cubic splines allow for precise tracking of cognitive decline over time, while summary measures capture key properties of the progression curve, including rate, acceleration, and inflection points, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of disease evolution. This approach is applied to data from the PREVENT trial, examining treatment effects on cognitive decline in individuals with mild cognitive impairment at various risk of progressing to Alzheimer's disease. We demonstrate that cubic splines offer improved accuracy and flexibility in modeling data compared to traditional methods, such as linear mixed models and nonlinear mixed effects models, and that the new approach captures clinically meaningful information about the progression of cognitive decline in patients with mild cognitive impairment.

In complex systems undergoing a transition, multiple pathways can lead to the same outcome, where the dominant routes to this transition vary based on the system's history and environmental conditions. A new method has been proposed to identify these dominant pathways by employing a global optimization technique for determining the minimum action required for each pathway, with the assumption that the system's configuration energy is proportional to the action. This approach has been demonstrated on a system undergoing a martensitic transition, where the method successfully pinpointed the dominant pathways in the system's configuration.

This study focuses on parabolic equations involving the Gauss curvature on the first Chern metric of a closed, positive $(1,1)$ form, establishing estimates for specific solutions on compact, Hermitian manifolds with torsion. The investigation provides L∞ bounds for these solutions, as well as their derivatives and the associated metrics. Notably, the findings can be applied to the Gauss equation, yielding L∞ bounds for a symmetric, elliptic PDE on a domain of Rn.

Building on the fundamental work of Church, researchers have made significant efforts to develop function classes that extend beyond the limits of first-order logic and set theory, while maintaining a logical foundation for recursive functions. These extended function classes, including Scott's C.N, provide the necessary structure to support recursive function theory and its applications. In an effort to further develop these concepts, researchers have explored a broader logic system, which serves as a basis for the extended function classes. By incorporating advanced type theory concepts, such as dependent types and types for functions with multiple arguments, this logic has the potential to provide significant new insights into these mathematical structures. In this study, a logic system with a lambda-calculus framework has been introduced, which incorporates a type system to regulate the use of types and allows for reasoning about functions through preotypes. The preotypes in this system can describe functions with multiple arguments with shared local variables, while maintaining a first-order character through the Curry-Howard correspondence. The study demonstrates that standard functions, which have been extensively studied in recursive function theory, correspond to preotypes in this system, which in turn enables a preotype to be constructed for any given function class. The research reveals that every function class with a corresponding preotype can be used to define a corresponding function with the same domain and range, which in turn implies that function classes with preotypes can perform tasks that can be computationally executed. The study also explores the relationship between preotypes in this system and other mathematical structures for functions,

This note clarifies a disputed step in the proof of arXiv:2101.00005, specifically showing that for any non-negative, jointly measurable, and adapted process $(x_t, y_t)$, a conditional version of a Stratonovich integral can be transformed into an Ito integral. This involves creating a new local time process $(x_t, y_t)$ that governs the integrand, using a novel method for determining its distribution given existing research on the subject. This approach enables the integral to be conditioned upon an arbitrary, nonelementary $\mathbb{R}^2_{+}$ Borel set. This method has additional applications, including a simplified proof of arXiv:2101.00005.

In an arbitrary topological group I, the standard structure space is created by taking the Borel σ-algebra and applying a specific group operation to its Borel sets, which results in a new σ-algebra. The standard structure space is then considered as a topological group with a continuous action by the original group I. This work involves examining continuous subgroups, one-point extensions, regroupings, quotient maps, free products, and homeomorphism relations on the standard structure space of groups.

Recent breakthroughs have demonstrated the ability of sequence-to-sequence models to effectively translate natural language into formal query structures. However, existing techniques often rely on in-database training and are sensitive to changes in the data distribution they were trained on. This paper presents a novel approach to tackle the challenging task of text-to-SQL query interpretation in an out-of-database setting by leveraging auxiliary tasks and a novel multi-task model. The auxiliary tasks include a cross-domain database pointer and a cross-domain column selection task, which help guide the sequence-to-sequence model towards a solution. The model itself incorporates a novel auxiliary column pointer to guide the user to relevant columns and has shown significant gains in interpretation quality and expressiveness when compared to a baseline sequence-to-sequence model when evaluated on the SparkSQL dataset.

In complex multi-robot environments with competing interests, developing effective navigation strategies is extremely challenging. To address this issue, our research investigates the application of a data-driven model predictive control approach, grounded in convex optimization, to ensure the safety of individual robots in multi-robot systems and reduce costs. This method involves generating an offline data set of trajectories, followed by real-time planning using a constructed polyhedral quadratic program. By leveraging a data set of safe and cost-effective trajectories, this method enables rapid computation of feasible and optimal solutions, even in situations where real-time data is limited. We validate the efficiency and scalability of this method with multi-robot navigation scenarios.

Recent research into Andromeda XXV, a faint dwarf galaxy in the Andromeda galaxy's satellite cluster, has yielded new data. Our research has produced new photometric and spectroscopic data that has allowed us to update the 3D galaxy map and calculate key metrics, such as the galaxy's luminosity and metal content. Our findings show that Andromeda XXV has a relatively low density of dark matter at its core compared to similar galaxies, with a density reaching only half of the world average at a certain radius. Our research has also revealed a relationship between the galaxy's metal content and its shape, with Andromeda XXV's metal content and shape differing from the average of similar galaxies. Our research suggests that the galaxy's shape may be the result of interactions with other nearby galaxies, such as Andromeda XX1, as part of the process of absorption in the Andromeda galaxy's satellite cluster.

In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), grant-free access channels with low complexity allow numerous devices to share a single resource block, with low complexity being a crucial factor for successful massive connectivity. To achieve this, radio frequency front-ends must support massive connectivity without requiring significant changes in hardware. To address this challenge, this paper presents an innovative two-stage genetic algorithm for designing non-orthogonal sequences that meet the requirements of single RF front-ends. Initially, a genetic approach optimizes a matrix with low power profile, reducing interference between users and groups. Next, another genetic algorithm is used to create distinct features for each group, minimizing inter-group and intra-group interference. Simulations show that the proposed method surpasses existing solutions in terms of overall performance, with an improved probability of successful detection by up to 25% and lower false alarm rate by 14%.

Several thermodynamic models for water vapor and suspended water droplets, often referred to as water vapor-binaries and trinaries, can be employed in atmospheric modeling. Traditionally, the most straightforward approach to defining the properties of mixtures is utilized, but this method has been criticized for its inaccuracies due to its failure to adhere to thermodynamic principles. In an effort to address these criticisms, the article undertakes a comprehensive evaluation of the conventional method and identifies an alternative, more accurate approach to describing water vapor and cloud water mixtures in the atmosphere. This revised method is based on the concept of "natural invariants," which relies on the use of specific thermodynamic variables to describe the system. By adopting this approach, the article demonstrates that a standard approximation used in atmospheric modeling is actually incoherent with established thermodynamic theory. In response, the article proposes a revised version of this approximation that is grounded in the "stability criterion," a fundamental principle of thermodynamics. Additionally, the article explores the use of "local consistency" as a further refinement of this revised approximation.

In 2019, two mathematical objects called algebraic loops and algebraic ideals were introduced in matroid theory by Laszlo Mauro, offering a geometric interpretation of the minimum rank of transversal designs. Building on Loerinczi and Toczko's work on external algebras in projective geometry, Mauro's concepts can be generalized using these external algebras, providing novel geometric interpretations of transversal designs and spanning trees. This leads to new geometric applications of external algebras in matroid theory.

In spoken language understanding, word error rates are a commonly used metric. However, when speaker recognition or confusion occurs, this measure can be misleading. Word confusion networks offer a more accurate representation of spoken language understanding by encoding uncertainty. It is suggested that these confusion networks should be used in place of traditional transcripts for training and evaluating dialogue state trackers. We propose a method for generating confusion networks from automatic speech recognition output and demonstrate an implementation of the Kalman filter using Word Confusion Networks. Our approach outperforms the baseline that assumes perfect accuracy by 11% when applied to the multi-domain ASR output of SAMSPA-DA. We also outperformed the baseline that uses Thompson sampling when the distribution of the hidden state is uniform by 8%.

We establish an approach for calculating the number of bundles on curves that have a specific determinant. For curves of type (0), our method yields an exact calculation; in the case of curves of positive genus, our approach leads to an expression with significant asymptotic growth as the genus (g) or degree (d) increases, making exact calculation infeasible. Nonetheless, for specific circumstances - a curve being non-hyperelliptic with iit* equal to 0 or 1, or a curve being hyperelliptic with a particular property - we are able to overcome these limitations and achieve precise results.

A universal access structure, denoted as $\mathcal{U}$, is a specific type of access structure where the intersection of all participant groups, collectively known as $G(\mathcal{U})$, results in a subset of $E(\mathcal{U})$, which represents the minimal subset required to secure the secret shared among the participants, $P(\mathcal{U})$. Furthermore, for every $S \subseteq G(\mathcal{U})$, $S \cap E(\mathcal{U}) \subseteq G(\mathcal{U})$, indicating that no additional participants, beyond those in $S$, are needed to secure the secret, nor can any group of participants, beyond those in $S$, be excluded from the secret sharing. This paper explores the properties of universal access structures, specifically their intricacy, which is defined as the minimum size of the smallest group, $G \subseteq G(\mathcal{U})$, required to secure the secret, $E(\mathcal{U})$.

Quantum systems can be more precise than classical systems in certain tasks, but certain measurements can reveal less information about their properties than others. A study has found that entangled qubits can achieve optimal accuracy in certain measurements by avoiding certain types of coherence, influencing how interactions with the environment impact entanglement. By exploring the effects of interactions with different environments, including thermal and non-thermal cases, the research shows that non-thermal environments can preserve entanglement optimally. Moreover, the research provides a method to assess the optimal entanglement-assisting capacity of quantum channels.

The recent discovery of palm tree modes in the JET tokamak is significant, as these structures appear to contribute to radiation buildup and fuel penetration, ultimately limiting the performance of the plasma. To gain a deeper understanding, we examined all palm tree mode episodes collected within the CTQ experiments, where the plasma was run in hydrogen and helium blend scenarios. Our findings show that these modes develop closest to the X-point in the lower mantle plasma, with growth rates that are highest when the nearest magnetic field field line passes through regions of the plasma that contain plasma currents. Notably, we discovered that these modes tend to weaken the magnetic field stabilization near the X-point, while also increasing its complexity in the outer poloidal direction. Our observations suggest that these modes are likely a result of a specific type of ideal mode of instability, triggered by small disruptions to the magnetic field, such as those that occur during the injection of gas fuel.

Continual Learning (CL) research aims to develop AI models that can adapt to successive tasks in a sequential learning setting. Despite ongoing efforts with sophisticated AI models, these efforts have yet to yield results on real-world datasets using state-of-the-art transformer models, even when fine-tuned on previous tasks. Given the significant resources required for training these models, it's surprising that no basic models have been tested on real-world datasets in the CL context. This work investigates the potential of a simple model, which does not employ CL techniques like experience replay or memory restriction. Our results show that this basic model outperforms the current best approaches on real-world datasets. Furthermore, when using a multi-layered version of the basic model, it's possible to achieve CL results on real-world datasets that are comparable to those achieved through the use of sophisticated CL methods.

Detecting abuse in online social media is crucial, but current models face limitations due to inconsistent annotation and limited data, particularly in non-English languages. The lack of detailed expert annotations in many datasets hinders the development of transparent and trustworthy models. In this study, we present a solution to address these challenges in a widely used dataset through precise feature extraction and implementation of modular, transparent, and energy-efficient models. The proposed approach enhances the model's linguistic analysis by employing a neural network that leverages the structure of abuse language, while incorporating additional modalities, we achieve significant improvements in abuse detection rates, exceeding current benchmarks by 10%. The detailed design and implementation of our model enable efficient replication and adaptation.

We examine the effects of different degree distributions on the dynamics of homogeneous networks of Type-I neurons, where each neuron forms a connection with a certain number of other neurons. We use a mean-field approach to develop and solve a system of differential equations that describes the phase transitions in these networks. We find that networks with a Poisson degree distribution exhibit a transition from subcritical to supercritical behavior as the connection strength increases, whereas networks with an alternative degree distribution exhibit a more complex transition with subcritical, bistable, or supercritical patterns depending on the parameters. We also observe that networks with fixed degree distributions can exhibit robust patterns such as biphasic and bistable behavior in response to different types of stimuli. These findings can be applied to understand the varied responses of different brain regions to external inputs.

The objective of the Abstract Symmetry Program Repair (ASPR) challenge is to find repairs for bugs in programs written in C, a repair process that is inherently challenging due to the language's complexity. Previous approaches to ASPR repairs have leveraged gradient-based methods, but these methods struggle due to the program's complex syntax and semantics, a problem that can be likened to optimizing under ambiguous transformation representations. To overcome this issue, we propose a novel repair method, adversarial mask generation, which translates the source code into an intermediate representation, simplifies the optimization process, and introduces ambiguity into the target transformation representations by masking the source code. Our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results in the ASPR challenge, outperforming all other methods that have participated in the challenge.

This paper presents an information spectrum method for determining the capacity region of a Gaussian interference channel with common information. By employing power splitting and interference channel coding techniques, the capacity region is found to encompass all pairs of achievable rates based on $\mathcal{L}(\alpha,\beta)$. In contrast to previous approaches, the proposed method eliminates the need for difficult calculations of mutual information spectra. It provides a straightforward and direct method for describing the capacity region, while also enabling a simpler characterization of the region.

Using advanced numerical simulations, we study how fluids and gases behave under extreme conditions, and how this behavior relates to their physical properties. We investigate the properties of a system in three dimensions, and how this approach differs from two-dimensional studies. By examining the system's geometry, we can identify key characteristics that influence its behavior, and can use three-dimensional data to pinpoint critical attributes. Additionally, we can use three-dimensional flow simulations to conduct experiments and assess the properties of different materials, and can provide valuable insights for real-world experiments and observations.

The COVID-19 pandemic has been managed using contact tracing, which relies on determining the close contacts of infected individuals to prevent the spread of the disease. Managing such contacts effectively requires accurate detection of infected individuals from available health data, using machine learning models. However, detecting infected individuals from patient records while maintaining data owner confidentiality is a challenge. In this context, our study explores the use of machine learning models to identify COVID-19 infections based on health data, while maintaining the confidentiality of such data. A particular concern is the risk of data breaches, which could compromise both the health data and the identity of the individual. To address such risks, our study employs adversarial training techniques to develop a system that learns to separate infected and non-infected individuals, while also learning to represent individual records as distinct entities. This approach enables the use of machine learning models in detecting infected individuals while maintaining the confidentiality of both the health data and the predicted diagnosis.

In wireless communication systems, Graph Neural Networks have shown potential as sequence prediction tools, capable of leveraging channel state information and adding value to existing wireless technologies. Graph neural networks can be applied to diverse wireless applications such as wireless chaos coding, intelligent wireless resource allocation, and wireless sequence forecasting. However, traditional graph neural networks have limitations in large-scale systems due to their centralized architecture, which can lead to high communication delays and processing burdens. To overcome these challenges, a new study explores decentralized machine learning and fusion methods for reliable sequence prediction in large-scale systems. The researchers' approach involves dividing a large system into smaller subgraphs and using a decentralized graph neural network model to enable robust sequence prediction. By employing a decentralized learning strategy, the model's network nodes can independently update their parameters, which can then be combined through a consensus algorithm to improve overall prediction accuracy and resilience to node failures. The benefits of this approach were validated through simulations on real wireless data, which showed that it can reduce processing and communication overheads, providing reliable sequence predictions even in failed or faulty nodes.

The trend in homicides in Goias, a region of Brazil, has diverged from the rest of the country. While the national homicide rate has experienced a significant increase, within Goias the numbers have fluctuated and differ substantially from the national average. This study aims to gain a deeper understanding of the variations in the frequency and distribution of violent crimes within Goias by using spatial analysis and identifying patterns of similar crime incidence. The analysis reveals distinct patterns in the occurrence of violent crimes, including robberies, assaults, and homicides, as well as property crimes like burglaries and thefts. The findings suggest that factors such as geographical location, urbanization, and socioeconomic conditions play a crucial role in determining the frequency of crimes within the area.

Stochastic Gradient Descent's (SGD) effectiveness in machine learning relies heavily on the quality of random sampling. In this study, SGD's capacity to leverage noisy samples for optimization is explored, along with a mathematical framework to quantify variance. A theoretical model demonstrates that noisy SGD can achieve accelerated convergence, provided the noise level and sample quality meet specific criteria. A mathematical condition is also formulated to gauge sample quality and saddle point evasion. We develop an SGD variant that capitalizes on noisy samples while maintaining robustness against corrupted samples, utilizing the concept of hypercontractivity. Experimental evaluations involving various noise models confirm the convergence properties of noisy and accelerated SGD.

Axions emerge as a logical outcome of the Peccei-Quinn mechanism, the leading explanation for the strong CP problem's resolution. Various theories suggest axions may possess properties that make them suitable for dark matter and/or bosonic components of the WISPs Dark Sector. Depending on the axion's behavior within astrophysical contexts, either algebraic or differential cross-section models apply. Algebraic models predict non-relativistic particle pairs, while differential models involve relativistic particles. We examine the implications of these possibilities on axion searches, arguing that both scenarios are feasible and that constraints on the axion decay constant should be reconsidered. We outline a modified version of the IAXO demonstrator, BabyIAXO, designed to test both algebraic and differential models.

In this study, we investigate non-equilibrium systems that exhibit self-sustaining oscillations. By focusing on the mean square displacement of the system's energy as a key indicator, we define and differentiate two distinct types of self-oscillating systems. One type is characterized by negative values in the mean square displacement, while the other displays positive values. Using the two-dimensional nonlinear complex potential of the Rayleigh system as a basis, we generate the oscillating mechanism for the system. Subsequently, through modification of the complex potential in three dimensions, we develop the corresponding 3D analogue of the Rayleigh oscillator. Additionally, we identify system conditions that give rise to self-oscillations in conservative forces such as the parabolic and harmonic potentials.

Developing robots with skilled hands that can effectively grasp and manipulate objects is a crucial yet difficult task. This research paper presents DexGraspNet, a vast dataset of simulated data, designed specifically for robotic grasping. Unlike other datasets, which are limited to specific items or shapes, DexGraspNet includes a diverse range of objects with complex geometries, resulting in a dataset of 144,000 unique grasps on 2,400 objects with over 13 million simulated observations. Our proposed approach employs a combination of deep neural networks that utilize inverse reinforcement learning, generating grasps with the highest possible success rates. The performance of our approach was evaluated in multiple experiments and demonstrated significant improvements over existing methods. Additionally, we have made DexGraspNet available, allowing researchers to train their algorithms on a diverse and expansive dataset of robotic grasping.

A novel turbo spin-eco sequence for assessing T2-weighted body imaging has been developed with an emphasis on free-breathing acquisitions and motion compensation. The research data reveals that using a low flip angle expansion technique results in minimal signal loss when employing higher flip angles, thereby enhancing image quality. The integration of left-right lateral symmetry correction significantly improves image accuracy by mitigating effects from non-uniform beam hardening and inter-leaf susceptibility artifacts. The addition of phase correction also provides further refinement. The proposed method demonstrates superior image quality when compared to traditional breath-hold turbo spin-echo acquisitions. The research data is based on data from 20 patients undergoing abdominal scanning. The resulting 4D compressed sensing algorithm achieves high resolution with a resolution of 2.5 x 2.5 x 30 mm^3. The research data also indicates that using this technique results in minimal signal loss with an average signal loss of 2.1% at high flip angles. The proposed method has been successfully applied in clinical practice and has shown high utility in various applications such as liver imaging and renal stone detection.

We introduce a new method for compressing neural networks, specifically designed to handle tasks that require a deep understanding of input data, such as natural language processing and sequential analysis. Our approach, known as InDistill, leverages an approach called soft pruning to identify and eliminate less critical information flow within a model. Unlike other model compression techniques, InDistill is unique in that it trains a smaller'student' model to replicate and mimic the information flow within a larger 'teacher' model, rather than simply replicating its output. By doing so, InDistill is able to achieve superior performance when processing data with significant background noise, and is particularly effective when there are large discrepancies in model size. Our results demonstrate that InDistill is able to achieve superior results on a range of challenging natural language processing tasks when compared to other model compression techniques.

Two submersion functions from the set of two-dimensional real numbers to the set of real numbers are defined, and their respective level set foliations are examined. It is demonstrated that these functions topologically resemble each other if and only if their corresponding foliation structures are topologically equivalent.

Ecosystem models that incorporate individual plant movements often overlook the role of local interactions, assuming that plant-to-plant contact is non-significant. This oversight may be premature, as new experiments suggest that local interactions could have a substantial impact on ecosystem behavior. To explore this possibility, we developed a simple model of dry-land vegetation dynamics that takes into account the effects of local plant movements and changed circulation patterns. Our results indicate that local plant interactions can dramatically alter the behavior of the ecosystem, even when the changes in circulation patterns are small. This, in turn, can significantly impact plant spacing and circulation velocity. Our model also exhibits a first-order phase transition that is reminiscent of the classic Henriquez-Ureya mechanism, which is a hallmark of density waves. However, under realistic conditions, the phase transition is obscured by the presence of turbulent circulation patterns, which are stabilized by plant interactions.

A well-known randomized algorithm, CountSketch, offers an efficient way to approximate a vector's heavy hitters by utilizing multiple, randomly configured projection matrices that direct input data into a compact space for closer examination. Notably, the development of more sophisticated algorithms that tailor these matrices to the input data has led to improved heavy hitter approximation. Nevertheless, these adaptive algorithms have a significant limitation: they are vulnerable to manipulation by malicious data that deliberately alters the matrices to undermine the approximation. In this study, the potential of non-adaptive algorithms that randomly configure the matrices, like the standard CountSketch, is explored. Specifically, the algorithm's resistance to being misled by carefully crafted input data that adapt to the matrices is investigated. A rigorous analysis demonstrates that non-adaptive CountSketch offers a form of 'robustness' against these adaptive attacks, with only a minimal decrease in accuracy, with the degradation inversely related to the number of matrices used. This study confirms a long-held suspicion and provides a rigorous mathematical proof, with the result also applicable to more general projection matrices.

A Python-based program, ipie, has been developed for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations, along with its integration with CUDA and cuPy for unified execution across CPU and GPU systems. The flexibility in design of ipie allows for the incorporation of various Python modules through its Python_interpreter interface, while its CUDA_interpreter interface accommodates CUDA modules. Furthermore, ipie features a portable mode with minimal language switches, enhancing its overall adaptability. In addition to analytical derivatives support, ipie also provides interactive visualization tools, including Berlu, Bereso, Berqua, Bereso_rso, Bereso_t, Beresop, Bereso_p, Bereso_t_p, Beresot, Bereso_t_s, Bereso_ts, Bereso_dt, Bereso_dts, Bereso_md, Bereso_mds, Beresom, Bereso_m, Bereso_m2, Beresor, Bereso_r, Bereso_r2, Bereso_rr, Bereso_rrr, Bereso_rrr_t, Bereso_rrs, Bereso_rrs_t, Bereso_rrt, Bereso_rrt_t, Bereso_rrt_s, Bereso_rrts, Bereso_d, Bereso_d2, Bereso_cd, Bereso_cd2, Bereso_cd2_t, Bereso_cd2_s, Bereso_cdts, Bereso_cdts_t, Bereso_cdts_s, Bereso_cd2ts, Bereso_cdts2,

High-frequency trading could greatly benefit from quantum computing due to its extensive use of algorithms. This research examines how quantum phase noise can be applied to facilitate communication between machines, utilizing the two-qubit system. A classic prisoner's dilemma game and a high-frequency trading algorithm are then implemented to demonstrate the advantages of quantum networks. Results show that quantum networks can achieve significant improvements over traditional networks, particularly in scenarios with high frequencies of communication.

A platform owner's revenue maximization is a common optimization goal, 
but in practice, it's complicated by the role of intermediaries and the lack of direct control over them. In this research, we focus on a specific scenario involving these intermediaries and demonstrate that, in a revenue-maximizing equilibrium, their costs are covered by the platform and their profits come from the platform as well. This finding motivational leads us to develop a more efficient method for the platform to maximize revenue.

To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've introduced a planning stage to guide text generation. Current planning methods often provide signal-based prompts that aren't tailored to specific texts. In response, we've developed a prompt generation method called Acquired Entity Prompt (AEP), which automatically creates prompts for given texts by identifying key entities. Our AEP prompt framework combines prompt and text knowledge to train an acquisition model that finds the most relevant entities. These entities are then incorporated into the prompts for a generative model. When applied to the Summarization Open-ended prompt for Long documents dataset, our method led to notable improvements in long document summarization, surpassing the benchmarks set by the original prompt and top-performing pre-trained T-5 model.

This research demonstrates that if a function with specific properties is differentiable almost everywhere in certain circumstances, then the function's derivative is differentiable in those same areas. In particular, the study shows that if a given $n-1$ variable function is differentiable almost everywhere on a particular domain, then the resulting function of $n$ variables, defined with one variable held constant and the rest varying, is differentiable almost everywhere on the same domain. Furthermore, the investigation provides sufficient criteria for differentiability in this scenario, including criteria related to Ljapunov and Lebesgue points.

Previous studies have suggested that people's voices synchronize with each other when they converse, and that this synchronization may be linked to stronger social connections. However, research on vocal synchronization in everyday conversations is limited, and it's unclear whether it's meaningful. To better understand this phenomenon, we've developed a new approach to measure it in real-world conversations without assuming it has a specific meaning. Our approach uses complex mathematical analysis to detect when two people's voices are synchronized, and we've found that this happens more often in people's romantic relationships than in acquaintanceships. This research provides a more precise method for studying vocal synchronization in any context.

A category called lambda-S1 has been introduced and extensively studied in previous research. This paper will delve into the quantum manipulation within the unitary sphere and establish a categorical model based on lambda-S1 for the U1 category. The U1 category consists of U1 spaces and U1 morphisms that meet specific conditions. The U1 morphism definition requires the satisfaction of two laws, alpha and beta, which are derived from the corresponding lambda-S1 category. The U1 category possesses a monoidal structure and its biproduct is denoted as lambda-U1. The alpha law applied to the biproduct has been further analyzed in this paper, demonstrating that it results in the addition of U1 spaces with the absorption of U1 morphisms. The U1 category has a monoid structure, and the beta law applied to the monoid yields a commutative and distributive monoid. The U1 category contains U1 endomorphisms that meet the condition of being epimorphisms, and the beta law applied to these endomorphisms results in the addition of U1 spaces with the distribution of U1 morphisms. The U1 category possesses a monoid homomorphism that meets the condition of being a coequalizer, and the beta law applied to this homomorphism yields a distributive and commutative monoid.
