A new superdeterministic theory known as Invariant-set theory (IST) has been proposed in the context of quantum systems. This approach posits that all possible outcomes of an experiment are predetermined, and thus no Bell value can be measured, as it would imply one of the possible outcomes. We explore a hidden-variable framework for IST by adapting a local hidden-variable theory that restricts its values to specific, bell-value-compatible sets. Surprisingly, we find that this theory cannot surpass the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt bound, and thus IST cannot surpass the CHSH bound, even in a hidden-variable framework. We further demonstrate that IST is not capable of surpassing the All-quantum bound, and thus cannot surpass the CHSH bound, even when considering all possible quantum models.

This study investigates whether Neural Networks can efficiently recognize key phrases from excessive text, while being capable of functioning on standalone units such as smartphones and tablets. It compares two models: the pre-trained BERT and a streamlined, lightweight version of BERT, which is referred to as BERT-Lite. BERT-Lite is based on a previously proposed Mobile BERT framework and was initially designed for speech recognition tasks. Our analysis demonstrates that BERT-Lite requires significantly less memory and computational power compared to the traditional BERT model. Furthermore, our key phrase spotting models, which incorporate a text encoder and a detection module, can efficiently operate on various IoT devices such as smartphones, tablets, and even low-powered smartwatches. It is worth noting that our study focuses on the performance of the text encoder, which is critical in determining the overall quality of the key phrase detection results.

We examine the dimer model on an Aztec diamond-dominated partially filled Aztec diamond lattice, specifically focusing on a two-player strategy to eliminate all monomer-dimer pairs. In the process, we derive an exact dimer density for the Aztec diamond area outside a primary diagonal, ultimately connecting this finding to the Dirac fermion density in a zero-background gauge field, with the gauge field being generated by randomly placing keron (altitude) lines in the Aztec diamond domain. We also calculate the dimer density in a diagonal, linking it to the level of occupation of the fermions, which is equivalent to the number of keron lines crossing the diagonal. We apply our model's insights to the semi-filled Aztec diamond, utilizing it to calculate the semi-filled area and its relationship to the gauge field. We conclude by outlining the Aztec diamond's transition to the Conformal Field Theory (CFT) fixed point, based on the SLE loop network that emerges during the dimer model's tiling process.

In high-dimensional data sets where categories have varying effects, improving upon the group Lasso's outcomes is a key objective. Building upon Chatterjee's 2012 insights that the group Lasso's performance issues stem from incorrect handling of categorical data, a new regularization technique has been developed. This new method produces a more accurate estimation of beta vectors and, as such, relies on a separate penalty for each categorical variable. A novel approach utilizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence, enhanced categorical group Lasso, is introduced to address this challenge. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through simulations and real-world applications, offering a more reliable and accurate alternative to the group Lasso.

In modern embedded systems, virtualization technology has become a common approach to manage complexity and improve performance. The increasing demand for virtualization-based embedded systems has led to the need for hypervisors that can meet the real-time requirements of such systems. In this paper, we present T-Visor, a hypervisor designed to provide hardware virtualization for embedded systems requiring real-time guarantees. Our evaluation of T-Visor on the BeagleBone Black platform shows that it can achieve context switching times of 43.56 microseconds and allow guest OS performance degradation of up to 20% when compared to native execution. Additionally, we demonstrate the security of T-Visor by showcasing an attack on a virtualized system using a malicious guest OS, which fails to breach the system.

We introduce a new method for resolving panoramic joining problems by leveraging a prior on the gravitational field. This approach involves initially assuming the direction of gravity as unknown, and subsequent Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations are conducted to iteratively update the probability distribution of the gravitational direction, as well as the orientation and scale factors of each image sequence, until convergence is reached. Key innovations include the utilization of the inverse Wishart distribution as a prior for the rotation matrix, and the employment of the Wishart distribution for modeling covariance matrix estimates, thereby allowing the integration of prior knowledge on the gravitational field as a pseudomeasurement. This method has been successfully tested on image sets captured from moving platforms, including a K1 plus-wheel test run, an urban drive, a ferry journey, a mountain drive, and a snowy drive.

Our analysis explores chimeras in two distinct settings: coupled populations where individual units receive the same information, and mixed populations where each entity is connected to different sources of varying stimuli. In the uniform variability population, chimeras exhibit robust behavior, characterized by a single, dominant time scale, and a coherent, synchronized macroscopic view, despite the absence of complete internal synchronization among component parts. Contrasting this, coupled populations featuring diverse time scales of variability display the chimeric state only when a specific threshold is met, known as the chimeric threshold. Below this point, systems fall into two distinct groups: either fully synchronized, or separate entities operating independently. In a recent study, it was discovered that large time scale differences between these populations lead to the chimeric state, but only when the chimeric threshold is met. Our research now demonstrates that this conclusion holds true for a system where individual units can transition between different states, a model applicable to a wide range of fields including biology and medicine.

We examine the issue of model-based policy search being too sensitive to variations in its models of the environment, and find that this can be mitigated by incorporating a degree of uncertainty into its state estimation. By introducing a probabilistic dimension to our models, we transform the focus from finding the single most optimal action to finding the most efficient exploration-exploitation equilibrium, taking into account the uncertainty of our knowledge. This shift in perspective allows us to leverage powerful techniques for approximating distributions and our experimental results show that this approach compares favorably with state-of-the-art methods in terms of resilience to errors in our environmental models.

Building on the concept of higher dimensional algebras introduced by Baez and Lumsdaine, this work extends the multi-layer diagrams framework from one-dimensional to higher-dimensional algebras. In this expansion, we derive a higher-dimensional version of the Stasheff diagram, and show how multi-layer diagrams relate to comonads through the cubical model. A key aspect of this work involves demonstrating that the structure of multi-layer diagrams in higher dimensions adheres to a theory, and that these diagrams form a distinct category of algebras for higher-dimensional monads. A preliminary application of this framework is a connection between the diagrams and the homotopy type theory concept of higher slice categories.

We explore the theoretical boundaries of reflected information in random tensor networks, particularly in one-dimensional models, where a single boundary separating the system's parts is present. Using the concept from entanglement blockchains and Monte Carlo simulations, we establish reflected entanglement entropy as an additive conserved quantity in random tensor networks, regardless of the model's specifics or specific tensor definitions, thereby generalizing previous findings. Additionally, we discover that for a class of uncorrelated and uniformly-truncated tensors, reflected entanglement is directly proportional to the Haar random tensor's overlap with a given state, perfectly capturing the system's entanglement when thermalized. Nonetheless, we identify limitations to using reflected entropy as a proxy for the system's entanglement in general random tensor networks, where violations of additivity are possible.

We analyze heritable information in random systems following patterns similar to pattern formation in laminar systems, like the interaction of heat with the rotation of a planet. Random systems can mimic these patterns, but the information they carry is not necessarily transferable from one generation to the next in a consistent manner, unlike their deterministic counterparts. In a simple model, our research demonstrates that introducing a degree of order can lead to the preservation of this information over time. Utilizing a graph-based approach to study this model sheds new light on the distinction between pattern maintenance and information transfer.

The three-dimensional generalization of the H\'{e}non model has been extensively examined due to its complex dynamics and diverse behaviors. This paper focuses on the dynamics of the three-dimensional general H\'{e}non model with two parameters under different conditions. The paper's findings demonstrate that this model can exhibit period and quasi-period solutions, as well as chaotic solutions with positive Lyapunov exponent. Additionally, the paper's visualizations using phase portraits and time series analysis confirmed that the model's behavior is consistent with previously published research.

The Riemannian holonomy is a fundamental concept derived from the general linear connection. This connection is based on the Levi-Civita connection, which is inherently determined by the Riemannian metric. As a result, the Riemannian holonomy is solely a product of the general linear connection's fundamental properties. This paper demonstrates that the Riemannian holonomy possesses only one characteristic component, which is entirely comprised of linear transformations. Consequently, the Riemannian holonomy's structure is equivalent to its maximal 1-dimensional representation. This paper further reveals that the U(1) gauge field holonomy is derived from the Riemannian holonomy and is consequently also unidimensional in representation.

For specified values of $a$ and $b$, or $c$, which include the cases where $a$ and $b$ are both odd or $c$ is a multiple of 3, we establish the limit shapes of the respective two-parameter and three-parameter Ferretti distributions. These limits are specifically defined over the squares of the line segments where $a$ and $b$ or $c$ increase, but in the cases where $a$ and $b$ are both odd or $c$ is a multiple of 3, we find that the rate of increase of the distributions at the boundary of these regions is specifically determined by the Poisson distribution. These findings are further linked to the asymptotic behavior of Young diagrams with bounded height.

Using Larmor clock measurements, we investigated the tunneling duration through a potential barrier influenced by a spin precession field. Our analysis begins with a Larmor clock-based detection method for tunneling, followed by an analysis of tunneling duration in a spin-preceding potential barrier context. We derived an expression for tunneling duration as a function of the Larmor clock's accuracy $\epsilon$, the potential barrier's height $V_0$, and the spin precession field's strength $\Omega$. Notably, tunneling duration is directly proportional to $\epsilon/V_0$ and $\Omega^{-1}$ and is independent of the electrons' mass and kinetic energy. This demonstrates that accurate Larmor clock measurements can reveal spin-fluctuation effects, even in scenarios where fluctuations are minimal or undetectable to Larmor clock measurements.

We examine the leading twist distribution functions for P-wave nonrelativistic mesons, focusing on specific examples: mesons composed of one heavy and one light quark, and those which are purely relativistic (Q balls). For these cases, we generate kernel functions which relate light-cone sum rules (LCSRs) and nonlocal symmetries and calculate the first moment of the LCDs. Moreover, we establish a connection between LCDs and renormalization group behavior. Our calculations also reveal that P-wave LCDs contribute Affine symmetry constraints.

A Bose-Einstein condensate provides an ideal setting for illustrating key principles of quantum mechanics, particularly linearity and superposition. When a system is described as undergoing multiple, distinct transitions is not accurately represented by linear equations. There have been various suggestions for nonlinear operators in quantum mechanics but these have not been widely accepted. We propose a set of nonlinear operators for quantum mechanics that can be applied consistently, effectively, and accurately. We demonstrate this by applying these operators to the study of a Bose-Einstein condensate, which allows us to solve a complex problem of interest to researchers in the field. We compare our solution to other existing solutions that use linear operators to describe this system.

Recent findings at the quantum level have reinforced the importance of specific mathematical structures, including soft theorems and BMS symmetry. A key connection was established between high-energy soft theorems and a specific subset of these symmetries, with the latter's consistency requiring a more detailed understanding of the underlying theory. This paper demonstrates that soft charges are protected from algebraic non-compactness through the specific mathematical structures, and this property further reinforces the consistency of the BMS symmetry. It then explores an enhanced version of the BMS algebra, incorporating additional elements and shows that this enhancement is consistent with the principles of asymptotic symmetry. This upgraded algebra allows for transition to a finite-dimensional algebra with robust properties, and this paper examines the principles governing such transitions. These findings have significant implications for theories beyond general relativity, including systems with vector fields and higher-dimensional analogs of the Higg's mechanism.

This paper addresses the challenge of online ensemble continual learning from multiple classification tasks. The key characteristic of such learning is that it regularly receives new tasks over time, and typically updates the model incrementally in real-time as it performs predictions. The solution proposed in this paper is an efficient and adaptable ensemble method that can be learned incrementally, along with a theoretical explanation for its performance guarantees. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods both in theoretical terms and practical experiments.

In metric-affine geometry, a particular four-form derived from the Cartan calculus, inspired by Cartan's method, possesses Ricci dual metrics with a Ricci flat character, suggesting a fundamental role in this theory. A generalized form has been introduced, analogous to the Cartan four-form, yielding Ricci flat metrics when applied to covariant derivatives. These discoveries lead to the creation of enriched metrics, combining Ricci flat and arbitrary components, and their associated dual newtons. A new class of Ricci flat tori has been established, and it is demonstrated that the geometry of tori is defined by the Ricci flat character alone.

In the context of function fields, a total permutation polynomial is a function that applies a permutation to every element of a specific field. Our study involves analyzing these types of polynomials in three specific field types: those raised to the 3rd power of a prime field, raised to the power of a prime number, and those raised to the power of a product of two prime numbers. Additionally, we identify necessary and sufficient conditions for specific polynomial types, such as permutation polynomials with small degree terms, to be total permutation polynomials in the first of these field types.

A recent study revealed that school-aged attendees in Ibadan, Nigeria, were afflicted with a high prevalence rate of intestinal parasites. In response to the severe health issue, a computational vision-based system was developed to automatically categorize intestinal parasites. This paper details the system's implementation, using images from the NumPy/Parasite dataset, and a Deep Belief Network as the chosen model. The DBN model achieved an accuracy of 86.67% in both its training and testing phases.

This paper addresses a critical issue in non-zero-sum investment and reinsurance games characterized by complex stochastic environments. Specifically, it involves two players, an insurer engaging in reinsurance and a capital holder investing in a fund subject to stochastic fluctuations. Their financial returns are linked by a common stochastic process featuring both continuous and abrupt variations. To tackle this complex problem, the paper proposes two approximation methods, leveraging regression analysis and a nonparametric approach. These methods yield stable and computationally efficient solutions by constraining approximations to target marginals under specific conditions. Numerical experiments reveal notable improvements in solution accuracy relative to existing approaches.

This research presents advancements in the development of Probabilistic Dual Simplex Algorithm (PDIA) and Genetic Filter (GF), initially designed by [Nishimura et al. 2020]. The enhancements to the algorithm address convergence issues in non-smooth problems, while the genetic filter was refined to rectify incorrect state variables. Key features of the updates include the integration of the QP module to facilitate convergence towards the optimal solution and the incorporation of a correct-state detection mechanism in the GF to identify and fix maladjusted filter settings. The efficacy of the enhanced PDIA and GF was demonstrated in real-world flight scenarios using a fixed-wing glider.

Historically, pion-nucleon interactions have played a significant role in the development of nuclear physics. Low-energy pion-nucleon scattering, in particular, has presented a challenge for theoretical models, hindering understanding of this interaction and, by extension, nuclear physics as a whole. We examine the essential requirements for low-energy pion-nucleon scattering and discover that it is inherently impossible to neglect resonance production when interacting at low energies. Furthermore, we find that a nucleon resonant state is essential for maintaining the consistency of pion-nucleon phase shifts. We use this discovery to correct an error in the phase shifts reported by the CBPF pion-nucleon phase shift analysis group and find that an additional sheet of pion-nucleon T-matrix unitarity is necessary to achieve consistency.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment is one of the primary detectors for the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), which is based in Geneva, Switzerland.  For the initial phase of LHC operations, a specialized module was developed for the CMS system.  This module was constructed from a titanium alloy and contained 4 distinct sections, which were later tested in separate experiments to verify the results.  The results showed that the CMS system was able to achieve nearly 100% efficiency in processing data, even at extremely low temperatures.  The total number of signal hits recorded during the pilot module's operational phase was significantly higher than expected, suggesting that the CMS system was able to efficiently convert signals from hits above threshold.  The total number of signal hits recorded during the pilot module's operational phase was significantly higher than expected, suggesting that the CMS system was able to efficiently convert signals from hits above threshold.  The total number of noise hits recorded during the pilot module's operational phase was relatively low, indicating that the CMS system was able to efficiently filter out noise.  The total number of single impact hits recorded during the pilot module's operational phase was relatively low, indicating that the CMS system was able to efficiently filter out single impact hits.  The total number of double impact hits recorded during the pilot module's operational phase was relatively low, indicating that the CMS system was able to efficiently filter out double impact hits. Detailed galaxy morphology information is vital for grasping how central black holes in galaxies relate to their host galaxies. We employed a machine learning technique, combining three different models, to identify the shapes and characteristics of inactive galaxies with black holes in the XMM-LSS and COSMOS regions. We then used this information to analyze how active galaxies with black holes in these regions relate to their host galaxies. We discovered a correlation between the host galaxies' bulge-to-total mass ratios and the active galaxies' sizes. Additionally, we found that active galaxies in this sample generally have fewer stars than inactive galaxies with similar masses. We found this phenomenon to be more pronounced in galaxies with smaller masses and those that are actively growing. We observed no significant relationship between the active galaxies' sizes and the amounts of star formation occurring in these galaxies.

In this study, we utilize the Vlasov method to explore the impact of short-range correlations in heavy nuclei. Two distinct wave functions are employed to model the nuclear ground state, namely the standard Hartree-Fock wave functions and wave functions derived from the Vlasov equation, which account for the dynamics of short-range correlations. By comparing the energy spectra and density distributions of both approaches, we demonstrate that the Vlasov wave functions can effectively capture the characteristics of short-range correlations. Notably, our findings reveal that the Vlasov equation is capable of formulating a new effective interaction, which aligns with the Hartree-Fock results. Furthermore, we observe that the Vlasov wave functions yield a more localized equilibration time for correlations than the Hartree-Fock approach.

In deep complex networks, where complex numbers are used as inputs and outputs,
we investigate co-domain equality. This equality, unique to real and complex number systems, allows us to constrain predicted outputs within a specific range.
Our analysis shows that equalizing co-domains for complex outputs requires a more stringent approach than for real values, involving restrictions on predicted outputs and their conjugates.
We demonstrate that achieving co-domain equality in complex networks is challenging due to the necessity for predicted outputs and their conjugates to lie within defined ranges.
This necessity leads to suboptimal solutions in optimization problems, hindering the performance of complex-valued deep learning models.
To address this issue, we introduce new classes of complex numbers, allowing predicted outputs to be constrained based on either their real and imaginary components or absolute values.
Based on these new classes, we reevaluate the co-domain equality and constrain predicted outputs based on either their real and imaginary components or absolute values.
This reevaluation leads to relaxed optimisation problems, and we show that for specific types of complex number systems, these problems are equivalent to their real-valued counterparts.
To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct experiments on two binary classification datasets, finding that our method outperforms traditional co-domain equality in complex networks.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per transverse area known as the saturation momentum.  In certain large-energy conditions, such as in heavy ion collisions, saturation momentum becomes accessible and influences DGLAP evolution equations.  In such scenarios, saturation momentum can be estimated by comparing saturation momentum to a scale aDGLAP, approximately 1-2 GeV, and also by comparing it to a scale set by a virtual photon virtuality, approximately 1 GeV, in cases of large Bjorken-x values in ep scattering.  In addition to saturation, a distinct phenomenon called geometrical scaling often arises in gluon distribution and it has been extensively studied in various gluon distributions both theoretically and experimentally.  In heavy ion collisions, this phenomenon has been identified in single-particle and multiparticle observables and it has been shown to have a universal behavior known as geometrical scaling that occurs at a certain energy density known as the energy density of the QCD string, approximately 0.5 GeV per Fermi, and it has been found to persist even at a kinematic range far from a GeV per Fermi where traditional gluon distributions do not apply and it has been shown to be a key component in understanding the emergence of a quark-gluon plasma in a theory of a string model.

Recent studies of low-metallicity stars using the low-resolution Hubble Space Telescope Wide Field Camera 3 Spectograph have observed significant dispersion among duplicate measurements, ranging from 0.05 to 0.17 \ensuremath{\mathrm{km\,s}^{-1}}\ with a median of 0.10 \ensuremath{\mathrm{km\,s}^{-1}}. Through an in-depth analysis, we have isolated the source of this dispersion from various factors and found that it is primarily due to variations in the measurement process itself, accounting for 66% of the total. We have also determined that changes in atmospheric conditions contribute 21%, while motion of the telescope contributes approximately 11%. The remaining 2% can be attributed to uncertainty. This discovery has led us to implement a strategy to reduce the overall dispersion to 0.05 \ensuremath{\mathrm{km\,s}^{-1}}\ by improving the thermal stability of the instrument and increasing the use of secondary calibration sources.

A novel machine learning approach has been developed for evaluating the sensitivity of predictions in classification tasks. The algorithm utilizes a Condorcet-efficient rule and demonstrates enhanced performance compared to existing methods. Initial testing on synthetic and real-world data confirms its efficacy. Specifically, the algorithm was applied to a large dataset of adults in the United States, examining the relationship between economic outcomes and financial literacy. Results indicate that individuals with lower financial literacy tend to experience more extreme economic hardship. Further analysis revealed that a financial literacy assessment can accurately distinguish between pro-poor and anti-poor economic policies, suggesting that targeting low-literacy groups may be an effective means of reducing poverty.

A foundational task in quantum machine intelligence involves training quantum models to execute machine learning operations. However, generating training data for this purpose in a quantum format is a highly complex and computationally expensive process. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative approach utilizing a Squared Unitary Dynamics (SQUID) algorithm that produces square square matrices through iterative applications of random unitary transformations. This method enables the creation of large-scale, computationally efficient datasets for quantum machine learning operations. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of SQUID in producing datasets for classification and clustering tasks, ultimately leading to the identification of optimal parameters for superior task performance. Notably, SQUID offers significant advantages over existing methods, allowing it to produce quantum datasets at a much lower computational cost. To facilitate the adoption of SQUID, our team has developed an open-source library that provides a visual implementation of the algorithm.

This research investigates warped product manifolds in relation to almost contact manifolds, specifically examining pointwise submanifolds and their properties. Pointwise submanifolds are found to be geometrically significant, and a new definition for warped product pointwise submanifolds is introduced. Key objectives of this study include understanding the characteristics of these new structures and establishing relationships with other existing mathematical concepts. To achieve these goals, the concepts of pointwise slant submanifolds and warped product pointwise slant submanifolds are also introduced. By defining and differentiating these concepts, this research provides insight into the properties of pointwise slant submanifolds as a subset of pointwise submanifolds. Furthermore, examples and case studies are conducted to illustrate the relationships between pointwise submanifolds, pointwise slant submanifolds, and warped product pointwise submanifolds.

The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to improve the detection and identification of low-energy nuclear recoil events, such as those involving dark matter, by utilizing color center systems in minerals as highly sensitive and isotopic detectors. A preliminary analysis of existing experiments suggests that Paleoccene-based systems could potentially detect individual MeV-scale nuclear recoil events, and further research could lead to the identification of nuclear recoil spectra in various reaction processes, such as radioactive decays and particle collisions at astrophyiscal energies. This could include the measurement of individual reaction events triggered by neutron scattering, such as the production of single gamma rays via coherent elastic scattering and subsequent beta decay. Furthermore, Paleoccene could potentially enable the study of inverse neutrino reactions and inelastic scattering, such as the scattering of neutrinos off electrons and subsequent gamma-ray emission. This could be achieved through Paleoccene's ability to enable the selection of specific initial nuclear states, such as the ground state, and its highly sensitive response to recoil energies, which could potentially allow for the identification of the final state of inelastic scattering, such as the 126Sn state.

Colloidal particles connected through virtual threads, can be used to study and mimic the behavior of bacteria moving towards a favorable nutrient source. By analyzing the movement patterns of these pairs, researchers can observe how different factors, including particle size and the strength of the attractive force, influence their path and speed. The path taken by these "molecules" tends to be unpredictable at short distances but becomes more directed and straight at higher distances or velocities. The reason behind this shift is that these "molecules" can either be controlled by near-body or far-reaching interactions. When near-body interactions dominate, their path is random, but when far-reaching interactions take over, their motion becomes more guided. This property can be used to develop new methods for navigating without reference to the direction of the gradient, the flagellum, or the environment.

In a detailed study, we examined the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with four sites and an applied magnetic field, focusing on regions where the density of states exhibits singularities known as magnetorotons. The emergence of these features corresponds to specific collective excitations that are constrained by both parity and spin. Notably, our findings reveal the existence of diverse magnetorotons that arise from collective excitations involving opposite spins, as well as collective states that arise from interactions between spin and orbital angular momenta. The latter behavior is a distinctive characteristic of systems that are placed in a fractional quantum Hall state. Using a total-rule condition, we identified a set of collective excitations that can generate magnetorons, and found that this rule is complete in systems that exhibit time-reversal symmetry. The application of this total rule also enabled us to systematically count the number of magnetorotons in systems with time-reversal symmetry, and this approach proved to be complete for systems with four sites and applied magnetic fields.

When analyzing a spreading process on a network, determining whether an existing outbreak will persist when interventions are implemented is a crucial question.  This issue can be resolved through the application of a percolation analysis, where the effect of various cluster patterns on persistence is investigated.  A novel geometric approach is presented, enabling the transformation of clustering patterns into simple geometric shapes.  This enables the identification of patterns that prevent large outbreaks by eliminating the largest cluster, while also allowing for gradual intervention strategies that transition between different patterns.  This new geometric framework is demonstrated through its application to two models: the process of Schweitzer and Wooley for percolation analysis and the epidemic process of the SIR type on networks.

A peculiar feature appears in maps of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) at the location of strong point sources, such as quasars, due to the flat plateau resulting from the likelihood function. This anomaly resembles an 'X' shape and affects the reconstruction of lensing patterns, which shares similarities with the point source signature. To rectify this issue, a straightforward correction can be applied to the likelihood function by subtracting the mode of the point source shape. This modification not only removes the point source contamination but also improves the estimation of the primary CMB and lensing maps by utilizing a more informative likelihood function. Additionally, we propose an alternative method using Gaussian processes to mitigate this problem.

In goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, agents learn to achieve a variety of objectives by leveraging past experience.  A crucial element of this process is that the agent can reference its prior experiences when approaching each task.  While prior experiences contain information about rewards and states, the agent only has access to a limited view of this information, which can include observables such as states, actions, or rewards histories.  However, even with these views, the agent may still face ambiguity in experiencing multiple goals with similar state or reward histories.  To address this challenge, we introduce a novel method that uses a supplementary memory with goal descriptions, which allows the agent to disambiguate goals based on relevant information.  We implement this method in three different settings: transfer learning, multi-task learning, and online goal setting.  By analyzing our results across these settings, we find that our method outperforms alternatives in achieving a higher return on investment while achieving better results in fewer steps.

Quantum channel shadow space provides an effective framework for organizing various quantum channel metrics and offers an alternative approach to reconstructing quantum states. In contrast to traditional quantum state tomography, which focuses on reconstructing a single quantum state, shadow procedure tomography involves deriving the shadow epistemic map, which represents the collective behavior of multiple quantum states across an ensemble, and leverages this information to evaluate metrics such as maximum fidelity and Hölder continuity. Our method for shadow procedure tomography involves combining experimental data from multiple quantum channels and using a least-squares approach to derive the most accurate shadow map. Our experimental results demonstrate the feasibility and precision of this new approach.

For a function $h$, defined on the unit disk $\mathcal{D}$ and ranging from $0$ to $1$, this research explores tight bounds for the inequality relating the $h$-isoperimetric function to the $p$-isoperimetric function, for $p \ge 1$, within the unit disk. This investigation has connections to similar problems in shape optimization and geometric inequalities, particularly with regard to the Cheeger factor, which is a geometric inequality on the unit disk and can be seen as a special case of the $h$-isoperimetric function when $h$ equals the Cheeger factor. As a result, this research also yields new inequalities involving the Cheeger inequality and its sharp forms.

This study investigates the most effective flight path for an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to follow in order to minimize total travel time while keeping its position in three-dimensional space within a specified range of a ground-based reference point. The three-dimensional movement of the UAV is modelled using B-splines, allowing its position to be constrained to a specific range of values. The optimization problem is converted into a problem with a non-linear objective function and subject to a quadratic constraint, for which an efficient analytical solution is derived using the method of Lagrange multipliers. The proposed method is found to outperform other techniques, including Newton-Raphson iteration and a genetic algorithm, particularly when dealing with complex and diverse flight paths.

A comprehensive study of Coulomb interactions in bilayer graphite is conducted through the renormalization group approach, considering all possible interlayer and intralayer excitations. Calculations reveal an increase in correlations between layers due to Coulomb interactions, ultimately leading to the destabilization of undistorted bilayer graphite to a pair-density wave state with in-plane ferromagnetism and interlayer coherent electron-hole pairing.

Tb and Sc-based fullerene-based systems have shown potential in stabilizing various structures due to the presence of a Tb atom at the core. By studying the Tb and Sc arrangement, researchers have discovered several configurations that could influence magnetic properties, such as a room-temperature stable Sc2TbN@C80 arrangement. This work employs density functional theory to investigate how this arrangement changes in response to temperature on an h-BN/Ni(111) surface. Results indicate that initially stable Sc2TbN@C80 changes to a less stable configuration, ScTb2N@C80, at high temperatures. This transition is a thermally driven phenomenon that occurs due to the substitution of Tb and Sc positions. Additionally, the study finds that the Sc2TbN@C80 structure exhibits enhanced stability on an h-BN/Ni(111) substrate. By comparing experimental and theoretical data, researchers have validated the reliability of density functional theory. This work's findings also highlight the significance of employing surface science approaches to analyze magnetic fullerene structures.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is an emerging network of interconnected devices that allows them to exchange information with a central server following a specific protocol. Such a network is comprised of a high number of low-power, budget-friendly, and compact devices, including security measures to safeguard confidential data during transmission and storage. These security measures must also consider the devices' limited resources, including processing speed, memory, power consumption, and size restrictions. To address these requirements, we are proposing a novel compact method of encryption that is highly efficient, using lightweight algorithms and utilizing the chaotic behavior of systems with a hyperbolic tangent response. By integrating the device ID into the encryption key, the user can ensure the integrity of data by verifying the device's authenticity and detecting any potential tampering along the communication channel.

In this study, we explore the application of the sequential Bayesian technique as a key component in the process of arranging experiments for the most informative outcome, particularly beneficial in the context of the Ramsey sequence measurement. The Ramsey sequence involves sweeping a magnetic field to determine the spectrum of hyperfine levels in atomic gases, and enhancing the spectral resolution can be achieved by minimizing uncertainty in key parameters, particularly the atom-trapping frequency. Our findings indicate that the Bayesian technique can efficiently achieve this level of minimization more effectively and efficiently than traditional methods, and can be complemented by a method that adapts to changing environmental conditions, and can serve as a supporting tool in the process of arranging experiments for the most informative outcome.

Network centrality metrics evaluate node importance using various geometric and diffusion models, often focusing on local or global perspectives. To address this limitation, a new approach, the Gromov centrality, offers a multi-scale measurement of network importance that complements existing methods. By leveraging triangle inequality excess, this metric naturally adapts to local, global, or intermediate scales, making it suitable for a wide range of network analysis applications. As an intermediate-scale centrality, Gromov centrality can detect hidden patterns and features that other methods may miss, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to both synthetic and real-world networks.

This paper introduces a novel theory of gravitation, referred to as the Azimuthally Symmetric Gravitational (ASG) model, which deviates from Newton's law by a fraction in high-mass objects, as evidenced by the observed behavior of galaxies. The study provides a comprehensive comparison between the predicted gravitational force and the actual measurement, including an examination of the predicted rotation curves. The research reveals that the gravitational potential can be expressed as a series of Legendre polynomials, with the primary term contributing approximately 99% of the potential. The study also derives a mathematical expression for the mass of a sphere with uniform density.

Let $\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ represent the space of square real matrices, and let $\mathbb R_{\sigma(n)}[x]$ be the ring of polynomials with coefficients in $\mathbb R_{\sigma(n)}$. Here, the function $\sigma(n)$ has the property that $\sigma(n)$ increases as $n$ does, and for matrices in $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ that have at least $(\sigma(n)+1)\times m$ linear independence, a matrix operator is defined as a mapping $\mathfrak L: \mathbb R^{m\times n} \to \mathbb R^{m\times n}_{\mathbb R}[x] \subset \mathbb R^{m\times n} \otimes \mathbb R_{\mathbb{\sigma}(n)}[x]$ with specified properties. These matrix operators can be used to construct a bundle of matrix operators $\mathscr F$ over an open set when certain conditions are met, and multiple matrix operators define the same bundle if they are strictly equivalent.

A topological classification of D-branes in certain environments is achieved through abelian T-duality, which has been extensively studied in the past. This research extends topological T-duality to more complex situations, specifically to two-dimensional twisted cylinders. By using unitary representations of lattice, we topologically classify all D-brane configurations in two examples. In one case, the fundamental group of the twined cylinder is $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, while in the other case, it is $\mathbb{Z}/(2r)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(2r)\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. This work also provides a non-abelian version of topological T-duality for both examples. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the 1-cocycles obtained through the abelian and non-abelian classifications are equivalent.

Given a certain structure of a graph, we can develop a compact encoding that represents distances between all pairs of vertices using a specific number of variables, which depends solely on the graph's size and a specific characteristic. This compact encoding allows us to express distance metrics as polynomials using variables and basic algebraic operations. This distance representation has applications in solving optimization problems more efficiently by expressing them as polynomial optimizations in the variables. Specifically, we can prove that if a graph has a particular characteristic with a relatively small value, we can develop a compact encoding for distance metrics using a specific number of variables, which is close to this small value. This compact encoding helps us to prove a conjecture proposed by Dvorak, Kiss, Miller, and Seibert, which has been studied for multiple graph structures. This compact encoding can be further improved to represent distances using a specific number of variables, which is even smaller than the graph's size by a factor. This improved compact encoding helps us to prove a conjecture for graphs with a particular structure, which has been studied for multiple graph structures.

For C1-smooth, strongly monotonic discrete-time systems, we establish the prevalence of globally Attractor Repellors among all positively asymptotically stable equilibrium points. Additionally, we show prevalence of globally Attractor Attractors among all equilibrium points with positive asymptotic stability in the sense of Lienard-type stability. Our findings also apply to periodic points of almost globally Attractor Attractors, with similar results extending to universally Attractor Repellors and universally Attractor Attractors. These concepts and proofs are robust enough to include many nonlinear differential equations, such as polynomial, monotone, and Lienard-type equations.

A new quantum algorithm has been developed, which adapts to the strength of interconnects between nearby system components to enhance simulations of complex many-body systems on near-term quantum devices. By utilizing an iterative variational principle, this method adjusts a variational wave function to optimize a target measurement, such as the ground-state energy, with the option to utilize various measurement functions. To speed up convergence, this algorithm includes two key features: first, it uses an excitation operator-based initial state on the quantum device to gain insight into the system's Hamiltonian, without needing to know the exact eigenstates; second, it adjusts qubit measurements to maximize the algorithm's efficiency based on the Sorkin-Nir-Yacobi map and the Schwinger-Cucchetti map. To test the algorithm's effectiveness, simulations were conducted to fine-tune a parameter estimation on the quantum device and to study its ability to efficiently simulate complex many-body systems, with results indicating that it can significantly outperform existing methods by adapting to the system's characteristics and choosing optimal qubit combinations for parameter estimation.

A novel deep generative encoder (DGE) model has been developed to train deep generative models (DGMs) using large datasets without requiring extensive computational resources. This model utilizes a variational free energy lower bound to determine a maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of the latent representation, thereby driving learning. DGE can leverage pre-trained DGMs, apply transfer learning, and train on multiple datasets simultaneously, all without needing access to the corresponding log-likelihoods. Furthermore, DGE offers several benefits, encompassing enhanced interpretability of the learned representations, the ability to distinguish between multiple modes of a representation, and the capacity to sample data approximations. Experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world image datasets have demonstrated the effectiveness of the DGE in both learning and data generation.

We've developed a theoretical framework that combines stochastic gravitational waves from cosmic inflation and a cosmological constant to explain NANOGrav's observed signal and alleviate the Hubble tension. Our findings suggest that a cosmological constant with a non-zero fluctuation may not be necessary after all. Inflation-generated stochastic gravitational waves can alone account for NANOGrav's data, especially when amplified by a steeper power spectrum. This possibility could be verified by detecting primordial black holes produced by such inflationary events. Additionally, our model predicts that Advanced LIGO-Virgo should observe an even higher background frequency of stochastic gravitational waves.

Comets are ancient icy bodies originating from the solar nebula's outer regions. As they pass close to the sun, their ices sublimate and release gases into the solar system. Recent ALMA observations of a few comets intercepting Earth's orbit reveal molecular emission patterns that can be analyzed to understand their composition, temperature, and structure. One such comet, C/2015 ER61, was surveyed with ALMA in emission lines of CO, CS, C2H2, and H2CS. Our data revealed weak CS emission but no other detected lines, despite ER61 having a moderate CO to methane ratio. ER61's CS emission is thought to originate from a dispersed gas within its coma, possibly produced by non-volatile ice sublimation on its surface. ER61's CS intensity is comparable to that of C/2013 X1, but ER61's CO emission is significantly weaker. ER61's temperature is estimated to be around 10K based on CO and CS line ratios. We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach, focusing on enhancing
speech quality while maintaining high speaking efficiency. Our method
incorporates a novel, efficient representation technique that enables the
separation of speech and prosody characteristics without needing paired data.
Furthermore, we introduce a novel, unsupervised speech synthesis objective,
which enables the system to find an optimal balance between speech quality and
speaking efficiency without the need for labeled data or manual configuration.
Results from experiments on the LJSpeech dataset demonstrate that our method
significantly improves speaking efficiency while preserving speech quality at
near-native levels.

This work investigates the dark energy characteristics of the Tsallis holographic dark energy model, where the gravitational decoherence effect influences the infrared properties of space-time via a time-dependent Planck length. We examine the behavior of two parameters, q and a, which determine the model's properties, under the essence form of a time-dependent equation of state for this type of dark energy. We consider two approaches: the algebraic and exponential forms of the essence model, leading to distinct parameterizations for the equation of state. We analyze the model's thermodynamic consistency, stability, and cosmological constraints on the Tsallis holographic dark energy model under both forms.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in supply chain management. This research introduces a multi-objective optimization algorithm that combines NSGAII, which is typically used for non-linear problems, with a branch-and-bound technique for resolving mixed-integer non-linear programming components. Key aspects of the proposed algorithm include leveraging a fast and efficient local search method, maintaining diversity through NSGAII, and leveraging the strengths of GAMS for identifying initial upper bounds. The algorithm demonstrates its effectiveness with four real-world test cases from diverse domains.

We provide a foundational study on the internal characteristics of connected Lie groupoids when viewed within the framework of synthetic differential geometry. Key findings include demonstrating that connected internal groupoids have integrated completeness and are internally connected. Moreover, our research reveals that the internal form of a connected Lie groupoid exhibits linked internality. These conclusions form the basis of two important theorems which collectively showcase the utility of SDG in reinterpreting fundamental concepts in Lie theory.

The secure sharing of biomedical data plays a vital role in modern research, where numerous recent breakthroughs have been attributed to collaborative data-sharing initiatives.  Nevertheless, the process of data exchange remains a source of concern, particularly with regards to the protection of sensitive information and re-identification of individuals.  Data de-identification techniques have been employed to mitigate these risks, yet the effectiveness of such methods is subject to ongoing debate.  Consequently, researchers frequently hesitate to engage in data exchange due to concerns stemming from past data misuse and the inherent risks involved.  This study aims to address these concerns by examining the role of secure data storage and analysis systems, which provide researchers with the means to manage and perform data analysis using standardized data formats, while upholding data confidentiality through established security protocols.  By leveraging these systems, researchers can concentrate on data analysis and sharing without compromising its security, exemplified by our own research endeavors where the data analysis pipeline was developed using the Biospec gateway and the CADE platform.  This data analysis pipeline enabled an accurate COVID-19 diagnosis from chest X-ray images, while adhering to the security and confidentiality standards of the underlying data storage system.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining how strongly individuals feel about specific aspects of given items/situations. Emotions, being a fundamental part of human experience, can greatly impact opinions towards certain aspects. However, prior research has largely overlooked emotions in aspect-based sentiment analysis, even though some studies have explored their significance to this task. This study aims to investigate how certain implicit emotions influence word meanings and, consequently, the performance of aspect-based sentiment analysis models. We introduce a new method called ELS, which stands for Emotion-enhanced LSTMs for Sentiment analysis, to capture the effect of implicit emotions. Our method involves a two-stage process: first, it leverages a supervised contrastive pre-training approach to capture the implicit emotions and maintain the explicit emotions, and then it uses a multi-task framework with an LSTM structure to integrate the implicit and explicit emotions and improve performance on aspect-based sentiment analysis tasks. Our approach is tested on 7 popular datasets and achieves notable improvements, with up to 4.39% increase in accuracy compared to a baseline model.

Researchers in epidemiology often use a case-control design to examine the influence of risk factors on diseases through intermediaries. For our purposes, we focused on a specific scenario: a study that includes participants with a specific health issue, controls without the issue, and an intermediate factor that's present in both cases and controls, but only actively works in cases. We developed a method to assess how risk factors contribute to health issues via this specific intermediate factor, but only in cases, without considering the factors that might contribute to health issues to controls. We used data from such studies to test the influence of risk factors via this specific intermediate factor and found that our method can work even when there's no common baseline in controls, which is a problem with many other methods available. We also tested the accuracy of our method with simulated data and found that it's quite reliable. We also applied our method to real data from a study on the influence of risk factors via a specific intermediate factor and found that risk factors had a significant influence on health issues through this specific intermediate factor.

This research focuses on secure communication networks involving both legitimate users and an intelligent surface that reverts signals to maximize security. Since the surface's passive nature relies on the characteristics of the incident and reflected signals, an optimization problem is proposed to find the best signal re-routing configurations for each user, taking into account the degrading effects of hardware limitations on both transmission and re-direction efficiency. A complex optimization issue arises due to the non-convex nature of hardware limitations and the binary nature of re-direction variables, which are compounded by an additional non-convex constraint related to the surface's phase shift. A novel re-formulation of this problem is presented, decoupling the optimization variables and transforming the complex issue into a set of convex optimization sub-problems. A new algorithm is then developed to solve these sub-problems, combining the advantages of an iterative re-optimization method with the concave-convex approximation of the interference term to ensure robustness against hardware limitations. A comparison of the proposed method with other recent algorithms is performed through simulation results that demonstrate the efficacy of the new approach in achieving secure sum-rate levels even in the presence of significant hardware limitations.

We've developed an Executive Function framework that enables robots to adapt in unforeseen circumstances through a new relabeling strategy based on hindsight summary percepts. Through a comparative study, we demonstrated our method outperforms existing techniques in facilitating robot adaptation. Additionally, we showcased the potential of our framework in improving robot learning through a series of enhanced perception tasks.

The solar wind's behavior near the Sun remains largely unexplored, largely due to the limitations of past spacecraft. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers analyzed data from the Solar Wind Electrons Alphas and Light Ions Experiment aboard the Parker Solar Probe, which is now in its third orbit of the Sun and only about 27 solar radii from the Sun. To isolate the desired data, scientists employed a technique called "inner heliosphere solar wind" and used it to analyze data from the outer corona and the solar wind. After removing electrons and ions, they found the typical solar wind speed to be around 300 km/s. To calculate the energy flux, they assumed a 1.3 second period and a 300 km/s speed, yielding an energy flux of around 2 x 10^7 watts per square meter. To verify this result, they compared it to data from the outer corona and the solar wind, showing that the energy flux increases as one approaches the Sun.

The concept of noncommutative principal countable bundles is introduced as a direct extension of their commutative counterparts, found by considering two separate types of symmetry in noncommutative spaces. One type leads to K-theoretic invariance, resulting in a subcategory of noncommutative spaces that retain their topological characteristics. Another type enables the construction of noncommutative countable bundles from locally compact Hausdorff groups operating on C*-algebras. Examples are provided of both commutative and noncommutative bundles arising from classical torus actions on AF algebras with a specific type of finite measure. These examples demonstrate that the noncommutative and commutative bundles can be distinct even when their corresponding spaces have similar topological properties.

In this paper, we show that adding a select Cohen ultrafilter over a specific set of ordinals creates a model where the value of $g$ (a measure for minimal uniformity in the Boolean algebra of an infinite set) equals the cardinality of the set of ordinals, $\aleph_\omega$. Furthermore, within this model, every family of open sets with finite intersection properties has a nearly disjoint subset, a property we prove can be equivalent to the value of $g$ through the addition of a suitable ultrafilter.

We have theoretically analyzed an optomechanical system with quantum fluctuations in the medium, using the $q$-deformed boson approach. By considering single-photon and two-photon processes within the linear and nonlinear regimes, we calculated the transmission spectra in both the Schrödinger and Heisenberg pictures. These regimes exhibit quantum windowed coherent states with different features: the Schrödinger picture is distinguished by single-photon induced transparency and two-photon double transparency peaks, whereas the Heisenberg picture features single- and double-transparency peaks with enhanced visibility. Our analysis also shows that the transmission spectra can be manipulated by adjusting parameters such as detuning, central frequency, and transmission efficiency.

We investigate the origin of mirror symmetry breaking in deformed nuclei, focusing on the Adversity R-parity Scissors modes, which exhibit distinct behavior in the Two-Rotors model. Unlike the standard R-parity Scissors modes, Adversity modes display unique characteristics, including differences in their behavior under time reversal and particle number parity operations. Furthermore, in the limit of large deformations, the Adversity R-parity Scissors modes do not combine to form the R-parity Scissors modes, as defined by Isthmus states. This study's findings are compared to existing experimental data and can be validated through future measurements of specific transitions, which could offer valuable insights into the nature of R-parity Scissors modes and mirror symmetry breaking in deformed nuclei.

A novel numerical technique for solving parabolic and hyperbolic partial differential equations has been developed, centered around a network that estimates the average values of solutions within fixed spatial regions. This cell-average method demonstrates the ability to approximate solution paths in both parabolic systems with complete connection loops and more complex networks featuring nonlinear interactions. A key aspect of this approach lies in its ability to handle high degrees of uncertainty without prior knowledge of the underlying parameters, facilitating the simulation of solution paths even in systems lacking convergence to a steady-state condition.

The ALICE detector will take part in the LHC's third run period (2021-2028) to study proton-ucleon and lead-lead collisions at specific energy levels. Beyond this, the LHC will introduce a number of significant updates that will allow the ALICE detector to operate in an even more effective manner. These updates include the installation of the LHCb straw tracking system, a system detecting very weakly interacting particles such as neutrinos in the very forward direction, and very forward direction photon and electron detection facilities. These new additions will give researchers the opportunity to study previously inaccessible areas of heavy ion collisions, making the LHC an even more comprehensive research tool. These new opportunities will be presented in detail.

We investigate the relationship between the Berry phase and entanglement in a specific system defined by the Cauchy slices of a Minkowski spacetime, encompassing two steered Unruh modes, and find that these quantities are equivalent. Our analysis indicates that these quantities are mutually exclusive and that one can detect the Unruh effect by monitoring either the entanglement of these light cones or the Berry phase. This research expands upon previous findings by providing a concrete example of the connection between nonlocal entanglement and geometric phases in spacetime.

We introduce MEE, a large, multilingual dataset of extraction annotations related
to crisis incidents, to facilitate research in crisis extraction and to enhance
systems designed to process crisis-related data in multiple languages. Our
dataset contains over 20K articles covering over 1K distinct incidents in six
languages, annotated by expert researchers to identify relevant information
and to break down the data into manageable components for in-depth analysis.
To complement the dataset, we also introduce the MEE-BERT system, which leverages
pre-trained BERT models to effectively extract crisis-related information from
unseen test data, achieving an F1-score of 66% on annotated validation data. 
Our comprehensive dataset is now available to support research in crisis extraction
and related areas at https://github.com/CL4C/MEE.

Given a global vector bundle and a connection, we establish a formula that relates the pull-back of a Chern form to the push-forward of a Chern form, where the push-forward is defined using Schur's theorem. We demonstrate that this formula is sufficient to prove the positivity of Chern forms, which in turn verifies the Hodge conjecture for manifolds with specific characteristics.

The behavior of the wind in the vicinity of stars influences the surrounding interstellar medium and the properties of nearby supermassive black holes, yet the impact of the wind on the X-ray properties of these black holes is not well understood. This study investigates the effects of the wind from the hot companion star on the X-ray characteristics of the black hole in the hard state of Cyg X-1, specifically examining how it affects the shape of the X-ray spectrum and timing patterns. To this end, we simulated the wind using a two-component model and simulated X-ray observations with the RXTE satellite, finding that the wind produces notable variations in the X-ray spectrum and coronal features, as well as changes in the amplitude of timing patterns, particularly in the amplitude of low-frequency variability. The simulated observations suggest that the wind may be responsible for a 10-20% variation in the amplitude of low-frequency variability in the hard state of Cyg X-1, and may be detectable in other wind-fed low-mass X-ray binaries with the help of future low-background X-ray telescopes.

The Maxwell-Higgs model can be modified by introducing an ether-like gauge field that interacts with physical charges, leading to new gauge fields being absorbed into the Higgs vacuum expectation tensor, which now incorporates cross and curl terms. As a result, the ether-like fields give rise to thermally induced forces between static charges, in addition to creating massive gauge fields that influence particle interactions. It has been found that these gauge fields develop mass when the symmetry is broken both spontaneously and explicitly. Moreover, static charge-anticharge systems exhibit repulsive forces at high temperatures, which differ from the Heisenberg-Euler effect; interestingly, the ether-like fields' presence allows for non-trivial solutions to the Higgs field's vacuum expectation, which are preserved by charge conjugation symmetry.

Researchers have made significant progress in developing separate parsers for universal grammar analysis and semantic parsing.  However, when dealing with sequences of words that form a sentence, these parsers are often trained independently, leading to inconsistencies in their representations. This limitation is addressed in this research, which presents a joint framework for universal syntactic and meaning parsing. By modeling the syntactic and semantic parsers as a single sequence-to-sequence model, and utilizing a structured prediction technique called score-graphical model, the joint framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in grammar induction and semantic parsing.  Moreover, the joint framework enables the identification of meaningful patterns in the data without relying on annotated semantic labels.

Our research investigates the dynamics of merger remnants involving a black hole and a neutron star using magneto-hydrodynamics simulations. We focus on the impact of neutrino cooling in a dense, magnetized disk following the merger. Our simulations, including a three-dimensional model with outflow effects, reveal that a black hole can form shortly after a neutron star-Black Hole merger. We've identified key features of postmerger disks, including a variety of configurations depending on initial conditions and the presence of a disk. Our findings also demonstrate that magnetized disks can produce massive outflows, which can significantly influence the surrounding environment in terms of mass and energy. These outflows can further lead to the ejection of matter into space, potentially resulting in the formation of a jet that can power a gamma-ray burst. We've analyzed the composition of the outflow and found that it primarily consists of electrons and positrons due to the limited role of neutrino-driven processes in the disk. We've also calculated the luminosity of neutrinos and gamma rays in merger remnants and their subsequent decline as the disk collapses into an accretion disk.

Galaxies of a specific mass range in the present-day universe typically exhibit minor mergers with smaller galaxies that result in the development of stellar ridges or streams. However, a lack of early-type galaxies with these features suggests they undergo dynamic processes that remove or obscure evidence of such mergers. One possible explanation is that massive galaxies in the early universe had giant satellites which caused massive stellar losses, leaving behind early-type galaxies with fewer satellites and less dynamic environments. To test this theory, researchers used data from the Hyper Suprime Cam Subaru Strategic Program to identify 87 giant early-type galaxies with tidal features and 43 without them, based on specific mass and redshift criteria. They then calculated the fraction of stellar mass associated with these features in galaxies that exhibit them, finding a higher fraction for more massive galaxies and those at lower redshifts. By assuming this ratio applies uniformly, researchers were able to estimate that approximately 40% of massive galaxies in the present-day universe have undergone tidal processes, which would result in an average annual merger rate of approximately 0.015 per unit redshift. Our findings support the theory that massive galaxies in the present-day universe have undergone tidal processes in the early universe, resulting in a massive, giant-satellite environment.

The Azimuthally Symmetric Gravitation theory is an alternative approach that can explain gravity without mass, originating from a different distribution of space-time. This phenomenon is not tied to mass, but rather arises from the imbalance of space-time's distribution. This theory supports the concept of repulsive gravity and has been experimentally verified in certain situations. Research has demonstrated its ability to accurately predict the rotation curves of galaxies and the speed of stars in various galaxies, including the Milky Way. This is achieved by considering the curvature of space as a whole, rather than focusing on local mass concentrations. Additionally, the theory is able to identify and explain black holes and neutron stars, differentiating between these types of objects based on the magnitude of their space-time curvature. This is in contrast to the traditional concept of a black hole, where an object's mass is the primary determining factor. In the context of the Azimuthally Symmetric Gravitation theory, a black hole is not formed until the space-time curvature surpasses the threshold corresponding to a mass of 2.4 times that of our sun. This is typically only achieved in supernova remnants.

A key challenge in understanding fast radio bursts stems from their brief duration and low flux, which makes it difficult to identify their optical counterparts. Researchers have employed a variety of methods in attempts to detect these bursts optically, yet few successful detections have been achieved to date. This study employed a novel technique involving a UV-optical spectrograph on the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo to explore a distinct sample of 87 FRBs, which were selected based on their narrow bandwidth and proximity to the camera's field of view. The aim was to identify any optical activity linked to these bursts or their persistent emission. The study involved a dual approach, which included a real-time observation of 67 FRBs and an analysis of archival data from 20 sources. These included FRB 20160225A, a repeating burst from FRB 200428, as well as FRB 2011137, a burst with a narrow pulse and a broad profile. The results showed that the optical emission from these bursts did not exhibit any patterns, including flares, pre-burst activity, or persistent emission. The study's findings have provided new constraints on the physical properties of FRBs, which may be associated with magnetars. The research also highlights the performance of the spectrograph as a high-speed camera capable of tracking rapid changes over short periods. The study's constraints on the optical emission from FRBs have provided significant insights into their behavior, which may be associated with the radioactivity of neutron stars.

Over the past ten years, advancements in high-power laser technology have been driven by the increasing demand for advanced coherent imaging, laser communication, and other applications. Our research provides a comprehensive framework for designing, improving, and analyzing complex laser systems. By applying a unified mathematical model to characterize pump and signal interactions, we develop an analytical approach to assess the performance of amplifier and oscillator configurations. This enables us to identify the optimal configuration for achieving high-power output within given spatial and temporal constraints. Our model can be applied to various laser architectures, and we utilize it to investigate enhancements to existing systems, including the LIGO Upgrade and TALISMAN projects.

Recent studies demonstrate the capacity of language models to control text generation 
through embedded signals, either numerical or linguistic, but the potential for visual control remains unexplored. 
This research delves into the capability of language models to derive visual controls from image inputs and integrates this capability 
into text generation controls. We propose a new text generation framework that enables the combination of visual and semantic controls 
independently, allowing for the modulation of both visual and semantic controls simultaneously while producing coherent and semantically sound text. 
We evaluate our approach on different image-text datasets and find that it successfully extracts visual information from images and integrates it 
with embedded semantic controls to produce high-quality text.

Our proposed Delegated Ring Signature (DRS) scheme serves as a substantial contribution in the realm of anonymous ledger technology, enabling Delegated Ring Signatures to be created without the need for a shared secret between the ring members and the verifier. This innovation builds upon traditional ring signatures, allowing a designated entity, known as the issuer, to create unsigned transactions while maintaining anonymity for the actual signers. Our evaluation demonstrates the efficiency of the DRS scheme by comparing it to other ring signature and anonymous transaction protocols, showcasing its ability to reduce both transaction size and required computations when converting private keys to elliptic curves. This DRS protocol can be seamlessly integrated into existing cryptocurrencies, such as Monero, to create an upgraded version with enhanced performance, dubbed Delegated RingCT (DRCT).

Research into an innovative method of beam diagnostics is presented, relying on quick (nanosecond) brightness scans of the accelerated electron beam using an affordable low-cost flat photomultiplier. Theory supporting the diode and photomultiplier approach is outlined, along with experimental results from a self-made apparatus that uses a flat photomultiplier. Findings from these experiments suggest a possible alternative to traditional shot-range scans in probing the electron beam. A proposed architecture for an apparatus that carries out brightness scans is presented, with a basis for determining the beam's transverse size and density already established. A potential design for an affordable and efficient device has been conceived, with plans to integrate it into the Fermi@CNR superconducting cavity.

To manage complex systems effectively, a broad approach is adopted that integrates model-based and data-driven methodologies for optimization and simulation. This paper presents an innovative technique for simultaneous model identification and optimization using machine learning algorithms. It employs a deep neural network model to represent the system's behavior, which is trained using data from multiple sources including observed states and inputs, as well as their estimated counterparts. Model parameters are adjusted through backpropagation to minimize prediction errors, particularly differences between estimated outputs and actual states. This method has been successfully applied to a power generation system, which is subject to performance constraints.

Our research focuses on the two-body decays of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$ state and a $\pi^+\pi^-$ pair, where $n=1,2,3$. We've found that these specific decay processes have relatively large branch ratios. Notably, the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-$ and $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-$ pathways could potentially account for a substantial portion of the $\Upsilon(10753)$'s total branch ratio. We've also determined that $\Upsilon(10753)$ is likely a mixed doublet state under $D$ and $D^\prime$ symmetry. We've analyzed the two-body decays of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ under $D$ and $D^\prime$ symmetry and identified the specific decay mechanisms for a wide range of heavy meson states. In our study, the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-$ and $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-$ pathways were found to be dominated by hadronic loop mechanisms, where the intermediate states include $J/\psi\rho^0$, $\psi(2S)\pi^0$, and $\chi_{c1}\Upsilon

This paper presents a novel optimization technique for training neural networks with quantized weights to reduce computational costs at inference time. We develop a method, AskewSGD, which combines the optimization principles of SGD and the training method used by straight-through gradients. AskewSGD refines its estimates of optimal weights through SGD iterations, starting with an initial estimate based on the quantized coding structure. As iterations progress and the optimization process advances, the bounds of the estimated weights widen, allowing for generalization beyond the initially confined space. We derive the theoretical foundations of AskewSGD by analyzing the distance between the optimal weight and its estimated value in the context of uniform quantization. We demonstrate that AskewSGD converges at a rate of $O(1/t)$, similar to SGD on smooth convex problems, even when weights are quantized to $B$ levels. We also show through experiments that AskewSGD achieves superior performance compared to other quantized training methods, particularly when training models with large batch sizes and multiple epochs.
