We developed an interactive visualization, EXPLORO, to help analyze changes over time in multiple variables, long-term trends, and population distributions. Its unique features include an adjustable panel allowing to zoom in on specific groups while maintaining a overall perspective, comparative analysis of individual and group-time series, and long-term data visualization. EXPLORO's effectiveness was confirmed through user studies and real-world data analysis.

Recent breakthroughs in Graph Neural Networks (GNN) have led to improved performance in natural language tasks, but most GNN applications rely on homogeneous node graphs where connected nodes share similar characteristics. In contrast, electronic health records (EHRs) comprise diverse nodes such as patients, hospitals, and drugs, each linked by varying relationships. To tackle this challenge, we develop a novel approach involving a heterogeneous resemblance graph where nodes differ in their properties and connections. We then adapt node embeddings from an unsupervised perspective, taking into consideration both intra- and inter-domain relationships within EHRs. We further propose a node alignment mechanism to enhance patient similarity detection across multiple hospitals. We evaluate our approach on real-world EHR data, achieving state-of-the-art performance in patient similarity analysis.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform ion size effects and solvent electrostatic properties, we have analyzed the electric double layer (EDL) formed at a softly charged surface in an electrolyte solution. The results show that solvent polarization has a significant impact on the EDL structure, particularly at high electrolyte concentrations, where it modifies ion distribution and potential near the charged surface. The high charge density limit allows us to compare our findings with Poisson-Boltzmann theory, revealing underestimation of ion exclusion width by this model. The study also highlights non-uniform ion size effects on EDL structure and shows that these effects are more pronounced at low surface charge densities.

The importance of accurate software documentation cannot be overstated, as it serves as a common reference point for developers and users alike. While natural language processing technologies have advanced to improve search and retrieval capabilities, they still fall short of enabling non-technical users to create documents from scratch that are easily comprehensible by others. To rectify this, we have developed a method to automatically transform unstructured text into structured code snippets, accompanied by comments providing context and meaning. Leveraging a large dataset, we have successfully applied neural networks to extract structured information from everyday documents, exemplified by transforming a user story into a precise method signature, as exemplified in the accompanying figure.

This research investigates a scheduling technique at both the base station and relay in a multi-cell network where the base station schedules multiple user devices and the relay simultaneously schedules packets from multiple devices, enhancing spectrum efficiency. A technique called collaborative network coding is introduced to improve efficiency by allowing relays to encode multiple packets into a single message, reducing the need for additional transmission time. A new method aims to optimize energy consumption while maintaining quality standards through a technique combining these scheduling methods. To resolve a complex problem, an algorithm is developed to provide a practical solution by simplifying the problem and using a method to find the best solution. When compared to other methods, this technique reduces energy consumption while maintaining quality by up to 21% and 10% respectively, also improving spectrum efficiency and cutting energy consumption by up to 50% and 60% respectively.

A comprehensive theoretical framework, rooted in the electronic properties of materials, has been established to analyze the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states formed by magnetic impurities on a superconducting host. Specifically, the study focuses on Mn atoms and clusters on the Nb(110) surface, utilizing the DFT results from previous research as a reference point. By incorporating the effects of proximity-induced superconductivity and impurity magnetization into the Rashba band structure of Nb(110), the study demonstrates that the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states can be accurately described within a 1D tight-binding model. Furthermore, the theoretical framework enables a first-principles explanation for the observed splitting of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states as a function of magnetic impurity spin orientation and a systematic investigation of the energy dependence of YSR state positions.

A new neural network-based method is presented to eliminate bias in distribution-to-distribution scan matching. The approach leverages a deep neural network to learn and represent matching functions for diverse datasets, as well as generalise to unfamiliar settings. The novelty of this method lies in its ability to optimize a prior distribution of matches, eliminating the requirement for individual training datasets. By directly approximating a conditional distribution of matches given a prior distribution, this method bypasses the need for a direct supervision signal. Furthermore, it can exploit the natural statistical structure of data to improve optimisation, using a prior distribution as an anchor to facilitate convergence. A novel DNN Filter is proposed to correct biases in matching functions, using an optimal mean and variance of matches that deviate from the anchor distribution. The method has been successfully tested on a variety of datasets, demonstrating its ability to correct biases and reduce matching errors on unseen datasets.

Satellite images edge detection hold significant importance in various fields including geography, cartography, and intelligence, where deep learning based methods have shown remarkable advancements in this area, however, they pose a significant challenge due to their large size, multiple dependencies, and complex hyperparameter settings which make them unsuitable for deployment on devices with limited resources such as satellite systems, where images are processed in batches due to their large sizes, thereby rendering them susceptible to non-ideal effects including satellite blurring, atmospheric distortion, and data compression, where conventional methods have shown promising results under normal conditions, this research aims to develop an efficient and robust edge detection algorithm that can effectively handle poor image conditions, by leveraging advancements in embedded systems and computer vision to design a novel approach that utilizes a dedicated processor for edge detection, where the algorithm is broken down into two stages, the first stage relies on a high-performance image sensor with advanced signal processing capabilities to extract edges from satellite images, where the edges are refined using a compact and specialized hardware accelerator, that utilizes advanced algorithms such as LoG and Non-Maximum Selection, where the algorithm as a whole, achieves edge detection performance comparable to deep learning based methods while consuming significantly less power and resources, where the algorithm has been implemented using Verilog-HDL on a Xilinx Kintex-7 FPGA, where the algorithm has been evaluated on publicly available datasets including EDGES, U2, and U2M, where the algorithm has been tested across multiple metrics including edge precision,

X-ray absorption near-edge spectra, specifically the core exciton lines, provide valuable information about the electronic structure and interactions within materials, mainly due to the resonant character of electron groups involved. A new rate model has been developed to accurately simulate core exciton lines, utilizing electron groups generated through a non-linear rate equation solution that effectively models the multi-particle XANES regime. This model's validity is demonstrated by comparing simulated and observed resonance patterns of a Ge K-edge exciton.

We introduce an innovative approach, called Blend GAN, which combines two generators from a GAN model to generate more accurate synthetic data. Its application in machine learning has significant implications, particularly in the development of self-healing radios on aircraft. We successfully tested Blend GAN within the context of a radio that can automatically repair its modulation recognition system using machine learning. The results show that this method enables faster convergence and more robust classification capabilities against adversarial attacks compared to traditional GAN.

Segmentation of multiple sclerosis lesions is an important step for researching the disease's effects and testing new treatments. Due to the scarcity of public datasets containing lesion segmentation annotations, researchers often rely on small datasets like the RRMS2019 challenge dataset. Our study investigates the performance of state-of-the-art models when cross-validated across different hospitals using the RRMS2019 challenge dataset. We discovered that models may significantly struggle when adapted to images from another hospital, and even top-performing models overestimated lesions in test images from another hospital by 20% or more. Our analysis suggests that the main issues are (1) the presence of false positive lesions, (2) the difficulty of accurately identifying lesions in the brain's white matter, and (3) the need to retrain models on images from multiple hospitals. To address this, we developed an approach that combines the strengths of multiple models, allowing them to continuously learn from each other's predictions. Our results show that this approach can effectively transfer knowledge between hospitals, and when applied to the RRMS2019 challenge test dataset, it reduced the average Dice coefficient by half compared to cross-validation results.

Bipolar contrast refers to a distinction between two concepts or elements, typically denoted as Positive and Negative, which are mutually exclusive and defined through an inherent separation. Examples of bipolar contrasts include positive and negative temperatures, good and evil intentions, or left and right spatial coordinates. In most bipolar cases, we can establish a middle ground for neutral or mixed values. 

We are examining the impact of binary and bipolar structures on information, specifically focusing on how information is represented and transmitted. In this context, we are examining the differences between these two systems, which often result in distinct computational and cognitive processes.

We are arguing that many one-hot systems should be viewed as instances of bipolar structures. We are also exploring the idea that the distinction between binary and bipolar systems might be an artifact of limited representation, which we can overcome by considering more general threshold systems. 

We are proposing a general threshold system model that captures both binary and bipolar representations as special cases, which we can achieve by introducing a distinct Neutral element. In this context, we are considering the impact of temperature as a scalar value that influences the probability of Positive, Neutral, and Negative states. 

We are also examining the information-theoretic implications of binary and bipolar representations, which we can achieve by introducing a general threshold system model. In this context, we are considering the impact of temperature as a scalar value that influences the probability of Positive, Neutral, and Negative states.

In the realm of dynamical systems, accurately learning a model that anticipates future states from past observations is a challenging task. While deep learning methods have shown promise in solving this problem, they fall short when it comes to identifying incorrect trajectories resulting from model errors. To address this limitation, a new approach called Model-based Error Learning (MOEL) is introduced, which not only learns a dynamics model but also a set of probabilistic transition functions representing potential errors. By modeling these functions, MOEL accurately predicts incorrect trajectories and improves long-term planning capabilities in model-free settings. MOEL's effectiveness is demonstrated in both discrete-time and continuous-time settings for a variety of systems, including navigation scenarios.

The formation of massive stars occurs primarily in dense molecular cores that have not yet formed stars, although the exact process remains unclear. In this study, we used the IRSCUSS survey to identify and analyze a dense molecular core within the Dragon molecular cloud, which is located approximately 10 degrees away from the Galactic plane. Our observations of CCS, HC3N, and SO lines at millimeter wavelengths indicate the core's rapid expansion, likely triggered by the conversion of kinetic energy into thermal energy. This process is thought to be a precursor to massive star formation, as the core's density increases and its edges collapse under gravity. Our findings are consistent with theoretical predictions, providing the first direct evidence of core expansion in a massive star-forming region. This process is analogous to the expansion of the core in the central region of the Carina Nebula, where massive stars were born. In contrast, cores that eventually form low-mass stars through the disc accretion pathway, as opposed to stellar collapse, typically show a gradual decrease in velocity dispersion over time. Our data suggests that the core in question is in the initial stages of massive star formation, but the presence of low velocity dispersion also suggests that disc accretion may still contribute to star formation in this core.

A novel computational model called PopSyCLE, which utilizes Monte Carlo sampling, has been developed to simulate the creation of primordial black holes under various cosmological scenarios. This model has been utilized to generate a vast number of PBH realizations in multiple cosmological settings, producing predictions for PBH mass functions that align with current astronomical measurements and theoretical constraints. Subsequently, PBH mass function calculations have been carried out using 10 distinct cosmological scenarios, yielding a broad range of possibilities. To determine which of these scenarios are feasible, PBH-induced dark matter calculations have been conducted, revealing that PBH functions formed during inflation and rapid cosmological expansion offer the most promising prospects for PBH dark matter candidates. This includes scenarios such as primordial black holes born from primordial density fluctuations during inflation, born from a cosmological phase transition, born from a field with a slow decay rate, born from a tilted power spectrum, and born from a universe with early matter domination.

Using computer simulations, we investigate a system of virtual wedges constructed from rigid and immovable components, where one piece can rotate freely and the other remains fixed, mimicking the molecular structure of colloidal particles with pinched arms. We analyze a mixture of these wedges in a container with flat walls that allow specific particle arrangements. Our study reveals that as the size of the movable segment decreases, phases with both uniform and periodically modulated orientations emerge, while those with large movable segments only exhibit uniform phases. We also observe that varying the ratio of mixture compositions influences the presence and intensity of modulated phases. Furthermore, adjusting the space between particles can transition the system from one phase to another. We also found that as the size of the movable segment decreases, the transition to modulated phases becomes more complex. We also found that as the size of the movable segment decreases, the transition to modulated phases becomes more complex.

Recent breakthroughs in NLP have been largely attributed to the effectiveness of large language models pre-trained with extensive, general-text datasets. However, incorporating special tokens in these models leads to increased computational and memory burdens. Furthermore, fine-tuning on specific datasets often results in negligible improvements or overcompensation due to excessive adjustments, particularly when dealing with these special tokens. To mitigate these issues, we propose a parameter-efficient adjustment method that adapts large language models by reconfiguring token representations using orthogonal matrices. Notably, the adapted token representations enhance model performance without compromising its overall structure, as evidenced by our analysis. Our experiments on six datasets demonstrate that this method consistently yields consistent gains in accuracy while reducing the impact on original representations.

Our research focuses on the preference ordering problem for set addition tasks, where users view elements added to a core set one item at a-time, allowing context-dependent preferences. We compare our approach, utilizing context-dependent preferences, with a widely adopted non-contextual method and find that context-dependent preferences yield higher user satisfaction, complete tasks faster, and produce better results. A thorough analysis of our algorithm's time and space efficiency reveals its performance, along with a discussion of its potential enhancements, including the application of context-free preferences. We also investigate the impact of our approach using a low-level programming language and demonstrate its effectiveness through user studies, showing its superiority with both small and large item sets. A replication of our study is available at https://github.com/stevej2020/context-set-addition-icml2022  (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.08319).

To investigate thermodynamic properties in detail, researchers used X-ray fluorescence and analyzed the results along with calculations based on the radial distribution functions of polycarbonate and polyvinyltosene. This analysis, combined with previous studies on other glass-forming liquids, reveals a connection between the heat capacity and dynamic properties, specifically the time it takes for structural relaxation processes to complete. This relationship can be described by a formula that factors in temperature and a variable that depends on the way this property changes during the relaxation process. Additionally, researchers discovered that this formula can be used to predict how volume changes in response to temperature variations. This understanding of thermodynamic properties in glass-forming liquids provides new insights into the mechanisms of amorphous state formation and can inform models of glass dynamics.

While it's widely acknowledged that children's second-language acquisition is hindered by negative feedback, there's a notable scarcity of studies on how artificial intelligence models process and learn from rejection in second-language learning. This research investigates the ability of Transformer-based models to handle rejection as negative feedback and assesses their ability to learn from it. We compare two distinct methods of incorporating rejection feedback: labeling rejected sentences as incorrect and calculating similarity between input and output sentences. We found that both methods enhance model performance in generating grammatically correct sentences and that utilitarian approaches to evaluating performance often underestimate the benefits of incorporating rejection feedback. Notably, our study reveals that artificial intelligence models can efficiently process rejection feedback without relying on explicit conditioning.

To enhance neural machine translation (NMT) model focus, we propose a novel approach that utilizes future context to determine what parts of the sentence history to concentrate on. By considering only a subset of past words, our method demonstrates the NMT model's capacity to learn when relevant information is forgotten. In contrast to existing methods, our approach allows the model itself to optimize focus weights without compromising its translation accuracy. Experiments on multiple translation datasets demonstrate significant improvements over current state-of-the-art methods, particularly in challenging Cohesion and Word Order metrics.

The full graph series for symplectic structures was previously determined by Conley and Schlenker, and we extend their work to consider the weights for the connection and curvature graphs in the context of symplectic Poisson structures. Specifically, we utilize a symplectic structure based on the graph, and our calculations reveal a recursive formula for the weights that involves the structure's Laplacian and a transport matrix. Notably, when the transport matrix is identity, the formula simplifies to involve only the Laplacian's eigenvalues and the symplectic structure's characteristics, and this is reminiscent of the graph's characterisation proposed by Conley and Schlenker.

We examine the properties of an $N$-component scalar field's O(N)-symmetric model using large-N approximation, which has a non-trivial interaction term in the IR limit. This model maps onto an O(N)-symmetric non-linear sigma model, with the latter's IR limit featuring a 3D interacting conformal field theory, characterized by a specific mass scale, $\lambda$. When $\lambda$ is finite, the former model is an example of an exactly self-interacting CFT. By using the large-N approximation, we can calculate the CFT's viscosity and information of entropy in the deconfinement phase at any $\lambda$. This leads to a key relationship between the viscosity and information of entropy, which is independent of $\lambda$. This relationship aligns with the principles of holography, which states that the information of entropy is proportional to the viscosity, with proportionality dependent on the specific mass scale $\lambda$.

This paper builds upon a recent pricing framework for geometric Asian options that utilizes a Markov chain.  Our work extends this theory in two significant ways.  Firstly, we show that a similar Markovian structure can be applied to linear Asian options.  Secondly, by utilizing a time-discretized Black-Scholes model as an example Markov process, we derive a closed-form cumbaya polynomial for pricing both geometric and linear Asian options.  This cumbaya polynomial allows for a straightforward extension to multiple-dimensional cases, making it a more comprehensive solution than the standard Black-Scholes formula.

We examine the possibility that gamma-rays emitted by dark matter particles in galaxy clusters may be misinterpreted as coming from resolved point sources, when in fact they are scattered throughout the cluster. By utilizing the PISRES package, we calculate the dispersed gamma-ray flux resulting from annihilation or decay of WIMPs in galaxy clusters, taking into account standard model particles and their effects. Our findings show that a significant increase in predicted gamma-ray flux occurs when considering the impact of conventional annihilation mediators and standard model particles on a fixed cross-section curve. This results in a substantial increase in cross-product phase space compared to the simplified model assumption used previously.

Our analysis delves into the cosmic acceleration epoch when our Universe is filled with a Bose-Einstein condensation of inflaton quanta, long before the formation of the CMB. In this environment, the rapid motion of a heavy inflaton perturber creates virtual quantum fluctuations that can generate a classical inflaton background pattern, often referred to as "cosmic chaos." The study focuses on the gravitational wave signatures produced by these phenomena, revealing the presence of two distinct "cosmological colliders." One is the GIGA-collider formed by the massive inflaton perturber and the inflaton itself, generating a unique gravitational wave signature at the $N^{-5/2}$ scale, where $N$ represents the number of e-folds. In contrast, the second collider is formed by the massive QCD inflaton quanta and the primordial string modes, producing a unique gravitational wave signature at the string scale $\Lambda_{str}$, often buried beneath the $N^{-1/2}$ Planck scale, with $N$ representing the number of e-folds. The study also explores the detection of these unique features by the POG and PIS, revealing that pristine features generated by the cosmic chaos may be observable if the GIGA-collider generated signal is not swamped by the $N^{-5/2}$ Planck scale noise, with $N$ representing the number of e-folds. In contrast, the cosmic string-like features may be observable if

Recent studies in visual neural networks have shown promising results, but the logic behind their accuracy is difficult to grasp. Researchers have created post-hoc methods to make these networks more understandable, yet many existing methods focus solely on what the network sees, ignoring what it learns during training. To bridge this knowledge gap, a new study introduces the filter focus framework, combining the network's visual abilities with its learned characteristics. This method uses a novel, unsupervised approach to analyze the features extracted by the network, without requiring any additional training. By applying the filter focus to images, it is possible to see for the first time how the network's learned knowledge matches up with what a human would see in the same image. This framework is versatile and can be incorporated into various visual analysis models, including those that rely on convolutional neural networks. Extensive tests conducted on standard image datasets reveal that the filter focus is highly effective, accurately capturing the network's visual focus and explaining its decisions with remarkable precision.

The superconducting copper oxides offer the most extensive superconducting performance when they are doped. In order to understand how to induce superconductivity through interaction, it is crucial to analyze how electrons and holes interact in one-dimensional cuprates. We utilized first-principles calculations to find out that in one-dimensional cuprates, electrons and holes have a long-range attractive force due to the mediation of phonons. This force is strong and can be mediated even when there are significant amounts of other particles. We found that the force is primarily due to the interaction between the doped holes and the undoped electrons through the bending of the lattice. This is due to changes in the distance between the electrons and holes caused by the bending of the lattice. This is different from other mechanisms of interaction. We found that this force is strong enough to induce superconductivity and it can be mediated even when there are significant amounts of other particles.

This study presents a groundbreaking approach to uncover the underlying causal structure from data, which generates both informative hypotheses and causal graphs in an iterative framework. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated on real-world medical intensive care unit data, where it detects novel causal connections among 26 variables, leading to the formulation of 366 novel hypotheses with potential therapeutic applications. Notably, these hypotheses were validated by referencing existing medical literature and expert input. Our approach also leverages existing knowledge to validate the reliability and accuracy of the discovered causal structures and associated hypotheses without needing large pre-labeled datasets.

We investigated the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$, which exhibits a unique property where its magnetic order can transform from a non-topological to a topological state as it cools. Using microscopic analysis, we discovered that the transition from a disordered state to an ordered state of magnetization occurs through the formation of skyrmions, which initially grow and stabilize in a specific arrangement called a skyrmion lattice as the material cools. However, this stable arrangement of the skyrmion lattice itself transforms into an ordered state of magnetization as it cools further. We used scanning tunneling microscopy to directly observe the evolution of the material's magnetic properties and the resulting magnetic order. Our findings demonstrate that the material's magnetic order can be explained by the growth and transformation of skyrmions, which can provide new insights into the behavior of magnetic materials.

High-dimensional time-series data are becoming increasingly common in numerous fields such as finance, medicine, and climate study. A specific type of model called the high-dimensional dynamic variable selection model has gained significant attention in the statistical community due to its ability to identify important variables and capture complex relationships in such data. This paper will focus on recent developments in HDVMS models, highlighting the different estimation techniques and highlighting their respective strengths and limitations. Notably, the paper will touch on the generalization performance of these methods and suggest areas of research that require further exploration.

This paper investigates the application of a fixed point method to a nonconvex, nonconcave mixed variational inequality problem. To achieve this, a nonconvex, nonconcave mixed equilibrium problem was first defined. Assuming the existence of equilibria in the equilibrium problem and its dual, a nonconvex, nonconcave variational inequality problem was derived. To solve this problem, which does not satisfy certain conditions necessary for the existence of solutions, a fixed point method was considered using a nonmonotone operator. However, it was found that under the given assumptions, the fixed point method does not lead to meaningful results. Consequently, it was necessary to impose additional conditions to ensure the existence and uniqueness of solutions. To resolve this issue, a simpler approach was considered, starting with the derivation of the Lagrangian function of the equilibrium problem and its dual. To solve the dual problem, which does not pose a problem, the Kikuchi-Tachida method was applied to the Lagrangian function. To solve the primal problem, which does not satisfy certain conditions necessary for the existence of solutions, a smoothing method was considered. To solve the mixed variational inequality problem, which does not pose a problem, the Kikuchi-Tachida method was applied to the Lagrangian function.

In recent years, digital forensics has gained significant interest, with a particular focus on advanced mathematical techniques that enhance concealment and detection processes. This research proposes a novel application of Bayesian Neural Networks in reversible concealment, where the goal is to safeguard valuable data by embedding a secret message. An extended benchmark framework has been developed to thoroughly evaluate concealment and detection methods. Comprehensive experiments were conducted, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of BNN-based concealment in maintaining reversibility and substantially improving detection resistance, compared to traditional approaches.

By utilizing a global magnetohydrodynamics solver and comparing its results to a sophisticated mean-field model, our study reveals that multiple turbulent effects are essential for accurately capturing the dynamics of convection-driven dynamo processes. Excluding these effects or simplifying them can lead to a model that significantly underestimates the amplitude of magnetic oscillations and other convective phenomena. Specifically, we find that incorporating only one particular turbulent effect, believed to be crucial according to traditional dynamo theories, is insufficient to produce magnetic cycles similar to those observed in our reference simulation. This finding highlights the necessity of incorporating the full spectrum of turbulent effects for developing reliable dynamo models, especially when they involve complex processes like convection and rotation.

Our study presents the first ALMA observations of a molecular outflow from NGC4945, a starburst galaxy similar to those seen in galaxies like NGC253 and M82. Using the ALMA observations at 220 GHz, we detected molecular gas in two distinct components: one at 230 km/s and another at 260 km/s. We observed high velocity components redshifted and blueshifted from the galaxy's center, indicating a symmetrical outflow. We analyzed the brightness distribution of the molecular gas and found it to be resolved into 2-3 km in size. We also observed a decrease in intensity of about 10% over time due to an unknown effect, and this data will be further analyzed to determine the outflow's properties. Our analysis of the outflow's morphology and kinematics is consistent with a star-driven model, and we estimate that about 20 solar masses per year are being ejected into the outflow. We also observed a 1.5 parsec thick outflow, and we estimate that about 50% of this material is being ionized, and this process may be responsible for the galaxy's observed X-ray emission. Our study suggests that the outflow from NGC4945 is driven by star formation, and we estimate that about 20 solar masses per year are being ejected into the outflow.

A comprehensive numerical approach has been developed for systems governed by hyperbolic partial differential equations with relaxation terms. This versatile framework enables modeling of momentum and energy transport in cold plasma systems, as well as more complex magnetized plasmas, taking into account collisions and non-conservative processes. The approach employs finite element discretization with an implicit time integration scheme, ensuring conservation of key invariants, including energy and momentum. The method's robustness and accuracy have been demonstrated through a range of one- and two-dimensional numerical examples, including solutions to the Boltzmann equation, the water wave equation, hydrodynamic systems, the Vlasov-Poisson system, and magnetohydrodynamics.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative IMPLICIT METhods were developed for solving standard continuous initial value problems in ordinary differential equations, specifically those with continuous and continuously differentiable coefficients. Introducing variable stepsize SDIMSIMs leads to Method 1, which maintains second-order local truncation errors at every point, even if the required continuity is not met. Furthermore, a specific implementation of Method 1 is provided, along with an analysis of its behavior using Big-O complexity, demonstrating that it converges to the actual solution under certain conditions. Additionally, a numerical example illustrates the effectiveness of this implementation.

This paper investigates the relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T(t) and solutions to a Lyapunov equation in a Banach space setting. Specifically, we establish that if there exists a bounded positive (•) such that the exponential stability of T(t) implies the bounded positive solvability of the Lyapunov equation L(A, Q) = (•)T(t) (•) Q, our findings extend earlier work by P. K. Raassau and A. L. Sakhnovich who considered the case of a compact operator in the paper J. Funct. Anal., 2011, 261, 2873-2898.

MuMuPy is a software for simulating interactions between dimuonium (a bound state of two muons) and ordinary matter, allowing users to model scattering, ionization, and other processes. The program includes materials for calculating interactions with electrons, protons, and photons, as well as routines for simulating interactions with substances and environments in one and three dimensions. MuMuPy includes pre-built options for simulating interactions with hydrogen, alkali metals, and noble gases. Users can input dimuonium properties and the material or environment it is interacting with, and the program will calculate scattering and absorption cross-sections, as well as the rates of various processes. MuMuPy is also available in a web-based version, allowing users to input parameters and view results without needing to install anything.

This study investigates a robust portfolio strategy that involves comparing and combining absolute and relative market performances. Utilizing power utilities, we aim to derive the optimal weights for a portfolio consisting of a benchmark index and two dynamic asset allocation options - one focusing on absolute returns and the other on relative returns with respect to the benchmark. The absolute asset allocation is further enhanced by a convex utility function, which shields the portfolio from extreme market volatility. The relative returns asset allocation provides protection by minimizing portfolio losses in downward market scenarios. The proposed model has been validated by historical data from the S&P 500 index and has shown the ability to improve performance, volatility, and consistency compared to static and dynamic hedging methods, as well as a benchmark portfolio.

Using simulations of galaxy evolution, it's found that dwarf galaxies are formed through the merging of smaller, satellite galaxies. Their internal matter is similar to that of larger galaxies, but due to fewer mergers, their external gas is less heated, and the characteristic features of their rotation curves are less prominent. A study of simulated dwarf galaxy systems, including M33 and M32, reveals lower mass outflow rates compared to larger galaxies. However, the outflow from dwarf galaxies can persist for long periods, and may play a key role in their evolution. A proposed observation aims to detect the external gas of dwarf galaxies, including M33 and M32, by measuring absorption lines in the light from background QSOs. The success of this observation could significantly improve our understanding of the evolution of dwarf galaxies.

We investigate the impact of bosonic bath perturbations on the ground state properties of imbalanced Fermi gases. In the absence of bosonic influences, the superfluid and normal components exhibit distinct, separate momentum spaces. However, in the presence of a repulsive local bosonic potential, an unexpected phenomenon occurs: the normal component's entire momentum space becomes inaccessible, resulting in a reduced superfluid fraction. This unusual effect is ascribed to the increased density of bosonic impurities near the Fermi surface, potentially facilitating Cooper pair formation from widely separated momentum states. We provide a simplified analytical explanation for this phenomenon.

The Thompson's groups $F$, $T$, and $V$ exhibit unique properties, including being non-amenable and having infinite divergence. Introducing its generalized versions, denoted $F_\infty$, $T_\infty$, and $V_\infty$, this paper investigates their divergence properties within the context of maps on the one-dimensional Sierpi\'nski space $X_\infty$. It is found that the maps forming $F_\infty$ have finite divergence and that the groups $F_\infty$, $T_\infty$, and $V_\infty$ are all non-amenable, with $F_\infty$ and $T_\infty$ further characterized by their lack of coboundary actions. Furthermore, this analysis is extended to the braided Thompson groups $BF$, $BT$, and $BV$ defined on the braided Sierpi\'nski space $X_\infty^B$, with similar properties confirmed for their corresponding map collections.

This paper explores the enhancement of the Retrieval Augmented Generation model (RAG) by incorporating the DPR vector-embedding approach for its retrieval step. In doing so, the model's dependence on pre-existing knowledge graphs or tokenized text databases is eliminated. Furthermore, the model's architecture is adapted for question-answering tasks, achieved by replacing the original RAG's aggregation step with a multi-head attention operation, allowing the model to focus on relevant information on an individual-head basis. As an added improvement, the model's attention and log-probability layers are fine-tuned alongside traditional fine-tuning methods, achieving superior performance when evaluated on the SQuAD v1.1-benchmark.

This paper introduces a novel logarithmic weight function and a family of orthogonal polynomials associated with it. These polynomials have several distinctive features, including a complex gauge transformation linking them to Hermite polynomials, and a singular weight function that becomes all but a constant as the variable approaches infinity. Focusing on the asymptotic behavior of these polynomials as the degree approaches infinity, we derive an asymptotic formula for the zeros and develop a system of differential equations whose solution converges to the polynomials as the degree approaches infinity. Additionally, the paper examines the asymptotic behavior of the associated monic polynomials and the associated quadrature rules.

Crowdsourcing research on MTurk has become a standard practice, but finding and managing qualified workers is an ongoing challenge. Researchers face the daunting task of identifying suitable workers among a pool of over a million workers, many of whom lack relevant experience or have demonstrated subpar performance in previous studies. To overcome this issue, we examine two key problems: (a) discovering and recruiting top-performing workers for MTurk tasks and (b) designing instructions and tests to effectively filter unqualified workers. To address these problems, we outline a set of potential solutions, drawing from existing research and our own experiences. Specifically, we provide guidelines for discovering and recruiting top-performing workers, as well as strategies for designing and evaluating candidate filters. Furthermore, we offer recommendations for refining and adapting our approach to a variety of crowdsourcing tasks and populations.

We introduce TS2-Net, a novel approach for text-clipping retrieval using long-range dependencies, leveraging the strengths of both long and short-range attention mechanisms. We develop Token Shift, a layer-to-layer attention mechanism, to capture long-range contextual information. Additionally, we design Token Selection, a hard selection mechanism, to enhance the representation of critical tokens. We implement soft selection in TS2-Net to maintain inter-token dependency, while Token Selection pinpoints and amplifies the contribution of crucial tokens. We evaluate TS2-Net on diverse text-clipping retrieval tasks and find it outperforms other methods across multiple settings.

The top quark's taste, an underlying flavor characteristic beyond its primary flavor identity, can be altered by neutral currents not visible in conventional top quark experiments. We explore the effects of these neutral currents on taste-changing transitions in top quark physics. Our research demonstrates that taste-changing processes involving neutral currents are accessible to observation at the Large Hadron Collider, provided that they have a significant impact. This development offers a novel opportunity for taste-changing experiments to contribute to our understanding of neutral currents.

In the realm of network science, particularly with regards to preferential attachment, numerous stochastic models have been developed to capture the rapid growth and interconnectedness of complex networks. Notable examples include Apollonian networks, which exhibit a high degree of clustering and core-periphery structure, and Erdos-Renyi networks, characterized by random attachments. To combat the issue of core-periphery structure, a new class of hybrid random graphs has been proposed, blending preferential attachment and uniform attachment mechanisms. By incorporating nonpreferential attachment, these hybrid graphs prevent preferential attachment from dominating the network's evolution. We investigate the small-world properties, clustering coefficients, and core-periphery characteristics of these hybrid graphs and demonstrate their ability to exhibit unique small-world, homogeneous, or multi-scale architectures, depending on specific simulation parameters.

This research explores the application of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in identifying multi-labeled disturbances in power grid wireless sensor data. Each wireless sensor transmits real-time data containing data for interference, noise, and actual signals from signals of interest. To extract valuable information from these sensor data, the impact of interference and noise must be minimized. This paper presents a CNN-based method that employs multi-labeling to identify disturbances in sensor data subject to varying levels of noise and interference. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, the research utilizes data from two distinct sources: two sets of noisy signal data from National Instruments and actual wireless disturbance data from the Western Australian grid context. To address the inherent imbalance in the data from National Instruments, the method employs class-weight-based deep learning to balance the data. This paper demonstrates that the proposed method can accurately identify multiple disturbance types in both simulated and real-world data.

This research investigates how both quantum and classical Klein-Gordon particles behave in a cosmic string spacetime that includes a spatial defect and a massless scalar field impedance. We focus on a specific gravitational field model in which the gravitational potential depends on a mass parameter associated with the cosmic string. To grasp the effect of quantum defects, we utilize two localization functions: a spatial function with no dependence on time and a temporal function with no spatial dependence. Our analysis includes a semi-classical study, which shows that the defect parameters generate a correlation between the Klein-Gordon particle's energy and charge. We observe that this correlation depends on parameters such as the gravitational field, cosmic string, and spatial and temporal defects. In addition, our study reveals a relationship between the Klein-Gordon particle's average energy and the quantum mechanical uncertainty principle.

A compact metric measure algebra is considered locally usual if it resembles a measure algebra of continuous functions on a compact metric space in a narrow sense. Our study involves categorizing locally usual measure algebras through their representation as direct limits of measure algebra of continuous functions on compact metric spaces. This research also explores the distinct characteristics of locally usual measure algebras built from functions with specific properties such as continuity, Lipschitz, or uniform continuity.

This white paper introduces the concept of the Recoil Proton Polarization (RPP) as a novel observable in Deep-Inelastic Scattering experiments at a Electron-Ion Collider. It suggests that the polarization state of the recoil proton can be utilized to create a unique observable that complements existing measurements. Several potential methods for achieving RPP are outlined, involving advanced techniques such as specialized target nuclei or specialized detector configurations. RPP has the potential to serve as an independent model-independent probe of Generalized Parton Distribution functions and is particularly effective in measuring high-Born-scale GFs.

The fusion of synthetic intelligence and human augmentation paves the way for novel, advanced forms of augmented intelligence, which will be examined in depth through theoretical analysis and empirical investigation. A foundational model has been developed to understand this convergence and explore its implications for future research, informed by a literature review and empirical data from a panel discussion with 13 experts in the field. Key findings reveal that augmenting synthetic intelligence may lead to a more authentic form of human augmentation, which can alleviate existing limitations of the technology. A central theme arising from expert input is the potential of augmented intelligence to transcend human limitations, which can be achieved through the integration of distinct components, including cognitive enhancements, robotic body extensions, and virtual reality augmentations. By integrating these components, augmented intelligence may provide a more comprehensive and human-centered approach to decision-making, which will be demonstrated in a practical scenario.

Our study delves into the thermal behavior of the Bose-Hubbard model for bosons with strong spin-orbit coupling and inter-component interactions, resulting in superfluids with multiple quasiparticle excitations. These quasiparticles possess distinct internal states due to coupled spin and orbital motions, and their collective internal states exhibit collective internal states that contribute to the superfluid's energy. At low temperatures, this contribution results in an energy gap to higher-energy states, and as temperatures increase, this energy gap diminishes, and a critical point is eventually reached where the energy gap vanishes. Beyond this critical point, the energy contribution from the quasiparticles becomes proportional to temperature, and our calculations demonstrate that this critical temperature scales in proportion to the inter-component interaction strength, and inversely to the spin-orbit coupling strength.

Consider a finite abelian group $G$ of order $n$, represented by an $n$-vertex undirected graph $K(G)$ with vertex edges. Two groups $G$ and $H$ are said to have a similar degeneration if their graphs $K(G)$ and $K(H)$ exhibit the same Minkowski representation. The set of all groups of a given order that degrade in a similar way is denoted by $\mathcal{E}_n$ and its cardinality is determined. For a given order $n$, the characteristics of the family $\mathcal{E}_n$ are investigated. Specifically, for $n=2$, $\mathcal{E}_2$ comprises all the abelian groups of order $2$. For $n=3$, $\mathcal{E}_3$ consists of the direct product groups of cyclic groups of order $3$, the Sylow $3$-groups, and a cyclic group of order $3$. For $n>8$, $\mathcal{E}_n$ has a cardinality of more than $n/4$. For $n=4,5,6,7$, the groups $\mathcal{E}_n$ are described explicitly. The study of graphs $K(G)$ of finite abelian groups $G$ is motivated by a broad investigation of graphs of finite groups, initiated in a previous work.

Recent breakthroughs in AdS/CFT correspondence research, specifically in low-dimensional massive Type IIA string theory, are discussed. We explore how conformal symmetry emerges in low-dimensional solutions when the dilaton is constant, without involving the dilaton as a gauge field. We establish an alternative method for finding solutions by simplifying the massive Type IIA action and represent them in a gauge-invariant form. This method has significant implications, as it connects solutions with a vanishing three-form in the bulk to conformal theories on the worldvolume of D-branes. We use this approach to find solutions that are equivalent to the Gubser-Hofman-Polchinski string theory in low dimensions and demonstrate its relationship with the stress tensor. Furthermore, we show that the AdS/CFT correspondence in low dimensions results in a dual relation between the stress tensor and F-term density on the worldvolume of D-branes, consistent with a previously proposed stress tensor definition.

We introduce a kernel development framework based on fundamental mathematical expressions, and couple it with reinforcement learning to determine the optimal combination of expressions for Gaussian Process (GP) kernels. The chosen expressions enable modeling of positive semi-definite matrices, and our method can automatically discover and adapt novel kernels for given tasks. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through successful prediction in two challenging tasks: GP regression in 2-dimensional space and internet traffic forecasting.

Future high-energy muon colliders face a significant challenge due to in-flight decay
producing beam-induced backgrounds at the detector, which will be a major factor considering
low initial muon energies at these colliders to ensure adequate luminosity. In this scenario,
strategies to mitigate this background noise are crucial for successful muon collider design.
Here, various reduction methods are examined, including segmented beams, beam shaping techniques,
active background cancellation, and separate ring designs. Simulation results indicate that
segmented beams offer the most effective method in reducing background noise by approximately
two orders of magnitude. In separate ring designs, research shows that multiple small
accelerators can successfully mitigate background noise at the cost of increased resource
use, however the segmented beam approach appears to be the more optimal solution.

In numerous machine learning applications, introducing sparsity into representations proves beneficial. Previous methods often employed heuristics grounded in grasping the underlying causes of sparsity, either through examining the features or identifying patterns. A new approach, called Differentiable Sparseness using Regularized Transportation, or Spartan, provides a way to incorporate sparsity into neural network models in a differentiable manner. This method can be used in model training as a regularizer, promoting representation sparsity. A notable aspect of Spartan is that it does not attempt to locate the underlying causes of sparsity or measure its importance. Instead, it applies a global approach, encompassing all hidden representations, thereby making it a more comprehensive method. Spartan's effectiveness is demonstrated through its ability to induce sparsity in representations, improve state-of-the-art results, and provide more interpretable results in complex tasks such as image classification.

In an ordinary matter system, corresponding to a specific quantum state, the number of possible spin orientations is limited to two, imposing restrictions on interacting particles. However, in a study utilizing the Bose-Hubbard model, researchers discovered that an exceptionally large number of spin orientations, specifically 2^99, is possible in a system of 100 bosons interacting weakly. Such a distinction is attributed to the absence of a specific type of obstruction in this particular system. Notably, our results show that this type of obstruction can be present or absent in various spinor Bose-Einstein condensate systems of identical bosons, even for perfect isolation.

Software developers widely acknowledge the negative impact of test defects and test smells on maintenance expenses and overall project success. Building upon previous research that evaluated the severity of test smells from a maintenance cost perspective, this study gathers developers' opinions on the matter. The study involves a large-scale survey with over 530 Java developers and follows up with 67 in-depth interviews across various age groups, experience levels, and company sizes. The results indicate a significant discrepancy between the developers' subjective and objective perspectives on test smells. While the developers agree that test smells have a significant negative impact, they also report that only a few smells are severe and that other factors often outweigh the impact of test smells. The study's findings highlight the limitations of purely quantitative test smell detection and the importance of considering developers' unique perspectives and context. The study's empirical data and results are publicly available for replication.

A novel semi-implicit numerical method is presented for an integro-differential equation representing Brownian Brownian motion with refractive index variations. This method yields a highly efficient computational tool for simulating the physical phenomenon it models, including index variations represented by fractional Brownian motion. As a result, it enables the derivation of closed-form solutions for related integro-differential equations, offering an alternative to the Brownian Brownian motion model with spherical index variations. Furthermore, the proposed method is applied to model fiber process branching and provides accurate approximate solutions in a short amount of time.

We've developed a comprehensive Monte Carlo generator, called KKMCee, for simulating the creation of lepton and quark pairs in high-energy particle collisions. This event generator builds upon the established CTEQ5 parton distribution functions and the KKMC Monte Carlo program, which is responsible for mediating the processes of interest. Our novel KKMCee code extends the original KKMC to model not only charged current interactions but also neutral current interactions as well. To validate its accuracy, we have performed an in-depth comparison with the flexible PEP4Polar POMAPI Monte Carlo code for a range of processes. Our results, presented in tables, demonstrate the remarkable agreement between the two methods for a variety of observables in various cases. This study serves as a precursor to investigating radiative corrections in polarized colliders, an area that will be explored in greater detail in a forthcoming publication.

Cardiovascular disease is a major health concern worldwide, often linked to heart rate variability, which is in turn linked to inter-beat intervals (IBIs). Analyzing IBIs can provide valuable insights into a person's cardiovascular health. However, extracting IBIs from noisy data while minimizing errors is a complex challenge. To tackle this problem, we developed an innovative two-stage neural network model based on the Tiramisu architecture, which combines features from U-Net and ResNet. This network can extract IBIs from noisy data, outperforming existing models with lower average error rates.

A new approach has been developed for computing the Tensor Singular Value Decomposition (t-SVD) in a randomized manner. The algorithm requires a specified number of iterations, beyond which the approximate solution converges to a certain threshold. The method employs a repeated application of the higher-order power method to generate a low-rank subset of data points. The provided theoretical analysis justifies the algorithm's performance and establishes a specific number of iterations needed to achieve an approximate solution within a specified error margin. The method's efficiency relies on the effectiveness of the tensor inner product, which can be computed using the same methods as before. The algorithm was tested on diverse datasets and the results demonstrate its scalability for up to 20 dimensions in a reasonable time frame, with performance that is comparable to existing methods.

Real-world connections are frequently represented by networks that change over time. 
Embedding dynamic graphs, which involves mapping vertices to vector spaces over time, 
enables a range of applications, such as detecting evolving communities and managing networks. 
This paper offers a thorough review of techniques used to represent dynamic graphs and their associated challenges. 
It also identifies research gaps and potential areas for further exploration, including developing more sophisticated metrics for tracking change and embedding graphs that are adaptive to time. 
The distinction between supervisory and unsupervised embedding methods is highlighted, and the paper discusses the difficulties of preserving network structure in low-dimensional spaces.

A novel method is introduced to describe deuterium and hydrogen isotopes with no intrinsic angular momentum, utilizing a $^3$H ground state and four neutrons as building blocks. To describe the $^7$H isotope, we employ the $^3$H+4n combination, with calculations conducted via the $ab initio$ no-core shell model. With the inclusion of $L$-operators, which account for Pauli exclusion, our method yields an accurate ground-state energy of 7.273 MeV above the $^3$H base state, as well as a predicted spin-particle structure of $1^-$. This new method holds potential for significant reductions in computational demands when investigating deuterium and hydrogen isotopes with no intrinsic angular momentum.

The research paper examines Nirenberg type problems on the upper half spheres with increased dimension. A key constraint is that the gradient of the solution must vanish at the origin. This paper's main focus is on Nirenberg type problems with a positive constant term in the equation, and for which the blow up limit as the exponent of a defining variable approaches infinity must be nontrivial. It also explores related problems with similar characteristics, and demonstrates the existence of solutions that become infinite at specific points when a particular parameter approaches zero.

Deep Learning models are now widely used in unsupervised representation learning. A popular method in this area is Autoencoders, but they rely on traditional metrics like PCA and BP-based reconstruction, which can limit the potential for rich representations. To overcome this, a deep learning framework for unsupervised representation learning has been developed, using a novel objective based on Sinkhorn divergences and Laplacian regularizers. This approach outperforms other methods in most cases, providing more insights into deep representation learning.

In England, a comprehensive contact tracing system was established in early 2020 to monitor the COVID-19 outbreak, which involved both manual and digital components. The success of this initiative relied on collaboration between local public health teams, manual tracing teams, and the UK's Test and Trace program, all of which played crucial roles. Although the Test and Trace program has been the subject of previous evaluations, the contribution of local tracing partners and manual tracing teams has not been extensively assessed. This study aims to fill this gap by evaluating the performance of the COVID-19 contact tracing system in England, with a particular focus on local tracing partners and manual tracing teams. Our analysis reveals that local tracing partners and manual tracing teams collectively made a significant impact, with the former responsible for tracing approximately 40% of manual cases and the latter successful in tracing about 60% of cases assigned to them. Our findings also highlight areas for improvement, with manual tracing teams struggling to keep up with rising case loads and both local tracing partners and manual tracing teams encountering difficulties with increased cases during the winter of 2020-2021.

Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is essential for understanding their characteristics and evolutionary patterns. Utilizing the Gaia DR2 survey, we conducted a precise examination of the Melotte 72 star cluster (also known as NGC 104) using 15 to 20 bright cluster members. By implementing a specific approach to eliminate binary influences and a specific method for determining age and metallicity, we derived key cluster properties. The resulting findings indicate a cluster age of 6.95 billion years, metallicity of -0.16 dex (solar), and a red giant branch bump location corresponding to a 1.15 solar mass turn-off star. Additionally, our Gaia DR2 data reveal that Melotte 72 is rotating at 0.693 degrees per 20 years and is moving at 9.8 km/s relative to the LMC.

We are examining random fields $F_d(x;W)$ with $W$ representing samples from a Gaussian process on $\mathbb{R}^d$ for large $d$ where $W(x)$ has a law given by $W(x)\sim W(\cdot,x)\sim\mathbb{P}\otimes\mathbb{P}$. We are interested in understanding the behavior of persistence diagrams in the case when the number of dimensions $d$ is much larger than the number of points $n$. We show that the homology groups $H_{k}(F_{d}(T_{n}(\mathbb{R}^{d}));\mathbb{R})$ for the complex topological structure are non-zero only for $k\leq d-n$ and provide a formula for their dimensions.

We propose an eye-in-hand camera adjustment method that relies on a single image, 
allowing for an end-to-end trained solution that can be applied to various robots.
By utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, our system generates an image signature 
unique to each robot configuration and calculates the hand-to-camera pose based on 
that signature in real-time.
We evaluate our method's performance using a public dataset and compare it to existing 
techniques, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency; it is also presented as a 
feasible option for other robotic applications.
A video illustrating our method's capabilities can be viewed at https://youtu.be/ 
G6Q5Q5Q5Q.

In a typical reinforcement learning setting, the objective is often to develop an agent that achieves the highest possible rewards while operating within predetermined safety boundaries. However, in a corresponding reverse scenario, known as reverse reinforcement learning (RRL), the focus lies in generating a safe reward function that aligns with an existing demonstration of a safe trajectory. This reward function will then guide an agent in optimizing its policy to reproduce the target trajectory as closely as possible. Although RRL has been gaining attention, existing methods often rely on assumptions like smoothness or semi-marginal consistency, or require complex network architectures. This study presents a novel method, named Constrained Trajectory Neural Alignments (CoTraNA), that leverages a constrained neural network to replicate the target trajectory's semi-marginal rewards. By formulating CoTraNA as an optimization problem with a differentiable constraint, it becomes possible to employ iterative optimization techniques to find an appropriate solution while avoiding smoothness assumptions. Furthermore, CoTraNA enables the efficient exploration of a large space in both sample and parameter spaces. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments in both 2D movement and 3D robotic manipulation tasks.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission, a core objective of which is to create a detailed 3D map of the galaxy's various celestial bodies, was launched on the 19th of December, 2013. With two on-board telescopes, one of 60.3 cm and the other of 1.4 m diameter, the mission aims to create the most accurate 3D chart of the galaxy by observing a quarter of the Milky Way's stars in the visible and infrared regions of the spectrum. With a prime focus on determining the positions and movements of stars, the mission also aims to gather additional data on stellar properties, including the study of binary and pulsar systems, the study of moving stars and the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the study of the

To find the treewidth of a graph, we employ the algorithmic technique of incrementally defining a tree decomposition and calculating its treewidth. This method is based on vertex separators, which we have developed an O(nα(n)) space-efficient version of, utilizing O(α(n)) levels of memory hierarchy, for graphs with n vertices, utilizing an alternating direction strategy. This strategy is applicable to the parameterized versions of various treewidth parameters, including branch width, cut width, and genus.

Network analysis is a widely used method for examining organizational structures within various fields. In the last decade, researchers have introduced new types of networks, such as those based on inferred or measured data, which differ from traditional groupings of nodes. To accommodate these variations, we propose a general framework for directed network analysis, which allows for flexible definitions of edge weights, node groupings, and centroid calculations. By applying this framework to these specialized network types, we identify specific requirements necessary for meaningful analysis. Specifically, we find that inferred networks demand uniform treatment, measured networks call for a comparison with theoretical models, and heterogeneous networks need to be analyzed using the mean and median values of their connecting weights.

Machine learning's "black box" nature poses a significant challenge, primarily due to its lack of transparency regarding the prediction accuracy and reliability. To counter this issue, we are developing an approach that evaluates a neural network's certainty directly from its trained parameters. This framework, which we call "a posteriori error estimation," enables us to accurately forecast our neural network's mistakes before using them for predictions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by applying it to two datasets: handwritten digits and images of galaxy spectra. This method's success in increasing our confidence in machine learning models will likely pave the way for reliable use of neural networks in high-stakes scientific domains, such as astronomy.

Epidemiologic research relies heavily on air quality models, which are used to estimate and predict the impact of atmospheric pollutants on human health. In this review, we examine the performance and limitations of spatial and temporal air quality models, particularly in the context of big data and big science. In addition, we provide a concise overview of two emerging methods: geostatistics and machine learning. We also outline potential future directions for air quality modeling, including the integration of these two approaches.

To identify Majorana fermions through tunneling spectroscopy, distinguishing the zero-energy peak from other peaks caused by various modes is crucial. Given that non-Majorana peaks typically have energy-dependent components, our idea is to use ohmic dissipation in tunneling spectroscopy to reveal these characteristics. Ohmic dissipation, introduced by resistive electrodes, affects low-energy excitations, making it easier to distinguish different peaks. To demonstrate this, our approach was numerically tested and successfully identified the critical non-locality of this method, which enables distinguishing Majorana peaks from others even with ohmic dissipation in place.

Linear bandits, where actions result in noisy observations of unobserved variables, are studied with a focus on groups of actions that share similar properties. It is shown that when these groups are known and actions drawn based on past experiences are organized accordingly, a specific rate of exploration that is close to the lowest possible is achieved. This rate is determined by statistical constants and the minimum distance between groups. When the action groups are unknown, a similar rate is obtained by using algorithms that cluster similar actions together, despite potential deviations from the optimal performance due to additional errors arising from misclassification. This research provides the first theoretical justification for the use of clustering methods in linear bandits. Additionally, its findings have been verified through experiments.

Graphene with gaps can exhibit two unique properties: the orbital Hall effect and the valley Hall effect. Although they share some similarities, we found that the orbital Hall effect stems from a different cause - the combined effect of the sublattice symmetry and the Chern-Simons magnetic field on the Bloch electrons in monolayer graphene. This phenomenon is visible in the Bloch band structure where phase differences between adjacent bands create openings that can host orbital Hall states. Our theory also explains how these orbital Hall states emerge from the gapped states by applying a symmetry-breaking mechanism and demonstrate their existence in the gapped graphene under a uniform magnetic field. Our research also shows that the Berry phase plays a crucial role in determining the orbital Hall states and their properties can be manipulated by adjusting an external drive at low temperatures.

Big tech companies utilize Graph Neural Networks to make informed decisions about advertising placement, but current solutions are limited by their reliance on perfect training data, which is often compromised due to contamination during data collection. This issue is particularly pronounced in online platforms where ad serving data is collected. We address this challenge by developing Reinforcement Learning models that can identify and mitigate data imperfections in the graph, focusing on the case where node attributes are represented by a single vector called embeddings. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of these models in the context of the Maximal-Local-Average loss, which is a key metric in the field. The source code for our proposals can be found at the address https://bit.ly/rlggnn.

The process of matching objects between photometric catalogues is critical in modern astronomy, underpinning various applications like multi-epoch photometry and cross-matchings between catalogues. The photometric follow-up of Gaia, in particular, necessitates matching objects between the Gaia catalogue and other photometric catalogues to ensure accurate photometric observations. The photometry of the target objects typically precedes the matching process, making the task an iterative process. To improve the matching process, we propose utilizing the astrometry information in the target objects, as provided by Gaia, to gauge the match quality. To this end, we developed two indices: the first is based on the distribution of spatial matches and the second on the distribution of parallaxes and right ascensions matches. The performance of these indices was tested on mock catalogues and real data, showcasing the efficiency of the proposed method. The proposed approach significantly enhances the quality of the astrometric parameters by correcting the systematics, to the order of a few hundred microarcseconds. The proposed indices can also be applied to other matching processes between catalogues, to assess the match quality and to refine the astrometry of the target objects.

In this paper, we study the characteristics of the largest minimal vertex sets within infinite hypergraphs, and find that for a finite hypergraph H, the maximum size of minimal vertex sets in its infinite linear extensions is log2(n) with n being the number of vertices. However, this result does not apply to infinite hypergraphs, as proven by establishing an infinite hypergraph where the largest minimal vertex sets in its extensions have an upper limit of 1. Moreover, an infinite hypergraph was found such that the largest minimal vertex sets in its extensions have a size of 1 and n has a size of n. Furthermore, an infinite hypergraph was found such that the largest minimal vertex sets in its extensions have a size of 2 and n has a size of n. Additionally, an infinite hypergraph was constructed where the largest minimal vertex sets in its extensions have a size of k and n has a size of n, for 3 ≤ k < n.

In domains like medicine and materials science, ontologies with thousands of concepts have numerous practical uses, often necessitating tools to facilitate browsing and association discovery. While visualizations like circular maps and Sankey diagrams are beneficial for understanding hierarchical connections, they are not well-suited for handling non-hierarchical relationships. To address this limitation, we have developed OntoPlot, a novel visualization that showcases domain concepts as an interconnected network on an irregularly shaped map. Users can customize the layout to group related concepts together, making it easier to identify patterns and relationships, and OntoPlot includes features like focus detection, focus-based highlighting, and an interactive search function to enhance user experience. To effectively visualize large ontologies, OntoPlot employs techniques like hierarchical rendering, pre-computed image caching, and asynchronous loading to strike a balance between interactivity and visual clarity.

We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to leverage unlabeled data in semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. By applying CycleGAN to produce inter-domain alignments, we enable the ASR model to utilize both labeled and unlabeled data from asynchronous acoustic features. This enables the model to learn a unified representation that unifies the domains. To facilitate this learning, we propose an inter-domain loss function that maximizes alignment between the two domains. Our experimental results on the WSJ and Voxforge datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this method, with notable improvements in convergence speed and out-of-domain ASR performance.

This paper outlines our entry for the NYU Data Sprint, where we demonstrated
a real-time robotic solution that leverages deep learning. Our approach
enabled a robot to independently navigate and anticipate future events.
Through image analysis, our method identified targets of interest and
generated a path using a deep predictive model. The proposed solution
combined soft actor-critic methods for navigation and focus detection,
yielding a seamless and autonomous robotic system.

To analyze the Soret effect in flexible molecules, we employ the lattice dynamics model and calculate the thermal gradient along the diffusion process for n-alkanes. Our findings reveal that the Soret effect in low-molecular weight compounds is primarily driven by the internal degree of freedom in these flexible molecules. As molecular weight increases, however, this influence diminishes while the effect of the entire molecular translation/rotation degree of freedom comes into prominence. Consequently, the Soret effect in high-molecular weight compounds is largely determined by the movement of the entire molecules rather than the impact of internal freedom.

The application of deep learning in Automated Essay Assessment has gained increasing attention, with established methods employing multi-encoder architectures to compare student writing with a reference model. Despite their efficiency, these models can be resource-intensive and may not always utilize the information available in the essays they analyze. In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of transformer-based language models in Automated Essay Assessment, using a variety of architectures that often are underutilized in this domain. By leveraging a large dataset of essays and an advanced evaluation framework, we assess the ability of these models to identify authentic and inauthentic writing, while also examining the computational resources required. Our findings demonstrate that certain configurations of these models outperform the multi-encoder architecture, both in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

Highly accurate pedestrian detection models often come at a significant cost and can be resource-intensive to train or purchase, making them inaccessible for edge devices such as self-driving cars on demand.
